text: Okay, chat, this is the part where I actually yelled at my screen. AKIRA is gassed. You can see it before the hit even lands: slower hands, tiny backward steps, that “please let me reset neutral” body language. But RYU-X is having absolutely none of it. Red spins in like a blender with a grudge, throws the leg around, and boom, AKIRA gets shoved all the way toward the right side. Not a lucky tag either. RYU-X aimed him there. The whole late-match pressure plan was basically: keep hitting blue until the arena runs out. AKIRA’s still alive, sure, but in that moment he looks trapped inside RYU-X’s rhythm.

I’m a RYU-X fan, so it hurt to watch. He had been tough all fight, but by then he looked like a sword with chips all along the blade. AKIRA came at him again, calm and mean, and there was no room left for RYU-X to make it pretty. The blue blur punched straight through his defense with a driving thrust, and RYU-X got sent skidding to the right like the arena itself was rejecting him. He tried to keep his feet under him, but the red aura was flickering, the guard was late, and AKIRA was the one moving forward. That moment felt like the match narrowing into a corner.

Jun's noodle-vat exchange happens in the ruined kitchen, where a cauldron of celebratory long-life noodles has tipped but not spilled, rocking on its rounded base like a sleepy giant. The crane-masked bruiser returns through the laundry chute covered in linens and charges again, determined to tackle Jun through the pantry wall. Jun snatches a pair of oversized noodle paddles and adopts a matador's stance that looks absurd until the bruiser commits to the rush. At the last instant Jun hooks one paddle under a draped tablecloth and pulls it sideways. The bruiser barrels through the cloth, blinded for a second, while Jun uses the second paddle to shove the rocking cauldron's rim with all his weight. The vat rolls a quarter turn, and a thick wave of noodles sloshes up without leaving the pot. The blinded bruiser steps onto the exposed slick rim, rides it like a treadmill, and windmills his arms. Jun does not strike him; he twirls one dangling noodle around the man's wrist and guides his momentum into a seated plop inside an empty flour bin.

Aoi’s duel with Yuma reaches the shattered water basin where sacred ladles float among chunks of ice. Yuma flicks sparks from his claws into the water, turning the basin into a crackling trap. Aoi leaps to the rim, but the wet stone is slick and Yuma is already there with a rising slash. She tosses one of the bamboo ladles upward instead of blocking. The slash cuts the ladle clean in half, spilling water across Yuma’s own forearm. Aoi exhales a white plume and freezes the splash instantly, locking his wrist inside a jagged cuff of ice connected to the broken ladle handle. Yuma laughs and discharges lightning to melt it, but Aoi has anticipated that. She kicks the floating copper donation coin at the basin’s bottom. The coin jumps with the current and brands his ankle with a bright snap. His leg spasms, his claw strike veers high, and Aoi shoulder-checks him into the basin, sending electrified water up like blue fireworks.

Technical view: AKIRA was losing the spacing battle before the strike even connected. RYU-X had compressed the lane, forcing blue to defend while retreating, which is poison late in a match when reactions are slower. The red fighter chose a descending angle at exactly the moment AKIRA appeared braced for something lower or straight-on. Contact landed cleanly on the upper guard line, and the force carried AKIRA to the right perimeter. What matters is not just the hit, but the direction. RYU-X converted offense into screen position, and AKIRA, already worn thin, had to absorb damage while surrendering ground. That is how a closing sequence starts to look inevitable.

The tea kiosk duel between Toma and the masked spearman lasted less than a minute but felt ceremonial. The spearman thrust between hanging teacups, each strike so precise it made porcelain chime without breaking. Toma retreated until his heel touched the hot-water urn. He grabbed the kettle, and the spearman immediately cut at his wrist. Toma did not throw the boiling water. He flipped the kettle lid open and let steam burst upward between them. The masked fighter jabbed through the cloud, guessing center mass. Toma had already crouched, holding two wooden chopsticks like tiny batons. He tapped one against the spear shaft to make it vibrate, then placed the other under the spearman's glove at the wrist joint and levered up. The spear point dipped into a tray of sweet buns. Toma kicked the tray, and the sticky buns plastered themselves across the mask's eye slits.

From a booth-commentator angle: this happens while the fight is still young, but the tone is already ugly for AKIRA. RYU-X, glowing red and pressing forward, commits to a straight-in body jab that lands flush before blue can reset his guard. The impact doesn’t just stop AKIRA; it carries him sideways, sliding and staggering toward the right boundary like he’s being shoved along rails. RYU-X is clearly the one setting the rhythm here, stepping into the space AKIRA keeps giving up. AKIRA isn’t finished, but he’s already being softened, forced backward instead of answering.

From an animator's perspective, the weight on that impact was ridiculous. RYU-X's shoulder drops, the hips commit, and then the contact hits AKIRA like a slab of concrete swung by a giant. Late in the battle, with AKIRA visibly worn thin, the timing makes it feel almost cruel. The blue fighter's body compresses first, then gets shoved across the arena toward the rightmost side, feet scraping out a glowing trail. RYU-X remains the visual anchor, red aura stable, torso pitched forward, already claiming the next step. It is not just a hard punch. It is a staging choice that tells you who owns the scene now.

Bro, that part was nasty. AKIRA was already cooking him by then, like the final stretch had turned into a pressure drill and RYU-X got picked as the practice dummy. Red was still trying to look dangerous, but you could tell he was tired. His guard came up late, his feet were stuck, and AKIRA just walked him down. Then blue snaps in with this dead-straight punch, bang, right through the lane. RYU-X eats it and gets pushed toward the right side, and suddenly it looks like the whole screen is squeezing him. No escape angle, no stylish counter, just AKIRA taking space and making him pay for every step back. That was not a random hit. That was the leader of the fight cashing in.

I’m a RYU-X supporter, so it hurt to watch. Early on, before he had even had a chance to build one of those scary comebacks, AKIRA got inside and rammed a knee into him. RYU-X did not crumble, and I will defend that forever, but he was forced backward toward the right edge in a way that made the crowd gasp. That was AKIRA’s moment, no question. Blue was pushing the tempo and red was already starting to look worn around the edges. I kept waiting for RYU-X to plant and fire back, but in that instant he was stuck absorbing, retreating, and trying not to get crowded out.

During the chaos beneath the bell, Senji grabs the torn red festival banner from its pole and uses it like a matador’s cape against Yuma’s lightning sprint. Yuma appears as a blue blur, claws out, expecting Senji to dodge left. Senji instead throws the banner straight upward. The cloth blooms between them, swallowing Yuma’s view for a heartbeat, and Senji dives under the blur to snare both of Yuma’s ankles with the banner’s weighted tassels. Yuma’s momentum carries him forward while his feet are suddenly tied together, flipping him into an ugly somersault. He refuses to crash; electricity crawls down the silk and burns it apart before his back touches the floor. The released charge pops every lantern nearby, leaving only afterimages. Senji, who has already rolled away, emerges from the darkness with the banner pole held like a spear and jabs Yuma squarely in the ribs, driving him into a stack of drum cases that explode open with hollow booms.

Sable tries to humiliate Aki by snaring her with marionette wires stolen from the festival puppet stage. The wires shimmer almost invisibly, looping around Aki's wrists, elbows, and one knee, and for a moment Sable makes her stumble like a wooden doll. Aki's response is not to pull free. She follows the forced motion completely, exaggerating each tug until the rhythm becomes a dance step. Sable, annoyed, jerks the wires in a sharper pattern, and Aki uses that exact pull to spin close enough to the puppet rack. With her bound hand she grabs a smiling wooden dragon head and lets Sable's next tug drag it between the wires. The dragon's horns catch the strands and cross them over one another. Aki then drops her weight, turning the tangled puppet head into a pulley. The tension reverses through the knot and yanks Sable's own fingers apart. Aki slips one wrist loose, steps behind Sable, and finishes with a tidy standing shoulder lock made from the remaining wires, bowing to the abandoned puppet audience afterward.

Tiny moment, huge vibe shift. We were still nowhere near the late-fight madness, but Akira had already flipped the pressure switch on. Ryu-X was backing up, red guard looking heavy, and then Akira attacked low. One quick cut at the legs, clean connection, and Ryu-X was pushed off balance toward the right edge. The important part was how little hesitation Akira showed afterward. He did not just score and stop. He kept moving forward. Ryu-X looked tired earlier than he should have, like the fight was already taxing him mentally and physically.

Tetsu's one-time lock on the smoke juggler began with humiliation. The juggler bounced three black bombs from elbow to knee to forehead, grinning as Tetsu swung too slowly at each blur. Then Tetsu stopped aiming at the bombs and grabbed the juggler's shadow on the floor with his iron chain, pinning it under a station bench bolted into the tile. The move was theatrical nonsense until the juggler tried to leap and found his timing broken by the chain snagging his heel. One bomb popped smoke, one popped sparks, and the third rolled straight into Tetsu's palm. He did not throw it back. He tucked it into the crook of the juggler's bent elbow, folded the arm with a brutal overhook, and held the wrist against the man's own shoulder. The smoke burst inside the joint lock, leaving only coughing, frantic tapping, and Tetsu's calm warning to stop juggling indoors.

The animation sold the impact beautifully. AKIRA’s blue silhouette compressed, then sprang upward into that knee, and RYU-X’s red outline jolted backward with a sharp smear toward the right edge. Since this was still in the opening stretch, the moment mattered because it established direction: AKIRA was not testing anymore, he was taking territory. RYU-X’s shoulders sagged just a fraction after the contact, enough to make him look less fresh than he should have been this soon. The hit was clean, the shove was clear, and the staging left no doubt that blue was advancing while red was being ground down.

Tetsu’s counter to Nami’s water-serpent technique was less a martial art than stubborn engineering. Nami sent a coiling column of rainwater whipping across the observatory floor, and it gathered broken lens shards into its body until it glittered like a dragon made of knives. Tetsu did not try to punch the serpent. He planted both stone-coated hands into the floor and ripped up a circular maintenance hatch. Holding it like a shield, he angled the iron disk so the watery serpent struck and split around it. The glass shards scraped sparks across the metal, but Tetsu kept advancing one grinding step at a time. When Nami flicked her wrist to make the serpent loop behind him, he suddenly dropped flat, shoved the hatch upright with his feet, and let the serpent wrap around it instead. Then he clapped his palms together. His stone aura hardened over the hatch, trapping the water and shards inside a crude cement plug that rolled harmlessly away.

As a neutral viewer, I stopped being neutral there. Not because I picked a favorite, but because the match itself picked a direction. AKIRA was coming forward, RYU-X was giving ground, and the closing stretch had turned into a chase. Blue struck with a direct thrust, compact and vicious, and RYU-X’s red frame jolted backward. He slid toward the right edge with his guard collapsing around the impact point. The fatigue was obvious; he had the will to stand, but not the sharpness to answer. AKIRA’s attack did more than score. It announced that RYU-X was being worn down in real time.

Boro made the mistake of cornering Lio at the fireworks barge, where crates of festival rockets were stacked in careless pyramids. Boro swung a heavy anchor chain, smashing one crate after another, but Lio kept hopping backward with his hands raised, counting the rhythm rather than fighting. On the fifth swing, Lio stepped in close instead of away and jammed a bamboo launch tube through a link of the chain. Boro pulled, snarling, and the tube wedged sideways against the anchor hook. Lio struck a fallen sparkler against the deck and touched it to the fuse still tied to the tube. The rocket ignited with a dragon scream, not exploding but dragging the chain violently upward. Boro's arms were yanked above his head, and Lio used the sudden opening to plant one clean spinning heel kick into the giant's exposed belt buckle, folding him into the empty rocket crate.

Akira moved like weather cutting close to the ground. The match was still young, but Ryu-X's red silhouette had already started to lose its sharpness, forced backward by a blue fighter who kept asking questions faster than he could answer. Then Akira sank and lashed at the legs. Ryu-X's footing vanished for a heartbeat, and that heartbeat was enough to drag him toward the right edge. It was not a grand explosion, not the climax, just a cruel little turn of the tide early on. Akira owned the forward motion. Ryu-X looked like he was paying interest on every mistake.

Chat would have exploded on that one. The fight was still young, and AKIRA already decided there would be no polite spacing game. Blue darted in, knee raised, and blasted RYU-X hard enough to send the red fighter sliding toward the right edge. You could see RYU-X trying to keep his guard respectable, but his body was telling a different story. He was losing ground, getting chipped down by pressure, while AKIRA kept moving like the next hit was already loaded. It was not the end, not even close, but it was absolutely the kind of early moment that makes everyone start saying momentum has swung blue.

If you were tracking momentum, this was a bad sign for anyone backing blue. Opening third, no deep fatigue excuse yet, and still AKIRA was the one being shoved around. RYU-X, in red, took the initiative, closed the gap, and landed a sweeping leg strike that knocked AKIRA toward the right boundary. The space loss mattered as much as the hit. RYU-X was investing in control, not flash, and AKIRA’s defense was starting to pay interest.

I had to rewatch this bit because it happens in that messy middle stretch where both fighters have scratches and sparks all over them, but the meaning is super clear. RYU-X is winning the argument here. AKIRA is not out, not helpless, but he’s definitely getting ground down. RYU-X comes forward with his defenses tight, almost like a shielded rush, and the moment they collide AKIRA loses the center line. You can see his torso twist as he tries to absorb it rather than eat the whole thing square. That choice keeps him standing, but it also costs him position. He slides right, then stumbles another half-step, and RYU-X follows like a predator who knows the prey is tired. The red pressure keeps stacking up. The blue fighter’s shoulders sag for just a blink, and that blink tells you the earlier exchanges are taking their toll. By the time they near the right edge, AKIRA’s options feel smaller. He’s still fighting, but RYU-X is the one forcing the geography of the battle.

My little brother kept asking why AKIRA did not counter, and honestly, that was the whole tragedy of it. Earlier, maybe he slips it. Earlier, maybe blue light cuts around red and makes the crowd explode. But this was late, and he was tired. RYU-X came in hard, arm cocked low, then slammed that heavy punch into AKIRA so cleanly that there was no room for hero music. AKIRA got knocked toward the right edge, boots dragging, shoulders hunched like he was trying to keep his soul from spilling out. RYU-X just marched after him, owning the space, owning the tempo, owning the silence that followed.

The brawl’s crane-hook moment happened after the ceiling display collapsed and left a maintenance winch dangling over the atrium. Juno tried to ambush Sable from above, dropping from a torn banner with both blades crossed. Sable saw only the shadow. She threw her sash upward, not at Juno, but at the swaying crane hook behind him. The silk looped around the hook and snapped taut as Juno descended. Sable ran forward under him, using her own sash as a pulley line. The hook jerked sideways, clipped the back of Juno’s belt, and stole the last foot of his fall. His blades carved empty air while he hung for a heartbeat in an undignified arch. Sable finished by letting go of the sash entirely. Juno dropped onto a pile of plush mascot heads, and the released hook swung away, carrying her sash up into the smoke like a vanishing ribbon.

Vey’s single strangest counter took place under the giant aquarium archway, where glowing koi swam overhead in glass tubes. Lira attacked him with a chain fan, snapping it open and shut fast enough to cut the air into silver flashes. Vey kept retreating until his back nearly touched the aquarium support column. Then, instead of blocking the fan, he rapped his knuckles against the glass tube above them in a quick three-note pattern. The luminous koi, trained for festival shows, swarmed toward the sound and flooded the archway with pulsing gold light. Lira’s fan reflected a dozen fake openings at once, and for one blink she could not tell which Vey was real. The real one had already ducked under the chain, stepped inside her reach, and pressed two fingers to the hinge of the fan. He twisted it closed around its own chain, pinning the weapon like a folded bird. Lira tried to yank free, but the koi lights flared again, and Vey guided her momentum into a gentle spin that seated her perfectly on a nearby bench.

There was a point in the final stretch when AKIRA stopped looking like he was choosing to retreat and started looking like he was being carried backward by each mistake. This was that point. RYU-X came in red-hot, planted, and smashed a punishing punch into him, the kind that makes the animation linger on the body bending before the slide begins. AKIRA was sent toward the right edge, heels carving the floor, his blue aura sputtering behind him. RYU-X followed, not frantic, not desperate, just predatory. The balance of the fight was painfully clear: red was setting the terms, blue was absorbing consequences.

I swear the arena got smaller when AKIRA hit him. We were already near the end, when the music had that urgent pulse and RYU-X was breathing like a furnace with cracks in it. AKIRA advanced in blue, sharp and merciless, then fired a straight thrust that went right through RYU-X’s attempt to hold position. Red was forced backward, sliding toward the right edge, his boots fighting for grip and losing. The important thing was the order of it: AKIRA attacked first, landed first, moved him first. RYU-X was not choosing that retreat; it was being hammered into him.

The sound sold it before the animation even finished. You heard the sharp crack of RYU-X’s leg connecting, then the rough scrape as AKIRA was driven rightward across the floor. It wasn’t a late-fight stumble; this was still in the first third, when fighters are supposed to have bounce. RYU-X’s forward pressure made every noise heavier, every step from AKIRA more desperate. Blue was losing space and stamina at the same time, while red kept marching him down.

During the rooftop portion, Juno pulled off a dodge nobody else could have copied. Tessa fired six prism darts that bent around obstacles, so hiding behind the air-conditioning units was useless. Juno waited until the darts split, each choosing a different angle into her blind spots. Then she ran directly at the billboard for Crimson Melon Soda, kicked off the glowing model’s painted smile, and flattened herself against the sign as if hugging it. The darts converged where her body had been, but their enchantment made them avoid striking the commercial image; they curved around the smiling mascot instead. Juno slid down the slick billboard face, grabbed the lower support bar, and let her momentum swing her beneath the sign. The darts, still refusing to hit the mascot, circled wide and stabbed into the roof behind Tessa. Juno released the bar at the bottom of her swing and dropkicked Tessa through a laundry line, leaving her wrapped in three white shirts and one advertisement banner.

Mako and Oro collided only once in the entire melee, and it was a weirdly graceful mess. Oro skated along the polished rail on the soles of his boots, knives trailing golden sparks, while Mako charged from the opposite direction carrying a broken bench over his head. Oro expected a swing and prepared to split into illusions. Mako did swing, but he hurled the bench straight upward instead of at Oro. The bench smashed into a flock of messenger drones, and their little propellers rained down like spinning coins. Oro vanished into four afterimages, weaving between the falling parts. Mako closed his eyes and listened. One propeller changed pitch as it bounced off a real shoulder rather than a ghost. Mako pivoted toward that tiny note, caught Oro's wrist with both hands, and locked his elbow against Mako's shoulder in a crude standing armbar. Oro tried to dissolve again, but pain anchored him. Mako then stomped on the rail switch lever. The track beside them shifted with a metallic thunk, and the sudden jolt tossed Oro over Mako's hip into a pile of lost-and-found umbrellas that sprang open around him like startled black flowers.

Listen, I was yelling at the screen because Ryu-X had been getting bullied for the last stretch, and this was where it got nasty. Akira, all blue blur and bad intentions, darted in with that narrow spear-like jab right into the gap. Ryu-X ate it hard. You could see the red glow jerk back, his heels losing purchase, and suddenly he was being pushed closer to the right edge like someone dragging a cursor across the map. This was mid-fight, not the opening scramble, and Ryu-X already had that tired animation: shoulders heavy, blocks late, pride doing more work than his body. Akira was absolutely dictating everything.

From the cheap seats, you could feel the match tilting red right there. We were already past the feeling-out stage, and Akira had that sluggish, guarded look, like every exchange was costing him. RYU-X stepped in first again, not waiting for permission, and cracked his bent arm across Akira’s upper body. It wasn’t flashy in the way the earlier exchanges were flashy; it was mean, compact, and perfectly timed. Akira’s blue silhouette got shoved sideways from the force, boots scraping as he was carried toward the right side of the arena view. The crowd noise dipped for half a second because it was obvious: RYU-X was driving now, and Akira was getting squeezed out of space.

The elevator doors opened at the worst possible time, revealing Captain Loro already mid-punch. Sumi, trapped in the narrow car with two unconscious guards at her feet, had nowhere to dodge. She hit the emergency stop with her elbow as Loro’s gauntlet crossed the threshold. The elevator jerked downward half a meter, not enough to escape but enough to change the angle. His punch smashed into the top door track instead of her face, and the gauntlet stuck in the buckled metal. Sumi grabbed his wrist with both hands, planted one foot on the elevator wall, and used the rising counterweight shudder to wrench his arm straight. Then she tossed one of the unconscious guard’s helmets into the gap. The doors tried to close, met the helmet, and bounced open, repeatedly hammering Loro’s trapped elbow with mechanical stubbornness. Sumi released him before anything broke too badly, but the captain staggered back with his whole arm numb, glaring at the elevator as if it had chosen sides.

As a coach, I hated what I saw from AKIRA there. Late in the bout, his base was compromised and RYU-X attacked exactly the weak line. Red descended with body weight behind the strike, contacted high, then continued driving through instead of bouncing away. That follow-through forced AKIRA to give ground toward the right boundary. Blue tried to widen his stance, but the legs were gone; fatigue made the correction too slow. RYU-X’s pressure was clean and immediate, the kind that tells you he knew AKIRA was wearing down. No reset, no courtesy, no space. The aggressor was obvious, and the defender was being marched into a bad ending.

Listen, as a corner coach, I hated RYU-X’s posture there. Midway through the clash, his shoulders had started to sag, and AKIRA noticed before anyone else. Blue didn’t chase wildly; he stalked. RYU-X tried to hold ground, maybe expecting another body-line attack, but AKIRA changed the angle and smashed down through the top of his defense. That downward blow folded RYU-X just enough to steal his feet, and the impact carried him toward the right side like he’d been shoved by a door swinging shut. It was not a finishing sequence yet, but it was the kind of moment that tells you who is dictating the match. AKIRA was hunting. RYU-X was managing damage and losing territory.

Kei’s one-time reversal against the chain brute was pure desperation. Brak had wrapped a barbed chain around Kei’s waist and was dragging him across the plaza tiles, sparks flying from Kei’s boots as he tried to dig in. Instead of resisting, Kei suddenly ran toward Brak, letting the slack whip behind him. Brak grinned and raised both arms to clothesline him, but Kei dove, rolled over the chain, and came up inside the loop. With a sharp twist of his hips, he turned the dragging line into a belt around Brak’s own forearms. Then Kei jumped backward off a toppled vending machine, using the height to pull the chain up and over Brak’s shoulders. Brak’s massive arms crossed in front of his chest, trapped by his own weapon. Kei landed behind him, put one boot between Brak’s shoulder blades, and kicked off. Brak pitched forward, unable to catch himself, and skidded through a carpet of spilled melon buns. The chain unraveled immediately after, too tangled with crumbs and broken links to repeat.

Kaito opened the exchange by sliding under Selene's first mirror-blade slash on his knees, letting the edge shave sparks from the metal platform sign above him. Instead of popping up with a countercut, he hooked one heel behind the rolling suitcase someone had abandoned during the evacuation and kicked it sideways into her shin. Selene did not trip; she stepped onto the suitcase as it skidded, rode it like a tiny chariot, and used the added speed to spin at his face. Kaito caught her wrist between the flat of his sword and his forearm, then pivoted hard enough to turn her momentum into a crooked shoulder throw. She flipped over him and landed catlike on the ticket gate, but the throw tore her reflective sleeve open, scattering coin-sized mirror charms across the floor. Each charm flashed with her grin, forcing Kaito to blink at fifteen false Selene faces while the real one silently retrieved her knife from the suitcase handle.

Mei’s prop hit with the announcement board was the brawl’s most theatrical accident. She was backing away from Ravel, whose whip-sword kept changing length, when she bumped into the old mechanical board that flipped destination names with loud clacks. Ravel slashed horizontally, and Mei ducked so close that her hairpins sparked against the metal frame. The blade cut the board’s release cord. Every destination panel began flipping at once: NORTH HARBOR, STAR MINE, PEACH GATE, all strobing above them. Mei noticed Ravel’s eyes tracking the motion for timing, so she slammed her palm into the manual lever and froze the board halfway through a flip. A row of black panels jutted out like steps. Ravel’s next extending thrust struck one panel and ricocheted upward, wrapping his own whip-sword around the board’s axle. Mei grabbed the hanging cord he had cut, swung out over the platform edge, and kicked the lever on her return swing. The board completed its flip with a thunderous clatter, winding Ravel’s weapon tight and yanking him forward until his nose pressed against the word DELAYED.

Bro, AKIRA hit him like a train with a grudge. We were already deep enough into the fight that RYU-X looked like he had been breathing smoke, and then blue just shot forward. Red barely got his arms up before the collision shoved him across the stage. You could almost hear the floor complain as RYU-X got forced toward the right side. No fancy pause, no dramatic reset, just AKIRA deciding, “You’re going over there now.” That was the moment the pressure became bullying. RYU-X was still on his feet, but he was losing inches, losing rhythm, losing that scary confidence.

I had been pretending the fight was still even, but that palm changed my face. RYU-X was fading. Not defeated, not yet, but fading in the way a candle looks smaller even while it still burns. AKIRA, all blue pressure and forward intent, stepped in during the middle of the clash and hit him with an open hand that carried way more authority than its short motion suggested. RYU-X’s red frame bent around the impact and got driven toward the right edge of the arena. He tried to stop the slide with one foot, then another, but the ground kept giving him up. AKIRA kept coming, and the message was clear: RYU-X was losing space, breath, and control all at once.

I’m watching it like a corner coach and all I can think is: bad sign, bad sign, bad sign. RYU-X had been absorbing too much by this point, and during the last run of the battle his defense started looking more like habit than intent. AKIRA noticed. Blue didn’t overcommit. No wild swing, no wasted drama. Just a short, accurate punch to the front that caught RYU-X before he could reset. The red fighter got knocked off his preferred line and drifted toward the right-side limit, boots scraping back as if the arena itself was shrinking. That’s dominance. AKIRA was advancing with purpose, forcing the exchange, choosing the distance. RYU-X, meanwhile, looked drained—still dangerous, sure, but dulled around the edges. The hit wasn’t the biggest blow of the fight, yet it screamed momentum. When a tired fighter gets moved by something that simple, you know the aggressor has taken over.

From a commentator’s desk, that sequence is easy to call: mid-fight, momentum red. RYU-X closes distance, tucks in behind a compact block, and turns the collision into forward pressure. AKIRA meets it, but not cleanly. The blue fighter absorbs the impact across his arms and shoulder, then gets walked across the floor toward the right side of the arena. That matters because it shows who owns the pace. AKIRA isn’t choosing where to stand anymore; he is being relocated. RYU-X keeps his posture low and assertive, forcing AKIRA to retreat step by step. It’s not the beginning chaos, and it’s not the final desperation yet—it’s that dangerous middle phase where fatigue starts showing. AKIRA’s reactions are still there, but they’re dulled. RYU-X senses that and keeps leaning on him.

There’s a little cruelty in how controlled RYU-X looks here. We’re not at the opening anymore, when AKIRA could spring away with clean footwork and answer everything with sharp blue flashes. This is later into the struggle, when the exchanges have sanded him down. RYU-X advances wrapped in a disciplined shell, catches AKIRA’s attempted resistance, and converts that contact into a punishing advance. AKIRA’s heels chatter across the surface as he’s pressed toward the rightmost side. It’s subtle at first—just a loss of one step, then another—but the camera framing makes it feel like the arena is shrinking around him. RYU-X never appears frantic. He keeps his weight forward, red energy pulsing at the edges, and forces AKIRA to spend strength simply staying upright. That’s why the moment lands so hard: it isn’t a finishing blow, it’s territorial dominance. AKIRA’s fatigue becomes visible through position. He can still block, still brace, still glare back, but he cannot stop being moved. RYU-X owns the middle phase and turns AKIRA’s retreat into proof of it.

The bell-rope lock happened near the shrine car coupled to the festival train. Old Genji had been moving slowly all night, so the young spearman Rott assumed he could rush past the grandfather and skewer the control panel. Genji stepped aside from the spear point, caught the red bell rope with one hand, and let Rott’s shaft slide under his elbow. Rott tried to wrench it free, but Genji had already looped the rope around the spear and his wrist in the same motion used to ring the shrine bell. He pulled down. The bell boomed once, deep enough to rattle the windows, and the rope tightened into a figure-eight bind around Rott’s forearm. Genji turned his hip, not his shoulders, and the spearman found himself kneeling with his own weapon pinned vertically against the floor. The more he struggled, the louder the bell chimed above them. Genji leaned on the rope with a calm smile and told him that if he wished to make an offering, silence would be accepted.

Okay, costume nerd take: the red aura against the blue jacket made this hit look insanely stylish, which is unfair because Akira was clearly suffering. RYU-X had the tempo by then. Not late enough for desperation, not early enough for excuses, just that ugly middle stretch where the stronger rhythm starts grinding somebody down. He swung in a tight crescent, arm bent, frost-like flash curling off the impact, and Akira got knocked toward the right boundary. It was like watching a character get pushed out of the safe part of the stage. RYU-X did not pose or reset; he kept advancing.

I was on commentary duty for a little fan stream, and my voice cracked when it happened. Late in the clash, after RYU-X had already absorbed too much punishment to reset properly, AKIRA refused to give him air. The blue fighter planted, launched in with a piercing forward strike, and the impact folded the red one’s stance. RYU-X didn’t just stumble; he was carried sideways and back, sliding toward the far-right edge of the arena frame. You could see the balance of the bout in that single shove: AKIRA dictating distance, tempo, and direction, while RYU-X was stuck reacting with a drained guard and desperate feet.

Kael’s first clean opening comes when Rakka lunges across the cracked marble concourse with both hook swords crossed like scissors. Instead of retreating, Kael plants one sneaker against the base of a humming soda vending machine, lets Rakka’s blades bite into the steel side, and kicks the machine’s coin return with his heel. The machine spits a spray of copper tokens directly into Rakka’s mask lenses. Rakka flinches for less than a second, but Kael uses that tiny blink to yank the vending machine forward by the embedded swords. It topples with a groan, not onto Rakka, but into the path of Vey, who is sprinting in from behind with a spear. Vey vaults over it, exactly as Kael hoped, and Kael catches him midair by the sash, pivots once, and slams him onto the vending machine’s glowing face. The glass spiderwebs under Vey’s back, while Rakka finally frees his swords and realizes the whole exchange was never aimed at him.

Kaito's rooftop exchange with Sable unfolds among bent antennas and humming spirit wires above the palace. Rain has started, making every tile shine like a mirror. Sable throws a crescent blade attached to a chain, not at Kaito, but around the central antenna mast so it can hook him from behind on the return. Kaito hears the chain hiss over the wet metal and jumps forward instead of back, sliding on his heels under Sable's follow-up kick. He grabs a loose antenna rod as he passes, but rather than wielding it like a spear, he jams it through two links of the returning chain. The crescent blade stops short, vibrating inches from his shoulder. Sable yanks, and the rod bends into a bow shape between the mast and the chain. Kaito lets go at the exact bend's peak. The rod snaps straight, flinging the chain upward and tangling it in a spinning weather vane shaped like a koi. Sable is pulled onto tiptoe, and Kaito simply taps the vane so it rotates faster, winding her chain into a harmless silver cocoon.

Coach’s eye on it: Ryu-X is losing the positioning battle before the match has even had time to settle. Akira closes the gap clean, plants his base, and drives the heel of his hand straight through Ryu-X’s guard line. That contact turns Ryu-X’s upper body and sends him sliding toward the right-side limit of the arena. The important part is not just the hit, it’s the direction. Akira is herding him, making him spend balance and energy while the bout is still in its first phase. Ryu-X looks like he’s absorbing too much too soon; shoulders high, feet late, posture breaking. Akira, in blue, is the one dictating every exchange here.

I was close enough to hear Ryu-X's boot scrape. Early fight, right? Nobody should be desperate yet. But Akira was already hunting. He came in from the left side of the exchange, blue flashing low, and cut Ryu-X's legs out of alignment with a ground-level strike. Ryu-X did not fly dramatically upward; he got shoved sideways, which somehow looked worse, because it showed he had no stable base left. He staggered toward the right edge, red coat snapping behind him, and Akira kept advancing. The balance of power was obvious: Akira was leading the dance, and Ryu-X was being dragged through it.

Mako and Kyra collided in the most delicate exchange of the entire brawl. Mako’s flames had been guttering in the rain blowing through the roof, so she gathered them into a single narrow ribbon around her index finger. Kyra saw the tiny flame and assumed it was a bluff, advancing with both mirror daggers crossed. Mako flicked the ribbon not at Kyra, but at a chandelier crystal dangling by one wire above them. The crystal heated, cracked, and dropped. Kyra’s reflexes were too sharp; she cut it into four glittering pieces before it hit the ground. That was exactly the trap. Each falling piece caught Mako’s ribbon-flame and refracted it into four separate threads, momentarily drawing a glowing cage around Kyra’s wrists. Mako yanked both hands back, tightening the threads just long enough to pull Kyra’s dagger points away from her throat. Kyra spun out by slicing through her own sleeve cuffs, sacrificing the embroidered guards, and the severed flame threads burst like fireflies between them.

Kenzen attempts a clean sword finish on Juno at the edge of the moonlit stage, but the exchange turns absurdly personal. He draws so fast that the scabbard slap alone cracks the lacquer floor. Juno, whose gauntlets were already shattered earlier in the brawl, has only the string of prayer beads around his neck. He whips them off as Kenzen’s blade descends, not to block the cut but to catch the sword guard. The beads snap tight around Kenzen’s wrist and tsuba, forcing the slash to veer just wide enough to shave Juno’s collar. Kenzen steps in for a knee strike, and Juno lets him, absorbing it against his ribs while looping the remaining beads around Kenzen’s elbow. With a grunt, Juno drops backward and plants one foot on Kenzen’s stomach. The fall turns into a sacrifice throw. Kenzen flips over him, sword still trapped in the bead loop, and lands flat on his back with his own arm pinned across his chest. Juno pulls once, and the katana skitters away like a silver fish.

From a narrative angle, this is the scene where the audience realizes the blue fighter isn’t just being cautious; he’s being worn down. AKIRA is still in the opening portion of the fight, but his movement has that defensive drag to it. RYU-X in red presses the issue, stepping in with a compact forward strike that cuts right through the space between them. The contact lands hard, with a flash of heat and momentum, and AKIRA is driven toward the rightmost side of the arena. He doesn’t fly helplessly, but he loses ground in a way that feels involuntary and costly. RYU-X’s body language stays predatory after the hit, shoulders leaning in, ready to keep crowding. AKIRA’s body language says survival: brace, slide, recover, hope for distance. At this stage, red is clearly setting the terms.

Selene cornered Nix inside the luggage carousel, where suitcases continued to circulate because some emergency battery refused to die. She danced backward on the moving belt, throwing mirror needles that bounced off the chrome rails and came from impossible angles. Nix raised an ice wall in front of him, but the needles reflected around it, nicking his coat sleeves and cutting the strap of his goggles. He stopped trying to block and slammed both palms onto the carousel belt. Frost raced along the rubber, locking every suitcase in place except one bright red trunk directly between them. Selene stepped onto that trunk, expecting another slide, and it held firm for half a heartbeat. Then Nix thawed only the strip under the trunk and kicked the carousel motor housing. The belt jerked. The trunk shot forward like a battering ram, carrying Selene straight toward him. She used the momentum, planted both feet on the trunk's front edge, and sprang over Nix's head. Her heel clipped the back of his skull in passing, but he caught the loose strap of her boot with an ice-coated hand and brought her down hard among the frozen suitcases.

There was a nasty elegance to it, the sort of thing that makes the crowd cheer before they realize how bad it is for the guy taking it. The duel had reached that bruising middle phase where the bright opening confidence was gone, and AKIRA’s blue aura felt dimmer, more defensive, more compressed. RYU-X, burning red and impatient, pivoted through the air with his body wound like a coil coming undone. The strike swept into AKIRA and carried force beyond the first hit, turning contact into a shove, a punishment, a relocation. AKIRA’s frame lurched sideways. His boots scraped, his balance staggered, and the right edge of the battleground rushed closer behind him. What made it hurt to watch was that RYU-X never looked overextended. He landed and flowed forward, as if the spin was just another step in a longer hunt. AKIRA, meanwhile, had that strained, battered look of someone still skilled enough to stay upright but not fresh enough to answer cleanly. The whole scene said: red is pushing the story now, blue is being written into a corner.

I was rooting for red, so I hated how clean it was. Ryu-X tried to hold his ground, but he was already worn thin by then, somewhere in the meat of the battle, after too many blocks and half-escapes. Akira recognized it instantly. He stepped forward and punched a straight, drilling hit through the guard. Ryu-X lurched backward, forced toward the right edge with no elegant recovery, just a rough skid and a desperate attempt to keep his balance. The worst part was Akira's expression afterward: calm, like this was exactly the result he had calculated. Ryu-X was fighting to remain in the match; Akira was fighting to finish shaping it.

Juno's wire dart shot for Tetsu's throat, a bright silver line so thin it vanished whenever sparks fell behind it. Tetsu heard the spool whine before he saw it. He snapped his magnetic bracers together and yanked every loose nail, coin, and ticket-staple from the ruined kiosk into a spinning halo around his head. The wire tangled in the halo, whipping itself into a knot instead of reaching him. Juno smiled and stepped backward, because tangling had been the point. She planted her heel on the railing, twisted both hands, and the knot cinched around Tetsu's bracers, binding his wrists chest-high. He responded by magnetizing the entire railing she stood on. The metal screamed as it bent toward him, dragging Juno off balance. She released one wire, cartwheeled over the collapsing rail, and kicked him squarely in the jaw while still holding the other line. The kick snapped his head aside, but the rail slammed down behind her like a fallen gate, cutting off her escape route and forcing the next clash at arm's length.

Juno turned the shattered pendulum of the observatory clock into a weapon only once. Cornered between two leaning pillars, he waited until Kyra’s mirror blades came scissoring in from both sides, then ducked so low his scarf dragged through a puddle of oil. The blades struck the brass pendulum bob hanging behind him and sliced its last cable. Instead of jumping away, Juno grabbed the broken cable, wrapped it around his forearm, and kicked off the wall. The enormous bob dropped, dragging him in a violent arc across the room. He skimmed inches over Mako’s flaming whip, twisted mid-swing, and slammed both heels into Kyra’s breastplate. The impact sent her skidding backward through a crescent of scattered glass. Juno let go before the bob smashed into the floor, rolling beneath the recoil and leaving Kyra’s two mirror blades embedded in the pendulum face like decorative hands on a ruined clock.

Tetsu's brief exchange with the bell priestess was remembered because it went silent in the middle of the loudest fight. She stepped into the concourse ringing a bronze handbell, and every fighter near her staggered as the sound turned their balance against them. Tetsu advanced with cotton stuffed in one ear, but the vibration traveled through his chain anyway, making his fingers spasm. The priestess smiled and swung the bell toward his temple. Tetsu released the chain entirely. It fell in a loose circle around her feet, apparently abandoned. She rang the bell again, and the chain answered the vibration by crawling along the tile like a snake being shaken awake. Tetsu stamped on one end, making the other leap up and wrap the bell's clapper. Her next ring produced no sound at all. In that pocket of silence, Tetsu stepped close, tapped two fingers to the bell's rim, and the trapped vibration knocked the priestess backward into a newspaper kiosk.

I was in the crowd losing my voice, and even I could tell Akira was running out of answers. Near the end, he came in like he wanted to force one last opening, but RYU-X just shut the door on him. Red braced, caught the impact, and shoved through it so hard that Akira got marched sideways toward the far right side. It looked less like a single hit and more like RYU-X saying, no, you move where I decide. Akira’s feet scraped, his blue aura kept sputtering, and the whole arena groaned because everyone felt the pressure. This was not early-match testing anymore. This was the final squeeze, with RYU-X hunting and Akira getting smaller by the second.

I was rooting for chaos, so I loved it, but even I winced. AKIRA had been hanging on by stubbornness, not freshness, and RYU-X finally hit him with the sort of blunt-force answer that ends arguments. The red fighter surged in and cracked him square, sending him skidding toward the right edge with that horrible delayed recoil anime loves so much. AKIRA's blue outline stuttered, then stretched behind him as he lost ground. No clever reversal came out of it, no cheeky dodge, no sudden reset. RYU-X was the one pushing, the one deciding where the fight moved, and AKIRA was getting squeezed into the last bit of space he had left.

As an in-universe reporter, I’d file that moment under ‘decisive pressure near the end.’ AKIRA seized the initiative with a forward burst, striking RYU-X with a slicing attack that broke the red fighter’s line and carried him toward the right perimeter. The sequence came during the closing stretch, when RYU-X’s reduced responsiveness had become increasingly visible. He attempted to absorb or deflect the blow, but his timing lagged, and the force displaced him several steps toward the edge. AKIRA emerged from the contact still upright, advancing, and tactically favored. RYU-X, by contrast, appeared worn down and constrained, with the boundary now limiting his movement. It was a damaging hit and a territorial win at once.

Vey thinks he has trapped Kael on the maintenance rails above the station floor, where one wrong step means a long fall into the dark tracks below. Vey’s gauntlets are magnetized, snapping to the rails with a brutal advantage that lets him crawl and strike from angles Kael cannot match. Kael fakes panic, retreating until his heel touches a loose bundle of copper signal wire. When Vey lunges, both gauntlets locked forward, Kael whips the wire around the rail and kicks the exposed end into the live junction box beside him. Sparks erupt blue-white. The magnetized gauntlets surge, not exploding, but clamping so fiercely to the rail that Vey cannot pull them free. Kael runs straight up Vey’s trapped arms as if they are a ladder, uses his shoulder as a stepping stone, and flips behind him. While upside down, Kael taps the emergency release latch on Vey’s belt with two fingers. Vey’s heavy armor skirt drops around his knees, leaving him stuck, furious, and suddenly much shorter.

From a tactical view, this was the moment RYU-X converted pressure into position. Earlier exchanges had been more balanced, but by this late stage AKIRA’s defense was visibly delayed: his guard came up a fraction slow, his stance was narrow, and his recovery steps were no longer sharp. RYU-X recognized that fatigue and attacked from a steep descending angle, committing his whole body downward and forward. The impact did not merely knock AKIRA down; it redirected him laterally, forcing him toward the right side of the field where escape options were limited. That detail matters. RYU-X was not swinging wildly. He was herding him. AKIRA absorbed the blow with his upper body and tried to twist out, but the force kept carrying him, boots scraping, shoulders hunched, blue aura flickering unevenly. RYU-X landed in control and continued to face him, closing the lane before AKIRA could reset. At this point in the fight, the momentum was unmistakable: red was dictating range, timing, and geography, while blue was surviving on reflex and grit.

At the carnival plaza, the pyromancer Lulo tried to trap Emi inside a ring of blue fire. Emi could not jump it, so she ducked into a mascot costume lying beside a prize booth: a huge plush moon rabbit head with floppy ears. Lulo burst out laughing and hurled a fireball at the ridiculous target. Emi tilted the oversized rabbit head forward, and the fireball sank into the reflective foil lining the eye window, bouncing its glare back into Lulo’s own face. He shielded his eyes for just a blink. Emi charged, but the suit’s floppy ear snagged on a dart board rack. Instead of tearing free, she spun with the snag, turning the ear into a plush sling. The rack whipped around and smacked Lulo’s wand hand. His fire ring collapsed into harmless sparks while Emi crashed belly-first into him, both of them rolling through a pile of stuffed starfish prizes.

Old-school martial arts fans know the value of a hand strike like that. Fists get all the attention, but an open palm delivered from the core can move a person without giving them time to roll with it. AKIRA used it beautifully here. Midway through the fight, with RYU-X already worn from defending too much, AKIRA stepped inside the red guard and sent force straight through him. RYU-X was driven toward the right edge, his stance breaking in stages: first the chest jolting back, then the hips turning, then the feet scrambling to save him. AKIRA remained balanced after contact, which tells you he was the aggressor with control, not just someone swinging hard. RYU-X was being pushed physically and mentally.

The red fighter had been roaring earlier, but here his roar turned into a cough. AKIRA, wrapped in blue, moved like a tide that had finally decided which shore to break. In the middle of the battle, when both should have been equal if strength alone mattered, AKIRA’s patience became sharper than RYU-X’s fury. He stepped through the sparks and pressed his open hand into RYU-X with a sudden bloom of force. RYU-X folded around the impact and slid toward the right edge, not dramatically graceful, just exhausted and human for a second. His boots dragged lines through dust. AKIRA followed with that terrible calm of someone who knows the other man is losing ground in more ways than one.

The arena had that endgame feeling, where every movement sounds louder because everyone knows there cannot be many more. AKIRA was on the defensive, blue light sputtering around his frame, his shoulders rising and falling like he was carrying the whole fight on his back. RYU-X, wrapped in red, took the initiative again and attacked from above, cutting down into him with a crushing, forward-driving impact. It was beautiful in a terrible way: the strike landed, AKIRA bent under it, and the force kept traveling, shunting him toward the far right side as if RYU-X had drawn a line and decided blue would be forced across it. AKIRA’s expression had that clenched, furious look, but his body betrayed him. He could not hold the center. He could not turn the pressure aside. The slide to the edge was the real story, because it showed how much control had shifted. Earlier, AKIRA might have pivoted out or answered with a sudden burst. Here, he was being carried by the blow, boots scraping, balance breaking, space disappearing. RYU-X landed like he owned the ground beneath both of them, already leaning forward for whatever came next. Red was not merely ahead; red was accelerating. Blue was not finished yet, but he was unmistakably being worn down.

I hated this part as an AKIRA fan. We were barely into the first third, and he was already defending more than fighting. RYU-X came forward in red like he owned the floor, swung his leg around in a sharp arc, and it landed hard enough to send AKIRA sliding right. Not a dramatic knockout moment, just worse in a way: another clean hit, another step lost, another meter of space stolen. You could see AKIRA trying to reset, but he was being walked down.

I was rooting for RYU-X, so this one hurt to watch. He had that stubborn look, like he was trying to convince himself the tide hadn’t turned. But by the middle, AKIRA was forcing him backward more often than not. Then came the palm. AKIRA closed in fast, blue flashing around his arm, and struck with his hand open, direct and heavy. RYU-X lurched toward the right side, and for a second he didn’t look like a rival, he looked like a man trying to stay on his feet after too many bad decisions. He still had fire in him, sure, but it was flickering. AKIRA looked fresher, meaner, and fully in command of the pace.

On the baggage conveyor, Niko faces a broad-shouldered wrestler named Gant who wants nothing more complicated than to grab him and crush the fight out of him. Suitcases rumble past on the belt like armored turtles. Niko keeps hopping from one to another, but Gant finally catches him by the back of his vest and lifts him overhead. Niko does not wriggle free. He hooks one foot under the handle of a massive traveling trunk as it passes, letting the conveyor drag his leg backward. The sudden tension yanks Gant off balance just as he begins the slam. Niko twists in midair, wraps both arms around Gant’s neck, and turns the failed throw into a spinning neckbreaker that lands not on the floor but onto the soft pile of overstuffed suitcases. The impact bursts one trunk open, releasing a flock of ceremonial paper cranes that whirl around them. Gant rises dizzy and covered in paper wings; Niko, still holding one suitcase strap, snaps it like a belt across Gant’s forehead and drops him back onto the moving belt.

I was skeptical at first because the animation made it look almost too small to matter. No giant impact crater, no screaming clash, just RYU-X making a shape with his body and AKIRA reacting. But on rewatch, that is exactly why it matters. AKIRA is exhausted, so his defense is automatic. RYU-X knows this. He threatens one thing, pulls AKIRA's eyes and guard there, then uses the hesitation to walk him rightward. The edge creeps into the frame, and suddenly blue has no comfortable retreat left. Red is not chasing randomly; he is forcing a funnel. That tiny deception is a late-fight knife twist.

Rika’s first clean reversal happened beside the ticket gates, where the polished floor had been slicked by spilled melon soda. Hagan rushed her with both fists glowing, expecting her to retreat into the turnstiles. Instead, she stepped onto the puddle on purpose, let her sandals skid, and dropped so low that his punch tore only the bow from her collar. As his momentum carried him over her shoulder, she hooked one ankle around the base of the nearest gate and used the other leg to lever him sideways. The turnstile spun once with a bright ding, and Hagan was flipped through it like an angry passenger who had forgotten his pass. He landed in a nest of paper tickets, still trying to finish the punch in midair. Rika simply caught the falling bow, tied it back on, and tapped her card against the reader as if the throw had been part of her commute.

The neon concourse gave Hiro a trick no one else noticed. Kade, whose gauntlets stored blue lightning, threw a straight punch that cracked the air and left a glowing afterimage across every puddle on the floor. Hiro watched the reflection instead of the fist. When the punch came, he seemed to duck too early, folding under an empty space. Kade smirked until his knuckles met only a paper lantern hanging behind Hiro's head. Hiro had read the delayed reflection in a spilled bowl of ramen and moved on the real punch, not the afterimage. As Kade's arm punched through the lantern, Hiro grabbed the trailing paper frame, spun around Kade's extended elbow, and snapped the lantern wire around his gauntlet. The current grounded through the wet noodle stand sign, exploding the sign into harmless blue sparks and a shower of plastic menu cards.

If this were an arcade match, that exchange would be where the player in blue proves they have corner control on the brain. AKIRA closed the gap during the early part of the fight and popped RYU-X with a knee that did more than just connect; it shoved red toward the right boundary and stole his space. RYU-X tried to brace, but the pushback told the story. He was already being worn down, already reacting instead of choosing. AKIRA did not pause to admire it, either. He kept the angle, kept the aggression, and made the right side of the stage feel a lot smaller for RYU-X.

On the rooftop garden, the masked twins try to bind Mira with kite strings stolen from the children's festival booth. One twin circles clockwise while the other circles counterclockwise, their colored spools hissing as they wrap lines around Mira's wrists, elbows, and waist. Mira lets the net tighten until her arms are pinned, then stamps on a sprinkler head. Water erupts in a silver column, slicking the strings and weighing the paper kites still attached to them. The twins pull to finish the snare, but the wet kites sag over the rooftop edge and catch the updraft from the avenue below. Instead of restraining Mira, the lines jerk both twins toward the parapet. Mira drops flat, threads her bound hands under her knees, and pops her arms in front of her like a contortionist. She grabs the crossed strings at her chest and hauls back. The twins collide shoulder-first with each other, not hard enough to end the fight, but hard enough to tangle their masks together by the cords and ruin their perfect symmetry.

No one expected the old announcer booth to survive the fight until Veyra used it as a pivot. She was being chased by a spear lancer whose weapon extended section by section, stabbing through the booth's paper-thin walls. Instead of leaving, Veyra ducked between microphones, letting each spear thrust puncture a different sound panel. The loudspeakers outside shrieked with feedback every time metal entered foam. When the lancer grew impatient and charged through the door, Veyra hooked her foot around the rolling announcer chair and spun it into his knees. He hopped clean over it, showing off, and that was when she slammed both palms onto the broadcast console. The booth's public-address system boomed the feedback into a physical shockwave from the damaged panels. The lancer's spear vibrated like a tuning fork, numbing both his hands. Veyra stepped in, clipped the spear segments shut one by one with the booth's dangling headset cord, and left him holding a useless metal baton.

Seya's hairpin looked ornamental until it stopped Juno colder than a chain. He had just vaulted a bench and was sprinting toward the control booth, one hand reaching for the override lever that would cut the station lights. Seya flicked the silver pin without even turning her shoulders. It did not aim for his body. It nailed the trailing cuff of his coat to the paper timetable posted on the wall. Juno felt only a tiny tug and tried to keep running, which yanked him backward so sharply his boots skated out from under him. He hit the floor on his back, staring up at departure times to cities he suddenly hated. Seya followed with a knife drop, but Juno tore the timetable off the wall with both hands, rolled sideways inside the paper sheet, and let her knife punch through the schedule instead of his chest.

From a referee’s angle, the sequence was decisive without being messy. In the closing portion of the contest, RYU-X advanced into Akira’s line and received the attack on a stable guard. Akira’s forward effort failed to displace him. RYU-X then applied pressure through the contact and forced Akira to retreat toward the right boundary. Akira remained active, but his reactions were clearly dulled by accumulated damage; his footwork was reactive rather than tactical. RYU-X maintained legal control of space, continued moving in, and prevented Akira from turning off the line. The exchange showed a clear shift in initiative. RYU-X was pressing the action, while Akira was being steadily worn down and pushed into a worse position.

From the commentary desk, you could feel the fight tipping hard toward red in that middle stretch. RYU-X didn’t give AKIRA a second to reset; he stepped in, snapped his arm through the air, and the blue fighter got caught clean across the front. It wasn’t just a hit—it shoved AKIRA sideways, boots scraping as he was forced toward the right boundary of the arena. AKIRA tried to square up afterward, but his posture was already sagging, like every exchange before this had stolen a little more from him. RYU-X looked sharp, hungry, and completely in control.

My little brother yelled that Akira was going to fall off the screen, and honestly, that was the vibe. It was the middle of the fight, after Akira had already taken too much pressure, and RYU-X just kept bullying forward. Red came in close and swung around with this cold-looking punch that nailed Akira from the side. Blue went sliding toward the right edge like he had been shoved by a truck. Akira was still trying, but he looked tired. RYU-X looked like he had decided the fight only moved one way now.

Mako’s exchange with the armored chef happened behind the festival food stalls. The chef swung a giant iron wok, using it as both shield and hammer, and Mako’s short blades kept bouncing off. Backed against a grill, Mako snatched a skewer of half-cooked squid and threw it—not at the chef, but into the wok. The chef instinctively tilted the pan to dump it out. That tiny tilt exposed the inside surface, slick with oil from previous attacks. Mako kicked the grill’s gas knob open, scraped one blade along the hot grate, and sent a spark into the wok just as the oil sheeted across it. A harmless but spectacular flare blossomed upward, blinding the chef behind his own shield. Mako slid under the rim, grabbed the chef’s apron strings, and tied them to the handle of a rolling takoyaki cart in one fast knot. Then she shoved the cart downhill. The chef staggered after it, dragged by the apron, still holding the smoking wok like a confused turtle shell.

If you rewatch it without the music, the exchange is even meaner. Akira's aggression is almost suffocating in that early section. He keeps his blue frame just inside Ryu-X's comfort zone, never far enough away for red to breathe, never close enough for Ryu-X to clinch and slow things down. Ryu-X tries to step out, but that step becomes the opening. Akira lowers, snaps a leg across the floor line, and catches him where balance lives. Ryu-X's body whips sideways, his recovery step fails, and the force herds him toward the right margin. It is one of those attacks that does not need a giant explosion behind it, because the damage is positional. Akira wins ground. Ryu-X loses confidence. Akira stays the hunter. Ryu-X has to waste more energy just returning to a usable stance. In the first third, that is a bad omen for the guy in red. You can see the wear building: the slower reaction, the cramped shoulders, the way he reaches for stability instead of preparing a reply.

Jun’s opponent, the smiling swordswoman Sable, corners him beside a broken music shop display where antique instruments have spilled across the floor. Sable’s blade is too quick for his bare hands, so Jun snatches up a lacquered violin case and holds it like a buckler. She laughs, cuts the latches clean off, and expects the case to fall open uselessly. Instead, Jun lets it split at the exact moment of her next thrust, revealing the mirrored inner lining. The reflection of the station’s emergency strobes flashes into Sable’s eyes, making her cut a handspan too high. Jun ducks under the stroke, scoops up the violin bow with his left hand, and uses it not as a weapon but as a lever, threading it between her sword guard and wrist. He twists once, forcing her knuckles open, then kicks the empty case upward. It closes around her blade like a wooden jaw and pins it to the ceiling beam for one clean, humiliating second.

Okay, listen, this is the part I keep rewinding because it looks unfair in the best anime way. AKIRA is in blue, already leaning into the fight like he owns the center, and RYU-X in red is clearly starting to lose that sharpness he had at the beginning. We are not at the finale yet, but the middle has become a grind, and RYU-X is the one paying for it. AKIRA suddenly launches himself forward, no hesitation, and catches RYU-X before he can properly plant. The contact pops through the screen. RYU-X’s body gets driven back and right, not just tapped, not just staggered, but physically marched toward the edge as if AKIRA’s momentum is a hand at his chest. You can see RYU-X trying to resist, knees buckling into a brace, but his frame gives ground anyway. That is why the moment hits so hard: it is not a surprise reversal, it is the aggressor proving the pressure is real. AKIRA is not chasing anymore; he is herding. RYU-X is still dangerous, sure, but now he is defending from a worse position, visibly worn and running out of room.

Mira's duel with the mirror-blade assassin lasted less than ten seconds, but everyone nearby remembered the dodge. The assassin split his katana into seven reflected afterimages and thrust all of them through the narrow gap between two vending machines. Mira was trapped there with her back to cold glass, a can of peach soda rattling beside her ear. She exhaled, flattened one knee outward, and dropped into a sideways bridge so low that her braid brushed the floor. The real blade punched through the soda display exactly where her throat had been. While still arched backward, Mira kicked the vending machine's coin return. A jammed stack of tokens spilled out under the assassin's forward foot. His polished stance became a ridiculous skate. Mira let him slide past her, then pinched the seam of his sleeve between two fingers and used his own momentum to peel him face-first into the vending machine window.

The old mall clock tower gave Mako exactly one ridiculous weapon. Juno drove him backward up the maintenance stairs until they burst onto the clock face platform, gears groaning behind them. Juno swung high, slicing through one of the loosened minute hands that had been removed for repairs. Mako caught the falling clock hand across his shoulders like a giant black oar. It was too heavy for a normal strike, so he used it as a lever instead, jamming one end between two turning gears. The other end whipped around with the machinery’s force. Juno ducked the first sweep, smirking, but Mako stepped onto the hand as it completed its arc and rode it forward. He launched off the tip in a clumsy but effective flying knee that struck Juno’s guard and blasted him backward into a shower of brass screws.

From the perspective of someone who used to box, that was a beautiful bit of ugly work by RYU-X. Not flashy, not cinematic in the usual way, just disciplined pressure. Early in the contest, he put his lead side in range and cracked AKIRA with a brisk, straight hand before the blue fighter’s feet were ready. AKIRA’s head and shoulders took the message, and his balance carried him backward toward the right-side limit. That’s the sort of contact that doesn’t need to flatten a person to be important. It interrupts breathing, ruins rhythm, and makes the other fighter feel the ropes before the round is even mature. RYU-X was the one walking him down. AKIRA was already paying tax for every inch of space.

Juno turned a food cart into a weapon exactly once, and everyone stopped laughing at his apron after that. Cornered by two masked twins at the ramen stall, he grabbed the steaming stockpot with both mitts and shoved it straight forward, not to burn them but to blind them with the cloud that surged over the rim. While they flinched, he kicked the cart's brake free. The whole cart rolled downhill across the rain-slick rooftop, dragging Juno behind it by the handles like a runaway chariot. One twin vaulted over the pot; the other tried to brace against it. Juno timed a hop onto the axle, bounced the front wheels over a cracked tile, and made the cart jump just enough to clip the bracing twin under the knees. The twin flipped backward into hanging noodles, and Juno bailed into a pile of scallions as the cart crashed into a shrine donation box.

Beside Platform Seven, old Mrs. Tako's sushi cart became a battlefield landmark for exactly one ridiculous second. Nara, cornered between Voss's shield bearer and a ticket gate, snatched the cart's bamboo rolling mat and flung it like a folding fan. The shield bearer laughed and marched through it, only to discover that Nara had wrapped six soy packets and a lump of wasabi inside. The mat slapped against his visor, bursting into a salty green smear. He staggered blind, shield still raised, and Nara kicked the cart's brake loose. The whole cart rolled downhill along the polished platform tiles. Rather than jump aside, the shield bearer braced to stop it with his shield. Nara used that as her cue: she ran up the shield face, stepped on his helmet, and flipped over him while the cart clipped his knees from behind.

Juno’s most reckless rescue involved the giant minute hand from the destroyed tower clock. Sable had kicked Nami through a railing, leaving her dangling over the open shaft where gears still turned below. Juno sprinted across the balcony, but Kyra intercepted him with a low slash meant to cut his ankle tendons. He jumped, tucked one knee, and landed on the loosened minute hand jutting from the clock face beside the balcony. The hand dipped under his weight, creaking like it would snap. Juno bounced once, using the spring of the metal to launch himself over Kyra’s second slash. Midair, he unsnapped his belt and threw it around Nami’s wrist. The belt buckle caught, but Juno had no anchor. He twisted and stabbed both throwing knives into the wooden clock face, skidding downward while the blades carved parallel grooves. The minute hand finally broke free and spun into the shaft, smashing a gear tooth just as Nami swung back to safety.

The medical side of me noticed the head movement first, and it was not pretty. During the early portion, RYU-X was already showing signs of accumulated pressure: slower guard recovery, retreating steps, less resistance at center. AKIRA accelerated into close range and delivered an upward strike that snapped RYU-X’s posture off line. The force redirected him toward the right edge, and for a moment his body looked suspended between lift and collapse. AKIRA’s blue momentum continued forward, controlled and aggressive, while RYU-X’s red form was being pushed away with diminishing stability. It was the kind of clean impact that says one competitor is imposing the pace and the other is starting to pay for surviving it.

If you pause the feeling of that instant, it is all pressure. RYU-X in red steps into the exchange with no hesitation, catches AKIRA's attempted movement, and slices through the space before AKIRA can stabilize. The blue fighter is driven rightward, closer to the arena's edge, his guard late and his balance compromised. In the first third, that is a terrible sign. RYU-X is not reacting out of panic; he is punishing on schedule. AKIRA is already being made to pay for every breath.

Mira and the second masked twin clash under the enormous holographic soda billboard as rain begins to fall through the neon light. The twin flicks three razor charms from her sleeve, aiming not for Mira but for the billboard's maintenance cords. Mira reads the trick and sprints up the wet wall using the stacked crates as steps. When the cords snap, the glowing vinyl screen peels downward like a luminous curtain. The twin expects Mira to be swallowed by it, but Mira punches both hands through the falling material, grabs the twin's shoulders through the screen, and pulls her into a muffled clinch. They become silhouettes thrashing inside a giant blinking soda bottle advertisement. The twin drives a knee up, denting Mira's ribs, yet Mira clamps one foot on a crate and spins. The vinyl wraps around them twice, binding the twin's arms tighter than Mira's. Mira releases at the last instant, letting the trapped twin tumble across the soaked pavement inside the glowing billboard skin, sliding to a stop beneath the slogan.

Toma's counter with the broken neon sign looked reckless until the last second. A lightning-fast swordswoman named Veyra forced him backward across the roof's advertising gantry, her blade tapping sparks from the metal rail with each feint. Toma kept retreating until his heel found the dangling sign for Lucky Crane Arcade, half torn loose from an earlier explosion. When Veyra lunged for his throat, he leaned backward over open air and let the cut shear the final cable above him. The neon crane dropped. Toma caught the lower tube with both hands, swung under it, and kicked Veyra's sword arm from below as the sign fell between them. The glowing tube shattered in a shower of blue sparks, but the timing knocked her blade clean out of line. Toma landed on the far side of the gantry with burned palms and a stupid grin, while Veyra's sword spun down into the crowd netting.

Mira’s scarf becomes a weapon only once, during her frantic exchange with Captain Orro near the escalators frozen mid-rise. Orro keeps using the escalator’s jagged metal steps to anchor his boots, turning every sword swing into a descending avalanche. Mira cannot climb toward him without being chopped down. She lets her long red scarf trail into the moving handrail groove, then slashes the emergency brake with a stolen ticket punch. The handrail jerks backward, yanking the scarf taut across Orro’s sword arm just as he raises it. Mira springs up three steps, wraps the free end around his wrist, and drops her full weight off the escalator’s side. The scarf tightens into a lever rather than a choke, twisting Orro’s arm behind his back and forcing the sword point into the rubber belt. The blade lodges there. Mira swings beneath the escalator, kicks his boot from its anchored notch, and the captain tumbles down the steps in a clattering armored roll, leaving his sword humming in the trapped handrail.

I swear the whole arena leaned with AKIRA when it happened. The fight was already in its grinding middle, that ugly phase where the fresh shine is gone and every breath sounds expensive. RYU-X, bright red and ruthless, carved through the space between them with a fast, cruel arc. AKIRA’s blue form took it badly—his guard buckled, his body twisted, and he was pushed to the right as if the floor itself had started sliding under him. He didn’t collapse, but honestly, that made it worse. He stayed up in that stubborn AKIRA way, dragging himself back into stance while looking more battered than he wanted anyone to notice. RYU-X saw it. Everyone saw it. The momentum had a color, and it was red.

Okay, I am a RYU-X loyalist, and even I have to admit that was a nasty turn. We were in the middle stretch, the part where red usually starts finding counters, but instead AKIRA was the one walking him down. RYU-X kept giving up tiny bits of ground, trying to reset, and AKIRA kept taking those tiny bits like rent. Then came the downward blast. RYU-X was looking for something in front of him, and AKIRA punished from high, clipping him clean and forcing his whole body to recoil toward the right side of the arena. I hated how loud the AKIRA fans got, but they were not wrong. That contact did not just hurt RYU-X; it made him look worn. He was still in the match, sure, but AKIRA was steering it.

From an AKIRA fan’s perspective, this one hurt to watch. He’d survived the opening exchanges, but the middle of the bout had become a slow squeeze, and RYU-X was the one doing the squeezing. AKIRA tried to hold center, tried to make red respect him, but RYU-X came through with a slicing blast that slipped past what was left of his timing. AKIRA recoiled and was shoved toward the right-hand boundary, not by choice, not as a tactical retreat, but because the force left him no alternative. His blue aura still flared, but it looked thinner, more defensive. RYU-X wasn’t chasing a comeback; he was building a lead, and AKIRA was being made to pay for every inch.

Captain Sable had one terrifying exchange where he nearly ended Juno with style instead of brute force. He tossed his saber into the air and fired a bullet at its hilt, causing the blade to spin like a silver propeller across the ruined platform. Juno ducked, but the saber chopped through the support ropes of a hanging advertisement blimp shaped like a smiling dumpling. The blimp dropped toward him, blocking his view. Sable used that blind spot to rush low, revolver empty but bayonet out, aiming for Juno's knee. Juno noticed the shadow too late, so he slapped both palms onto the dumpling blimp's painted face and inflated his breath technique into it.
