The sagging prop ballooned violently, its grin stretching into a nightmare. Sable's bayonet punched into rubber instead of flesh, stuck, and the rebound snapped the rifle stock into his own jaw. Juno rolled over the blimp's top, caught Sable's airborne saber by the guard, and used the flat of it to swat Sable sideways into a popcorn cart, showering the captain in popping kernels and sparks.

The commentator in my head went silent for half a second because the contact was that blunt. RYU-X, wrapped in red aggression, steps forward while the fight is still young and sends a tight punch straight into AKIRA’s defense. AKIRA’s blue frame buckles, not dramatically enough to call it a collapse, but enough to show the punishment stacking. He slides toward the right-hand edge, heels dragging, guard rattled. RYU-X is the hunter here. AKIRA isn’t exchanging evenly; he’s being pushed, physically and mentally, before the match has even reached its middle stride.

The sequence had that awful inevitability where you realize one fighter is not merely attacking but steering the entire scene. AKIRA was drifting into survival mode already, even though the battle was only in its opening portion. He reached for a response, perhaps to break the pressure, and RYU-X answered with a perfectly timed steel sweep across his line. The contact snapped AKIRA's body to the side and dragged the action toward the right-hand perimeter. What mattered wasn't just the wound or the spark shower; it was the positioning. RYU-X made AKIRA give up more space. Blue was being compressed, scratched up, made smaller. Red, meanwhile, advanced with that calm predator rhythm, as if every defensive twitch from AKIRA was another invitation.

I was screaming for AKIRA, so yeah, this one hurt. He had survived so much by that point, but you could see the fatigue in every little flinch. RYU-X did not give him a breath. Red just stepped in, bullied the space, and dropped a crushing attack from above, straight over AKIRA's last bit of defense. AKIRA folded under it and got forced toward the far right side, not flying cleanly so much as being driven there, like the floor itself was dragging him into trouble. It was the final stretch, and my guy in blue was clearly running out of answers. RYU-X looked mean, sharp, and fully in control.

From my seat behind the blue banners, it felt like the whole duel had been tilting this way for a while, and then Akira finally made it obvious. He stepped in first, shoulder low, arm shooting straight through the tiny opening in Ryu-X's guard. The hit snapped the red fighter backward, not clean off his feet, but enough that his boots scraped and skidded toward the boundary on the right. This was not early testing anymore; by the middle of the fight Ryu-X already looked chipped apart, breathing too hard, reacting too late. Akira was the one choosing the distance, choosing the timing, and that stabbing impact was him herding Ryu-X exactly where he wanted him.

The crowd noise swallowed everything when Akira connected. I remember the blue flash first, then Ryu-X’s red silhouette buckling as if the ground jumped up through him. This was already well into the contest, after Ryu-X had taken enough punishment that his reactions were coming half a breath late. Akira, meanwhile, looked sharper with every exchange. He drove the blow through Ryu-X’s guard and shoved him across the platform, sending him skidding toward the right edge while dust curled around his feet. It was the kind of impact that makes the audience lean the same direction as the victim. Ryu-X tried to stop himself, arms flaring, one knee dipping, but he couldn’t cancel the force. Akira owned that moment completely: advancing, pressing, herding him into danger. Ryu-X wasn’t finished, but he was being ground down in public.

At the edge of the roof, Senji and Nero trade blows while tiles slide into the courtyard below. Nero feints a punch and instead clamps both hands around Senji’s jacket, trying to hurl him over the eaves. Senji lets himself be lifted but hooks one finger through the tiny metal ring on Nero’s chest harness. As Nero throws, Senji twists sideways and the ring catches on a roof nail jutting from a broken tile. For one breath, Nero is tethered to the roof while Senji keeps flying. Senji rips free of his own jacket mid-throw, leaving it in Nero’s fists, and lands on the curved end of a decorative dragon gutter. The gutter bends under his weight, springs back, and launches him straight at Nero’s side. Nero tears the harness ring loose just in time to turn, but all he sees is Senji’s bare shoulder crashing into his ribs. Both fighters skid along the roofline, shedding tiles like scales from a wounded beast.

From the announcer’s desk, this was the first clear sign that AKIRA was dictating the match. The fight was still in its early stretch when blue stepped in instead of circling away, lifted that knee through RYU-X’s guard, and caught him clean in the body. Red didn’t just flinch; he was shoved backward by the impact, boots scraping toward the right boundary like the whole arena had tilted. AKIRA followed through with forward pressure, shoulders square, while RYU-X looked forced to spend more energy just staying upright. It was not a finishing moment yet, but it made the balance obvious: AKIRA was pressing, and RYU-X was already getting softened up.

Toma's duel with the silver-haired archer occurred on top of the stalled sky tram, with the city lights spinning far below. The archer fired three glowing arrows in a staggered rhythm, forcing Toma toward the tram's rounded edge. Toma batted the first aside with his bracer, let the second graze his scarf, and seemed trapped by the third, which curved to follow him. At the last breath, he jumped straight up and kicked the tram's emergency hatch shut beneath him. The hatch bounced off its spring and popped open again like a metal tongue. Toma landed on it, catapulted sideways, and the tracking arrow chased the scarf he had deliberately unclasped midjump. The arrow pinned the empty scarf to an antenna mast while Toma crashed shoulder-first into the archer, sweeping both of them into a rolling clinch across the roof.

From my seat it felt like the match had barely finished introducing itself when Akira in blue decided the pace was his. Ryu-X, already giving up little steps and breathing like the pressure was heavier than expected, tried to plant near center. Akira dipped under him and carved at the legs with a low, fast kick that caught clean. The red fighter's stance buckled sideways, and he was shoved skidding toward the right side of the arena. It was not a huge finishing moment yet, more like an early warning sign: Akira was pressing forward, taking ground, and Ryu-X was already being made to look tired and reactive.

I swear the sound came before my brain understood what happened. We were all packed near the aisle, and RYU-X was pushing forward, red aura flickering like a warning light. AKIRA, poor guy, had been defending forever, and by then he looked less like he was choosing where to go and more like he was being herded. Then RYU-X snapped upward and brought the blow down over AKIRA's head. It landed with this heavy, awful thud. AKIRA slid toward the right end of the arena, bent almost sideways from the pressure. Everyone around me went quiet for half a second because it was obvious: this was near the end, RYU-X was the hunter, and AKIRA was almost out of room.

Nami had only one chance to use the aquarium tank, and she made it memorable. Vex threw her through the noodle shop window, and she rolled between overturned stools with soup dripping from her sleeve. Vex followed with a spear-hand thrust bright enough to leave a blue trail. Nami ducked behind the decorative tank full of moonfish, not to hide, but to bait him. His strike pierced the glass. The tank exploded outward, water, fish, pebbles, and a tiny ceramic castle blasting across the tiles. Nami spun under the wave, hooked one hand behind Vex’s neck, and shoved his face into the oncoming flood at the same time she swept his front foot. He slipped on the aquarium gravel, lost the spear-hand shape, and slammed chin-first onto the counter. The moonfish sailed over him in glittering arcs while Nami caught the little castle and cracked it against the back of his helmet, a humiliating bonus hit that made the crowd gasp more than the actual takedown.

Okay, as someone screaming at the screen, this was the moment where I started going, “AKIRA, please move left, please do anything.” The match was already in its middle stretch and you could tell blue was getting dulled down, not broken yet, but definitely sanded away. RYU-X, in red, spun into him like he’d been waiting for that exact angle all round. It wasn’t some clean heroic exchange either; it looked mean. AKIRA’s shoulders jerked, his footing scattered, and suddenly he was being pushed sideways toward the right side like the arena itself was helping RYU-X trap him. Red kept advancing with that predator energy, while AKIRA looked like he was trying to remember where the open floor had gone. Momentum was completely on RYU-X’s side there.

Coach perspective? AKIRA’s problem here is that he lets RYU-X decide the lane. Mid-fight, when you’re already worn, you cannot give an aggressive opponent a clean turning angle. But that’s exactly what happens. RYU-X steps in from red’s side of the rhythm, rotates hard, and his leg comes around with enough torque to knock AKIRA off his center. AKIRA tries to hold shape, but he’s late. Not catastrophically late, just tired-late, which is worse because it means the decline has been building. He gets driven toward the right boundary instead of absorbing in place. That tells me his base is compromised. RYU-X recognizes it instantly and keeps the pressure pointed that direction. If I’m in AKIRA’s corner, I’m yelling for lateral escape and a reset. If I’m in RYU-X’s corner, I’m telling him to keep steering him there, because blue is starting to fold under repeated pressure.

I swear the whole row around me stood up at once when Akira lunged in. It wasn’t some giant windup either, which made it nastier. One second Ryu-X was trying to hold his ground in red, the next Akira’s palm cracked into him and all that force just shoved him across the floor toward the right edge. We’re still in the early chunk of the battle, but Ryu-X already looks like he’s been made to answer too many questions. He tries to dig in, but Akira keeps coming forward like he can smell the fatigue. That shove felt less like a single hit and more like a warning: Akira owns the center, and Ryu-X is being pushed out of the story.

Master Hoshin’s strangest exchange comes when he is surrounded by the masked triplets after they crawl back from the pond dripping and furious. They rush him together this time, abandoning rhythm for a messy tackle. Hoshin stands beside a rack of ceremonial fans and plucks one open with a snap. The first triplet laughs at the paper fan until Hoshin angles it beneath the courtyard lamps, flashing reflected light into his wet mask lenses. The blinded attacker bumps the second. Hoshin closes the fan and taps the third triplet’s knee, folding him neatly to the ground. The second triplet swings anyway, but Hoshin slips the folded fan inside the sleeve of the punch, pinning cloth to wrist. He then opens the fan again. The sudden spread twists the sleeve around the attacker’s arm like a soft vice, turning the punch into a harmless bow. Hoshin steps aside, and the blinded first triplet barrels into both brothers, knocking the fan from his hand only after it has done all its work.

Nami used the collapsed planetarium screen for a trick nobody expected. Oren had her pressed against the southern wall, each stomp from his iron boots cracking tiles and sending chunks up like shrapnel. She retreated until her heel touched the torn canvas screen lying in a heap. As Oren lunged with both fists together, Nami kicked rainwater across the canvas, then snapped it upward with a wave motion. The soaked screen billowed between them like a dark sail, swallowing Oren’s punch and wrapping around his arms. He tried to tear through it, but the old projection paint on the fabric stuck to his gauntlets. Nami dove under the hanging cloth, slid between his planted feet, and pulled the screen’s lower cord as she passed. The canvas cinched around Oren’s torso, momentarily turning him into a thrashing cocoon painted with faded stars. Nami popped up behind him and flicked one finger, sending a ribbon of water into his ear to ruin his balance without seriously hurting him.

Okay, tactics-nerd read: RYU-X uses the opening phase to compress space, and this exchange is the proof. AKIRA is not losing because of one giant mistake; he’s losing because red keeps forcing him to defend in a straight line. On this entry, RYU-X closes with a direct stabbing motion through the center lane. AKIRA’s guard is late and narrow, so the contact drives into him and converts immediately into positional gain. The result is AKIRA being marched toward the right-side limit, unable to pivot out before the pressure has already moved him. RYU-X remains the active player, initiating and following through. AKIRA, meanwhile, looks progressively drained, stuck reacting instead of creating.

Okay, frame it without the hype: during the first phase, AKIRA had initiative, and RYU-X’s defensive options were narrowing. The blue fighter stepped in at close range and delivered a knee that connected solidly enough to displace RYU-X’s whole body line. Red was forced backward, not diagonally into safety, but toward the right edge, which is a terrible place to be when the opponent is already marching you down. RYU-X was not out of the fight, but the wear was visible in the way he yielded space after contact. AKIRA’s offense was not random pressure; it was pressure that was converting into position.

Here’s what killed me about that moment: it was not some giant cinematic finisher, but it had the weight of one because of when it happened. The fight was sitting in that dangerous middle portion where the first burst of adrenaline is gone and the real cost starts showing. Akira, all blue and stubborn, still had fight in him, but he was no longer moving like the guy who could answer every threat. His reactions were a fraction slower, his stance a little too narrow, his attempts to reset constantly interrupted. RYU-X, meanwhile, looked energized by every inch he stole. He pressed forward in red, shoulders square, refusing to let Akira circle out. Then he came in tight and drove the point of his elbow into Akira with a compact, punishing motion. No wasted spin, no dramatic windup, just a heavy collision at close range. Akira’s torso snapped from the impact and he was forced sideways, sliding toward the right side of the stage like the whole battlefield had tilted under him. That was the real cruelty of it: RYU-X wasn’t merely landing strikes, he was shaping where the next exchange would happen. Akira got shoved closer to the margin, where escapes become predictable and counters get cramped. You could see the fatigue in the way he tried to plant his feet and failed to fully stop the drift. RYU-X stayed on top of him, clearly the aggressor, turning pressure into damage and damage into position. By the end of that single elbow, the audience knew Akira was being ground down.

Hana used the quietest attack of the whole brawl when Kaito paused near the shrine alcove built into the old station wall. He expected her umbrella blade, her cane thrust, or some hidden dart. Instead she tossed a paper charm into the air, and it drifted lazily between them. Kaito cut it in half on reflex. The sliced charm released a puff of white powder that smelled like crushed mint and erased the sound of Hana's footsteps by coating the floor. She crossed the distance in silence and pressed two fingers under his sword elbow, aiming for a nerve pinch. Kaito felt the pressure a fraction too late. His hand spasmed open, and his sword began to fall. Before it hit the floor, he stamped on the flat of the blade with his boot, flipping the hilt upward into his other hand. The awkward left-handed slash forced Hana to abandon the nerve hold. She leaned back so far her hair brushed the floor, then swept his standing leg with the folded umbrella. Kaito hopped over the sweep, but the motion put him directly in front of the shrine bell, which Hana kicked once to stun him with its ringing boom.

Oro's one-time counter happened in the broken glass canopy above the station clock. Rika had chased him up there, and he tried to vanish by splitting into six golden afterimages, each darting along a different steel rib. Rika guessed wrong twice, punching through ghosts that burst into feathers, and Oro used the second miss to dive at her spine with twin hook knives. She could not turn in time. So she dropped. Not fell, exactly; she slammed her open palm against the glass under her feet and flash-froze a circular patch. The sudden cold made the pane contract and crack like a ringing bell. Rika slid backward through the hole she had created, letting Oro's knives slice only her trailing ribbon. As he overshot, she caught that severed ribbon in one hand, looped it around his ankle, and used her drop to yank him out of his dive. Oro crashed sideways into the clock face, knocking the minute hand loose. The hand swung down like a pendulum and clipped his shoulder, pinning him against the twelve until his afterimages flickered out.

Not gonna lie, I started this fight clowning on RYU-X for being too straightforward, but that late hit shut me up. There was nothing subtle about it, and that was the point. AKIRA looked like he was running on fumes, blue glow dim and twitchy, and RYU-X simply crashed through the front door. His fist caught AKIRA hard enough to send him skidding toward the right edge of the screen, like a cursor being dragged by an angry hand. The red guy had the whole arena leaning with him. AKIRA did not tumble into a comeback pose; he stumbled, absorbed it badly, and kept losing space. RYU-X was pressing the issue and everybody knew it.

I was in the crowd on the right side, so from my seat it looked like AKIRA was being herded straight at us. RYU-X kept coming, not rushing wild, just mean and patient. Near the end, when AKIRA already had that sag in his stance, RYU-X twitched his body like the big hit was arriving from the front. AKIRA flinched, and that was all red needed. He cut the angle, made blue defend empty air, and forced him another few steps back until his boots were almost scraping the edge. Everyone around me groaned because you could see AKIRA knew he had been tricked, but he did not have the energy left to reset.

I swear from my seat it looked unfairly quick. The match had barely gotten into its first stretch, and RYU-X was already bullying the lane. AKIRA tried to plant, maybe thinking there was room to breathe, then red just flicked that tight knuckle shot right down the middle. No windup, no drama, just impact. AKIRA’s blue frame jolted and slid toward the far-right side like the floor had tilted under him. That’s when the crowd around me started making that low noise, because everyone could feel it: RYU-X had momentum, and AKIRA was losing pieces of himself every time he gave ground. Not done, not broken, but definitely being worn thinner way too early.

From the commentary desk, this was where the ending started to feel inevitable. Akira tried to answer with blue sparks still flickering around him, but RYU-X had the cleaner read. The red fighter planted himself, absorbed the contact on a tight shell, and immediately turned that stop into forward pressure. It was not flashy in the usual way, but it was brutal: Akira’s body slid and stumbled toward the right boundary as if the stage itself had tilted. Late in the fight, after so much punishment, Akira did not have the legs to reset. RYU-X kept advancing, shoulders square, claiming space. Akira was still alive, still resisting, but the momentum had clearly swung red.

Okay, I rewatched that little sequence way too many times because it looks simple at full speed, but it is actually nasty. The match is still young, not even close to the desperate final stuff, and RYU-X already has that faint “I need a second” posture. His red aura is flickering tight around him, like he is conserving, while AKIRA is bouncing with that predator calm. Then AKIRA just cuts in. Not a normal run-up. There is this blue smear across the floor, a blink of empty air where he was, and then he is suddenly chest-to-chest with RYU-X, slamming through the guard and making him travel. The important part is that RYU-X does not choose to backpedal. He gets shoved, shoved hard, toward the right-hand limit of the fighting space, and his body language changes mid-slide. First he tries to plant. Then he realizes planting is not working. Then he turns his shoulder and kind of rides the force so he does not get flattened. That is when I knew AKIRA had the opening phase under control. He was not fishing anymore; he had found a rhythm that was chewing RYU-X up one exchange at a time. RYU-X still has power, sure, and you can see the danger if AKIRA gets reckless. But in this specific instant, red is being marched backward, blue is dictating distance, and the audience noise spikes because everybody can feel the pressure tilting.

Okay, tactical read: this wasn’t just damage, it was positioning. In the closing run, AKIRA forced entry while RYU-X was already giving ground. The blue fighter’s strike came from an angle that punished the red one’s weakened stance, catching him before he could pivot out. Because RYU-X’s weight was too high and his legs looked dead, the contact didn’t just stagger him; it redirected him toward the right edge. AKIRA immediately owned the center after it, which matters more than people think. RYU-X had less room, worse balance, and no initiative. The sequence screamed endgame pressure: aggressor advancing, defender fading, boundary turning into a threat.

As a former gym rat watching that exchange, I loved how simple and mean it was. No wasted motion from AKIRA. Late in the fight, when people start throwing wide because they’re tired, he stayed disciplined. RYU-X was already fading, shoulders heavy, reacting half a breath too slow. AKIRA pressed forward, planted, and sent a laser-straight fist into him, catching him square and forcing him to give ground again. The red fighter didn’t just stumble; he got walked backward by the force of it, sliding toward the right boundary with nowhere friendly left to retreat. That told the whole story of the final stretch. AKIRA still had enough snap to dictate range, while RYU-X was being chipped down into pure defense.

RYU-X was bullying him. That’s the recap. Still early in the match, AKIRA should’ve had space to reset, but red kept eating that space. Then came the clean forward punch: compact, hot, and mean. AKIRA caught it and got shoved toward the right boundary like he’d lost control of his own footing. You could see him trying to dig in, but he was already worn from the pressure. RYU-X didn’t just land damage there; he moved the whole fight where he wanted it.

If you slowed it down, you could see the cruelty of the timing. RYU-X inhaled, maybe hoping for half a second to breathe, and AKIRA took that half second away. Blue surged forward in the final exchanges, arm carving a bright path through the space RYU-X needed to defend. Red caught the impact across his front and was thrown off balance, sliding toward the right boundary with his boots fighting for traction. The old RYU-X would have turned that into a counter. This exhausted version simply endured it. AKIRA’s momentum didn’t break; he kept his center, kept his angle, kept the pressure. It felt like the fight narrowing to one conclusion.

Listen, as a commentator, you live for the giant explosions, but the cruelest stuff is usually compact. In the closing stretch, AKIRA didn’t need some grand windup. The blue fighter stepped into range, cut off RYU-X’s escape, and snapped a quick fist right through the red guard. It was the kind of clean contact that barely lasts on screen, yet it told the whole story: AKIRA had the rhythm, AKIRA had the initiative, and RYU-X was running out of answers. The impact slid him toward the far-right side of the arena, not enough to look theatrical at first, but enough to steal space. That was the important part. RYU-X wasn’t choosing where to stand anymore. His stance buckled, his guard came back up too slowly, and every inch he lost made the situation worse. Late fight, tired legs, pressure building—AKIRA was not merely hitting him, he was compressing the entire match into that one sharp, punishing shove toward the edge.

I don’t think RYU-X lost because of that single contact, but that was the moment the room understood he was being worn thin. AKIRA’s offense had a grinding quality by then. He was not chasing applause; he was removing options. The open-handed blow landed square and sent RYU-X across toward the right limit of the arena. What stood out to me was RYU-X’s recovery, or the lack of it. Earlier, he would have snapped back with fire. Here he staggered, shoulders turning before his feet caught up, as if the hit had separated his body from his will. AKIRA kept advancing, posture forward, expression locked. The balance had shifted blue, and everyone knew red was running out of space.

Veyl's one-off throw against Mako was savage and mechanical. Mako had been laughing too loudly after the umbrella pile incident, so Veyl stalked in through the steam with his ruined glaive shortened into a jagged staff. Mako swung first, a broad haymaker bright with orange aura. Veyl stepped inside the punch, let it skim his cheek, and trapped Mako's forearm under his armpit. With his other hand he hooked the back of Mako's belt, but he did not lift. He stamped the butt of the broken staff onto a moving conveyor belt used for cargo crates. The belt caught the staff and dragged it backward, turning it into a sudden lever against Mako's trapped arm. Mako's feet left the ground as if the station itself had flipped him. Veyl guided the motion into a brutal corkscrew throw, sending Mako spinning over the conveyor guardrail and into a stack of foam-wrapped porcelain dragons. The dragons did not simply break; their painted eyes flashed, and each one released a stored ceremonial firecracker. Mako vanished in a rattling cloud of pops, smoke, and dragon confetti while Veyl calmly shook feeling back into his bruised cheek.

Yumi's exchange with the masked puppeteer happened beneath the parade dragon, a huge segmented prop carried on poles by panicking performers. The puppeteer controlled razor wires from rings on his fingers, making the dragon's cloth body lash around Yumi like a living serpent. She ran with the movement instead of against it, ducking under one silk coil and stepping onto a carrier's abandoned shoulder pole. As the puppeteer snapped his fingers to tighten the wires, Yumi vaulted along the pole and grabbed the dragon's papier-mache jaw. Her weight pulled the head down, crossing two of the puppeteer's wires over a third. He tried to unwind them, but Yumi kicked the dragon's jaw shut on the knot. The crossed wires yanked his own hands together, and she landed in front of him just long enough to flick his forehead with one finger, toppling him backward into the drum line.

At the construction pit behind the festival stage, Sadao backs Juno toward a suspended crane hook swinging in the wind. Sadao keeps slashing with his iron fan in half-moon cuts, steering Juno step by step until the hook is behind his spine. Juno appears not to notice, raising his forearms to absorb each strike. When Sadao lunges for the final cut, Juno suddenly crouches and slaps the hook with his palm. The hook swings over his head and catches Sadao's open fan through one of its ribs. For a second Sadao is tethered to the crane cable by his own weapon. Juno grabs the cable and throws his weight backward. The crane hook yanks Sadao's arm high, spinning him onto his toes. Sadao avoids a dislocated shoulder only by leaping with the pull, flipping over Juno, and landing on a stack of cement bags. He tears the fan free, but the motion dumps the top bag open, coating his black coat in gray dust and giving Juno a clear target in the dim pit.

Okay, everyone keeps talking about the big power hits later, but this early low takedown attempt from Akira is the moment where I started worrying for Ryu-X. Akira had already been crowding him, blue constantly stepping into red's space, making Ryu-X guard, retreat, readjust, guard again. Then Akira goes down low and swipes through the support leg area so cleanly that Ryu-X's whole frame jolts sideways. It was not a total wipeout, but it was worse in a different way: Ryu-X stayed conscious, stayed moving, and still got bullied across the floor toward the right side like he had no say in the geography. That is the kind of exchange that drains a fighter. He had to scramble, twist, catch himself, and recover his stance while Akira was already chasing the advantage. In the first third of the fight, you want to establish rhythm. Ryu-X instead had his rhythm kicked out from underneath him. Akira looked sharp, mean, and proactive; Ryu-X looked like he was starting to feel all the small losses stacking up.

Rika’s first clean opening came beside the toppled takoyaki stall, where hot sauce was still dripping in red commas across the tile. Juno rushed her with twin elbow blades tucked low, expecting Rika to leap backward as usual. Instead, Rika snatched the vendor’s iron skewer rack with both hands, slid it under Juno’s wrists, and used the rack like a temporary ladder rung. She stepped onto it, forcing Juno’s arms down, then jumped off his shoulder in the same motion. The rack clanged loose, Juno’s balance tipped forward, and Rika’s heel snapped down onto the back of his knee. He did not fall dramatically; he folded in a sudden, ugly crouch, just long enough for her to flip over the stall canopy and escape the counter-swing of his blades.

Tetsu and Rook met in the central concourse with no tricks at first, just a collision that rang through the broken roof beams. Tetsu's magnetized fist slammed into Rook's stone guard, and both men dug trenches in the floor rather than give ground. Tetsu grinned and activated the bracers' pull toward the steel skeleton under the tiles, trying to drag Rook face-first into the concourse. Rook answered by shedding the stone plates from his forearms, letting them drop like dead weight so his hands were suddenly free and faster than Tetsu expected. He caught Tetsu's punching wrist, stepped inside, and rotated the arm into a brutal standing arm bar. Tetsu's knees bent, but he refused to fall. Instead he magnetized Rook's discarded stone plates by the rebar embedded inside them. The plates rose behind Rook like dull gray fists and hammered into his back. The impacts loosened the arm bar just enough for Tetsu to spin out. He left one bracer in Rook's grip on purpose; when Rook looked down at the empty shell, the bracer snapped back to Tetsu and struck Rook under the chin.

Akira was hunting. That was the thing you could feel midway through the clash: blue pressing, red surviving. Ryu-X tried to brace near center-right, but Akira slipped into range and drove a straight, piercing strike into him. The force folded Ryu-X's stance and shoved him sliding toward the far side, the right boundary coming up behind him like a wall. Ryu-X did not collapse, but he looked drained, his counter delayed and his guard sagging. Akira stayed planted forward, the aggressor, making that single hit feel less like a lucky connection and more like the next step in a slow squeeze.

At the burning curtain stage, the exchange between Pasha and Ren is decided by a single costume ribbon. Ren’s flame aura has set the velvet backdrop alight, and he advances through the falling embers with both palms raised. Pasha retreats while flicking sewing needles from her sleeves, but Ren melts them in midair. He corners her beside a rack of festival costumes and sweeps one flaming hand across it, turning masks and robes into a wall of fire. Pasha snatches a long blue ribbon from a dancer’s outfit just before it catches. Ren laughs because cloth is the worst possible weapon against him. Pasha throws the ribbon anyway, but not at his body. It loops around the overhead sprinkler pipe, which has been hissing uselessly since the ceiling cracked. Ren lunges to burn through it. Pasha yanks the ribbon, and the pipe tears open above him. A sheet of water crashes down, smothering the fire aura for one heartbeat. In that heartbeat, Pasha slides in on wet knees, wraps the soaked ribbon around Ren’s forearm, and twists it behind his back. The ribbon steams, but does not burn before she drives him shoulder-first into the costume rack.

Captain Orro’s most theatrical mistake is charging Jun beneath the old split-flap departure board. The board is broken, but hundreds of black-and-white destination tiles still clatter wildly, flipping names of cities that no longer exist. Orro uses the noise to cover his armored approach, raising his halberd for a chopping blow. Jun cannot hear him, but he watches the reflections on the polished floor: every flip tile flashes a tiny black rectangle in rhythm, except one patch that is blocked by Orro’s shadow. Jun drops at the last instant. The halberd buries itself in the wooden information desk. Jun kicks the desk’s crank mechanism, and the departure board shudders into a furious cycle. Loose tiles rain down like square hail. Orro lifts his shield overhead, blind beneath the metal. Jun slides under the shield’s rim on his back, jams a fallen destination tile into the hinge of Orro’s knee armor, and rolls away. When Orro tries to step, the tile locks the joint stiff. His next swing turns into a wobbling one-legged spin that ends with his helmet wedged in the board’s maintenance ladder.

As someone who rewatches footwork more than explosions, this moment was all about territory. AKIRA’s blue silhouette is already drifting backward in the opening stretch, not because he wants to bait, but because RYU-X’s red pressure keeps taking options away. RYU-X narrows the angle, shoulders square, and sends a direct fist down the centerline. It lands with that harsh fiery snap, and AKIRA’s stance compresses. The force carries him rightward, closer to the edge of the fighting space, which is exactly where you don’t want to be against an attacker who’s still fresh. AKIRA tries to stabilize on the slide, but he’s reacting late. RYU-X, meanwhile, doesn’t overextend; he simply steps into command. The exchange says everything: early match, red advancing, blue getting sanded down.

The arena camera never gives enough credit to how much territory Akira stole there. At that stage of the battle, still in the opening third, Ryu-X had not collapsed, but he was already being sanded down by repeated pressure. Every time he tried to reset, Akira stepped into him. Every time he looked for a counter, Akira made him defend first. So when the blue fighter suddenly dropped his center of gravity, it was less a surprise attack and more the natural consequence of all that harassment. He sent a quick, low sweeping motion across Ryu-X's path, catching the red fighter during a half-step. That timing was everything. Ryu-X's lead leg had no chance to root, his hips turned badly, and the rest of him had to follow the mistake. He slid and stumbled to the right, not with heroic resistance, but with that ugly forced travel fighters hate because it means the opponent is controlling both your body and the space around you. Akira's posture afterward said plenty: he was not relieved, he was expectant, already prepared to keep pressing. Ryu-X, on the other hand, looked like he was taking damage in layers. Not just physical damage, either. There was fatigue in the delayed guard, frustration in the way he tried to plant, and a flicker of panic as the boundary crept closer. For an early exchange, it was a statement: blue was dictating tempo, red was losing room, and the right side of the arena was starting to feel like a trap.

I’m going to sound dramatic, but the hit felt like a door slamming shut on AKIRA’s options. The battle hadn’t reached its middle yet, and already RYU-X was the one stalking, pressing, and demanding answers. AKIRA was absorbing too much, backing up too often, and when RYU-X finally committed to that direct fiery punch, blue couldn’t stop the consequences. The fist landed with a clean forward drive, and AKIRA slid toward the right edge of the screen, body bent back and feet fighting for purchase. It wasn’t just pain; it was displacement. RYU-X turned one strike into position, pressure, and psychological advantage. AKIRA looked like he was starting to feel the accumulation, while red looked ready to keep pouring it on.

From a camera operator’s point of view, the movement was perfect and terrifying. The frame had Akira drifting right already, battered and breathing hard, then RYU-X stepped into the foreground in red and cut him off. Akira made contact first, but the image told the truth: RYU-X’s stance barely buckled. He caught it, locked it, and the next motion was all forward drive. I had to pan right as Akira got forced back, not blasted away in one clean arc, but bullied across the floor. That is what made it feel late-fight heavy. There was no wasted animation, no big windup, just a hard denial that became a push. Akira’s blue trail dragged behind him like a fading comet while RYU-X kept eating up space.

Captain Sable's strangest loss came from underestimating the station clock's fallen minute hand. After prying himself free of the popcorn cart, he challenged Hana in the open concourse and shot the clock hand off the floor with a ricochet, making it spin toward her like a giant spear. Hana placed a talisman on her sleeve and stiffened the cloth into a shield, but the minute hand punched through and pinned her sleeve to a pillar. Sable advanced, reloading with his teeth. Hana did not pull away. Instead, she whispered a binding phrase into the hollow clock hand, using it as a speaking tube. The words traveled through the metal, came out the other end behind Sable, and activated the tiny paper hands still clinging to his coat from the ticket gate exchange. They yanked his ammunition belt backward. Sable fired, but the sudden pull ruined his aim, and the bullet struck the clock hand's base. The vibration freed Hana's sleeve and launched the hand upward. It flipped once, came down flat, and slapped Sable into the floor like a flyswatter. Hana stepped over him, sleeve torn but expression perfectly composed.

In the concert hall lobby, Nao was cornered beneath a chandelier by Viktor, whose mechanical jaw could bite through steel. He chased her behind a velvet rope barrier, snapping at her ponytail. Nao grabbed one of the brass stanchions and pretended to throw it like a spear. Viktor opened his jaws to catch it. Instead, she tossed only the attached velvet rope, letting the brass post drop at her feet. The rope landed across Viktor’s open mouth, and when his jaws clamped shut they caught the thick fabric between the teeth. Nao kicked the brass post, sending it skidding around his legs in a circle. The rope wound around his ankles, then tightened as the post struck the base of the chandelier display. The impact released the maintenance pulley. The chandelier did not fall; it rose, yanking the rope upward and pulling Viktor into a ridiculous tiptoe bind with his jaw and feet connected by velvet.

Mira's ice exchange begins when Naru cuts through the refrigeration talisman protecting the dessert sculptures, causing swans, towers, and a crystal dragon of carved ice to sweat into the fight. Naru uses the slickening floor to accelerate, skating on the flat of one sandal while his sword tip sketches cold arcs at Mira's waist. She cannot match his blade speed, so she stops trying to stand. She drops onto a silver serving platter, grabs the ice dragon's tail as she slides past, and uses it as a steering handle. Naru slashes the tail off, but that only frees the platter to spin. Mira becomes a whirling disk at ankle height, passing under his next cut and knocking one knee with the platter's raised rim. He recovers by stabbing his sword into the floor as a brake. Mira crashes into the base of the melting swan sculpture, sending its long neck tipping forward. Naru lifts his guard for a falling ice beak; Mira instead pops up behind the swan's body and shoves the whole slippery pedestal into his planted sword, levering it from his grip.

On the stage where idol holograms kept performing through the chaos, Rika faced Sable under a rain of virtual rose petals. Sable launched a thin throwing needle straight at Rika’s forehead, counting on the bright projections to hide its path. Rika slapped the hologram projector with the flat of her palm, skewing the image. The idol’s enormous translucent skirt flickered sideways, making Sable’s needle appear to bend. Sable followed the false line for a fraction of a second, and Rika used that beat to step inside. She did not punch; she yanked the microphone stand from the stage floor, caught the needle in the stand’s coiled cable, and spun it once over her head. The needle whipped back along the cable’s loop and buried itself in Sable’s own trailing scarf, pinning the scarf to a speaker grille with a neat little thunk.

Okay, I swear the crowd collectively leaned right when it happened. We were deep into the finale, everyone’s nerves cooked, and AKIRA just kept pressing forward like he had found a crack in RYU-X’s timing and refused to let it close. Then—snap. A quick blue-gloved pop, straight in, clean on RYU-X. Not a dramatic haymaker, not one of those screen-filling blasts, just a sharp little check that landed exactly when red tried to brace. And somehow that made it worse. RYU-X slid backward toward the right edge, visibly losing territory, and you could feel how exhausted he was. His body answered the hit late, like the command had to travel through static. AKIRA was walking him down at this point, almost measuring him with each step. Earlier, RYU-X might have planted and fired back. Here, in the final stretch, he just got forced closer to the boundary, wearing the whole fight on his posture.

From a fighter’s perspective, RYU-X gave up the worst thing after that impact: space. AKIRA entered close and slammed the knee in at the right time, catching red before he could anchor properly. The result was immediate displacement toward the right-side limit. Early in a match, you can survive a strike like that, sure, but being forced backward so visibly changes how everyone reads you. AKIRA looked like the hunter. RYU-X looked like the man being walked down and made to pay for every step. The damage was not just physical; it was positional, and AKIRA owned that exchange.

For the gamblers in the back, that exchange moved the odds without needing a scoreboard. Early round, fresh crowd noise, lots of fight still ahead, but AKIRA had already made RYU-X look like the one paying interest on every mistake. RYU-X took a half-step back, probably trying to reset along the right lane, and AKIRA read it instantly. Blue closed the gap, dropped low, and hammered upward. RYU-X got clipped under the face and bounced toward the right wall of the arena, limbs trailing a beat behind his torso. The nasty part was how composed AKIRA remained. No wild chase, no panic. He had control. RYU-X had impact shock and less room.

Hana's exchange with Oro at the shrine vending machines was a battle of misdirection. Oro flicked one knife and cut the strap of Hana's charm bag, sending dozens of prepared seals skittering under the machines. He smirked, certain she had lost her ammunition. Hana backed away, hands open, until her heel touched a fallen can of plum soda. Oro lunged for her centerline, blade aimed at her heart. She popped the can with a heel stomp. The pressurized soda geysered upward, sticky and pink, splashing Oro's eyes. He still slashed by instinct, and the knife grazed a lock of her hair. Hana used that severed strand as a brush, dipped it in the soda on her palm, and drew a hasty seal directly onto the vending machine's glass. The machine lit up like a festival lantern. Every bottled tea inside shot forward at once, hammering the glass from within until the front panel burst outward. Oro took the entire wave of cans and bottles to the chest. As he staggered, the machine cheerfully dispensed a single hot coffee onto his head.

From a tournament desk perspective, that exchange said everything about control. Late match, fatigue obvious on RYU-X, AKIRA still pressing. The blue combatant entered with a narrow thrust, clean contact through the front, and the red combatant yielded several steps toward the right-side perimeter. No scramble, no equal trade, no reset. It was forward pressure from AKIRA and forced retreat from RYU-X. You could see RYU-X attempting to brace, but his base had been compromised by all the earlier punishment. AKIRA’s aggression was not reckless; it was targeted, measured, and it shoved the fight exactly where he wanted it.

I watched it like a coach and hated what I saw from AKIRA. His weight was too high, his elbows late, and by that stage of the fight fatigue was making every correction arrive half a breath behind. RYU-X recognized it instantly. He stepped into range and landed a compact, brutal punch that drove through AKIRA's defense and shoved him toward the right boundary. The important detail is that RYU-X did not need a wild windup. He was already in command, already making AKIRA react, so the strike hit like an inevitability. AKIRA's blue energy dragged after him in ragged streaks. RYU-X's red pressure stayed centered and forward. That is what dominance looks like when the match is nearly done.

As someone who actually trains, the scary part was not the flash around AKIRA’s arm, it was the timing. RYU-X’s shoulders had dropped from fatigue, his lead foot was lazy, and he was trying to brace rather than counter. That is when AKIRA closed the lane. Blue entered on a straight line and speared through the center, landing clean enough to make RYU-X’s whole body give way. The red fighter was forced toward the right-side limit, not by theatrics, but by structure breaking under pressure. This was deep in the ending phase, and the initiative was completely on AKIRA’s side.

The sequence reads like a lesson in pressure management. Near the end, AKIRA has already established initiative: forward stance, faster recovery, cleaner entries. RYU-X is operating defensively, and more importantly, he is conceding ground before contact. AKIRA uses that hesitation perfectly. A compact hand strike lands to interrupt RYU-X’s attempt to stabilize, and the result is immediate displacement. The red fighter is pushed toward the right edge of the fighting space, not by brute force alone, but by accumulated fatigue and positional control. That is why the moment matters. A fresh RYU-X probably absorbs it, pivots, and counters. This version is worn down; his base is narrow, his response sluggish, his retreat predictable. AKIRA, in blue, remains the one dictating tempo. The punch functions almost like a punctuation mark on the late-match momentum shift: small contact, big consequence. RYU-X loses room, AKIRA gains certainty, and the arena starts looking much smaller for the fighter in red.

There was a cruel elegance to it. RYU-X, robed in red momentum, closed the distance as though the battle had already granted him ownership of the ground. AKIRA, the blue flame, had diminished into sparks, still bright but visibly losing air. Then came the falling blow, a dark arc from above, landing on AKIRA with the weight of the whole final passage. It did not merely hurt him; it displaced him. He was driven rightward, step and slide and stumble, toward the border where options go to die. The scene felt less like a single attack and more like a verdict. RYU-X advanced. AKIRA endured. The fight narrowed around them.

Hana's exchange with the masked twins happened on the elevated kite bridge, where festival banners whipped hard enough to sound like cracking sails. The twins tried their mirror assault, one diving low with hooked knives while the other sprang from the railing to slash downward. Hana did not block either blade. She stamped on the bridge's rope seam, making the entire walkway tilt three feet to the left. The low twin slid helplessly past her knees, and Hana caught his collar with her parasol handle, using his momentum to yank him into his brother's descent. Their masks clacked together in midair. Before they could separate, she snapped the parasol open beneath them, its reinforced ribs blooming like a shield, and bounced both twins over the railing into a vendor's mountain of plush dragon dolls below.

Nero tries to spear Daigo with the black iron flagstaff torn from the shrine gate. Daigo backpedals across the courtyard, too crowded to sidestep, while the staff point snaps holes through his jacket. At the last thrust, Daigo times the weapon’s flex. He claps his palms around the shaft, not to stop it, but to bend it downward until the iron point bites into a stone lantern base. Nero shoves harder, thinking he has pinned him. Daigo grins and stomps the middle of the trapped staff. The metal bows like a spring, launches the lantern cap into the air, and smacks Nero beneath the chin with the rebounding haft. Before Nero’s knees buckle, the airborne lantern cap drops. Daigo catches it by the rim, spins once, and rams the heavy stone disk into Nero’s chest like an improvised shield bash. Nero tumbles backward through incense smoke, the flagstaff still vibrating in the lantern base behind him.

Mira tried to rescue Juno from the clock-side melee by hurling a broken bench with a gravity push, turning the whole row of seats into a flying barricade. Selene intercepted it with a sheet of mirrors that unfolded from her sleeves like a fan. The bench struck the mirror sheet and appeared to vanish, reflected into a false corridor. For one breath everyone lost track of it. Then the real bench emerged from Selene's blind side, because Mira had bent its path around the mirrors rather than through them. Selene ducked under the returning bench, but the move put her in Juno's range. Juno, half-crouched with one damaged spool, flicked a wire around Selene's waist and pulled. Selene spun with the tug instead of resisting, using the wire as a dance partner's arm. Her rotation carried her inside Juno's guard, and she slapped a mirror charm onto Juno's forehead. Juno froze, seeing a perfect reflection of her next move before she made it. Mira broke the illusion by dropping gravity on a single loose bench leg, which fell upward and knocked the charm off like a thrown baton.

Coach’s read: AKIRA did the smart thing. No fancy reset, no wasted flourish. In the opening portion, while RYU-X was still trying to find rhythm, AKIRA shortened the distance and put the knee right through the center line. That is how you make a red fighter lose space fast. RYU-X absorbed it badly, his weight going behind his heels, and the impact carried him toward the right-side boundary. The important part was not just the strike; it was the body language after. AKIRA stayed hungry and balanced. RYU-X looked like he had to regroup under pressure. Early match or not, blue was already forcing the terms.

Kaito had just slid under the turnstile when Captain Ruga came down on him with both electrified tonfa crossed like scissors. Instead of blocking, Kaito planted one palm on the wet tile, spun his whole body flat like a compass needle, and hooked both ankles around Ruga's leading leg. The sweep did not simply trip him; it twisted Ruga sideways into the coin-operated locker row, making every door pop open in sequence. Ruga tried to recover by jamming a tonfa into the floor, but Kaito kicked the loose helmet rolling nearby into the tonfa's trigger. The weapon discharged into the puddle between them, forcing both fighters to spring apart. Kaito landed on a ticket counter with smoking shoes, while Ruga stood up with locker coupons plastered to his armor, furious and briefly unable to lift his numbed left foot.

Listen, I’ve been on RYU-X’s side all season, so this hurt to admit. But in that final stretch, AKIRA owned him. The blue guy didn’t wait for some opening from heaven; he created it by crowding RYU-X until the red armor looked heavy. Then came that sharp lateral cut, quick enough that RYU-X’s defense seemed to appear a heartbeat too late. The impact twisted him off-line and shoved him toward the far-right limit of the arena. You could feel his options shrink. No spring in the legs, no bite in the counter, no confidence in the guard. AKIRA was still attacking with purpose while RYU-X was negotiating with exhaustion.

I swear the crowd noise dipped for a split second when AKIRA connected. It was that clean. The battle was in its last, desperate phase, and you could see RYU-X trying to hold the line, trying to convince everybody he still had an answer. But AKIRA had seized the rhythm. He was advancing in blue like the fight belonged to him now, and RYU-X, all red and battered, was giving up inches he could not afford. Then AKIRA shot his arm forward in this brutally plain, centerline hit that smashed into RYU-X and sent him skidding toward the right edge of the stage. It wasn’t a flashy turnabout or a lucky clip. It was an aggressor punishing a tired opponent who had been made to block, brace, and retreat for too long. By the time RYU-X was pushed near the side, the mood had changed from “can AKIRA finish?” to “how long can RYU-X keep standing?”

My section was behind the right side, so we saw AKIRA coming toward us before the broadcast probably made it clear. RYU-X had him under pressure in those final exchanges, and AKIRA's retreat line was basically aimed right at our seats. The strike came from over AKIRA's guard, crashing downward, and the force shoved him closer and closer to the boundary near us. You could see his boots scrape for purchase. You could see him try to square up again and not quite manage it. RYU-X followed with that predator posture, red still leaning forward. It was not a lucky connection. It was a late-match squeeze, and AKIRA was the one getting squeezed.

If you freeze it in your memory, the composition is almost cruel: AKIRA advancing from the left in blue, posture compact and certain, while RYU-X in red is already angled backward, too close to being trapped on the right side. This is deep into the closing run of the fight, when exhaustion has made every decision expensive. RYU-X has lost the initiative. You can see it in how he waits for danger instead of creating it. AKIRA does not wait. He steps in and delivers a sharp, linear blow that lands flush and transfers all that forward momentum into RYU-X’s chest and stance. RYU-X is driven across the floor, not dramatically flying away, but shoved with enough authority that the side of the arena suddenly becomes a threat. The hit matters because of where it happens in the momentum arc. Early on, maybe RYU-X absorbs it and fires back. Midway, maybe he rolls with it and circles out. Here, late and worn down, he gets moved. AKIRA is the one asking every question, and RYU-X is running out of answers.

Hibiki’s encounter with the perfume assassin happened inside the luxury cosmetics store, where every bottle was a potential smokescreen. The assassin sprayed a violet mist that made reflections lag a second behind reality, turning the mirrored walls into a maze of false movements. Hibiki closed his eyes, but the scent itself guided the assassin’s blade, curling toward his breath. So Hibiki grabbed a display tray of sample cards and flung them upward. As the cards fluttered, he exhaled sharply through his sleeve, pushing his scent into a fan of paper. The assassin’s blade followed the strongest trace and sliced through three sample cards instead of Hibiki’s throat. Hibiki moved with the empty breath still held in his lungs, stepped behind her, and slammed his palm onto the atomizer in her hand. It sprayed straight down, coating the polished floor beneath her heels. One gentle ankle hook sent her slipping backward into a tower of gift boxes, which collapsed in a sugary avalanche of ribbons and tiny glass testers.

I swear the whole match tilted red right there. We were already deep into the closing minutes, with AKIRA looking like he was holding himself together on pure stubbornness, and RYU-X just smelled it. He came down from above like a falling spear, shoulders and weight aimed straight through AKIRA instead of at him. The hit caught blue clean, folded him backward, and shoved him skidding toward the right boundary like the arena itself was trying to spit him out. AKIRA tried to brace, but his feet barely answered. RYU-X did not pause, did not admire it, did not give him air. That was the scary part. It was not just damage; it was ownership of space. Red was pressing, blue was fading, and the end suddenly felt very close.

From the referee’s angle, it was all about forced movement. The fighters were no longer fresh, and RYU-X was showing accumulated strain in the delay between guard and step. AKIRA advanced with control, then delivered a crushing downward contact that landed over RYU-X’s line of defense. The red fighter absorbed it, but the force redirected him toward the right perimeter. No pause, no mutual reset, no clean separation. AKIRA remained the advancing party, and RYU-X was the one being displaced. In the middle of a fight, that matters more than spectacle. It showed who was commanding the tempo and who was being made to pay for every inch.

The coin storm was not magic, just terrifying accuracy. Sable, the gambler monk, emptied a whole pouch of bronze station tokens into one palm and snapped them at Aiko like shuriken. They rang against pillars, kiosks, and ticket gates, forcing her backward with every metallic flash. Aiko grabbed the nearest object, a round cafeteria tray covered in curry stains, and used it as a shield. Sable adjusted instantly, banking three tokens off the ceiling so they came down behind the tray. Aiko heard the clink above her head and spun the tray flat like a cymbal. The falling tokens skipped off its rim and shot back toward Sable's sandal straps. He avoided the first two with graceful hops, but the third sliced the knot of his left sandal. His next elegant step became a stumble, and Aiko shoulder-checked him into the automatic ticket gate.

I’m the person in the crowd who always roots for the underdog, so this hurt to watch. AKIRA had that blue-hero look, but at this early point he was already being forced backward, and RYU-X smelled it. Red pressed forward without hesitation. The punch came in direct and level, like a heated piston, and it landed hard enough to move AKIRA more than his own steps did. He skidded toward the right boundary, arms tight, posture dented. It wasn’t a wild combo or some flashy finishing attempt; it was worse, because it was controlled. RYU-X was establishing that every inch of space belonged to him, and AKIRA was paying for each retreat.

I was sitting near the right-side barrier, so believe me when I say RYU-X came flying our way. The match was past the feeling-out stage by then, and AKIRA had become the one asking all the questions. RYU-X’s answers were getting uglier each time. He raised an arm, maybe expecting a punch, but AKIRA slid inside and cracked him with a flat-handed thrust to the body. The sound was short and horrible, like a drum hit under water. RYU-X stumbled toward us, forced into retreat despite trying to dig his heels in. His red glow sputtered; AKIRA’s blue was steady. Everyone around me leaned back at once, because it looked like RYU-X might actually hit the edge.

Midway through the clash, the momentum clearly belonged to AKIRA. The blue combatant committed to a sudden forward burst and connected solidly with RYU-X’s centerline. The red fighter was unable to absorb it cleanly; his footing broke, and the force of the collision displaced him toward the right boundary of the battleground. What stood out was not only the hit itself, but the context around it. RYU-X had already been chipped down physically, his reactions less crisp than in the opening exchanges. AKIRA, by contrast, was dictating distance and tempo. This forward-driving strike confirmed the pressure pattern: AKIRA attacking first, RYU-X retreating second, the space behind RYU-X shrinking fast.

The final exchange before the observatory floor gave way belonged to everyone at once, but it still turned on one unique action. The central column cracked, and the suspended orrery of bronze planets began to fall. Mako saw the largest sphere dropping toward Juno and hurled a flame whip around it to slow it, but the heat made the old chain snap faster. Tetsu planted himself beneath the sphere, ready to catch it, while Nami flooded the floor around his feet to cushion the impact. Oren, refusing to help openly, kicked a fallen railing so it slid under Tetsu’s heels as a brace. Sable tried to exploit the distraction by throwing his broken chain at Rika’s back. Kyra intercepted it with one mirror dagger, pinning the chain to the incoming bronze planet for a fraction of a second. Rika noticed the new anchor and yanked the chain herself. The falling planet swung sideways instead of down, smashing through the remaining window and dragging Sable off his feet. Everyone stared as the bronze sphere vanished into the storm outside, still trailing his chain like a comet tail.

I swear the crowd inhaled all at once. Akira flashed in blue, not wild, not swinging huge, just cruelly direct. His hand shot forward and found Ryu-X before Ryu-X could bring his defense back together. The red armor jolted, and he went sliding sideways and back, closer to the right-hand limit of the battleground. You could tell this was the middle stretch because neither of them looked fresh anymore, but Akira still had bite in his movement while Ryu-X looked like he was wearing the whole fight on his ribs. It was a pressure hit, a bully hit, the kind that says: I am not letting you breathe.

Red-side fan here, and that sequence was pure dominance. RYU-X had Akira figured out by then. Late fight, everyone tired, but only one of them looked like he still had command of the arena. Akira tried to force contact, maybe hoping for a desperate momentum swing. RYU-X locked down, took it, and immediately shoved the blue boy toward the right edge with this cold, relentless pressure. No panic, no overextension, just a grounded stop that became a bulldoze. Akira’s feet kept searching for traction and finding none. The best part was how RYU-X kept his line after the clash, like he was herding Akira exactly where he wanted him. That is not luck. That is control.

Technically, this was RYU-X converting fatigue into territory. AKIRA had already lost a lot of his lateral sharpness by this late stage, and his guard was rising slower each exchange. RYU-X noticed the lag and attacked from the outside line, turning his torso into a violent circular strike that arrived around AKIRA’s defense instead of straight through it. The impact forced AKIRA diagonally back and right, leaving him nearly pinned near the edge of the fighting space. What matters is not only that the red fighter connected, but that he continued advancing immediately afterward. AKIRA’s balance recovery was delayed, his feet crossing awkwardly, while RYU-X stayed compact and forward-facing. Momentum was firmly red at that instant.

Kaito got the first clean throw of the rooftop-market brawl when Renga lunged at him between two stalls of glass wind chimes. Instead of meeting the shoulder charge head-on, Kaito hopped onto the brass lip of a noodle counter and snatched the festival bell rope dangling above it. He let Renga pass under him by half a step, looped the rope around the big fighter's forearm, and dropped backward like a pendulum. The bell boomed once, loud enough to rattle every paper lantern on the roof, and Renga was yanked sideways off balance. Kaito used the swing to plant both sandals on Renga's hip, twisted midair, and sent him skidding through a pyramid of steamed buns. The move only worked because the bell rope was exactly there, and afterward the rope snapped, leaving the bell rocking uselessly over the stunned crowd.

I’m not exaggerating when I say that hit sounded like the match ending early. Maybe RYU-X still had breath left, but he didn’t have control. AKIRA, in blue, was the one dictating everything by then. He stepped in and delivered a fierce blade sweep that cut through red’s attempted guard, forcing RYU-X to skid toward the right edge of the field. The important part was RYU-X’s reaction: no sharp comeback, no clean recovery, just a strained stumble and a desperate turn of the shoulders. Late-match fatigue had finally made him movable. AKIRA noticed and kept advancing like he meant to finish the job before RYU-X could find his legs again.

My little brother kept yelling that AKIRA should counter, but you could see why he couldn't. It was too late in the battle for clean hero reactions. He was breathing heavy, his stance kept collapsing for tiny moments, and RYU-X was all over him. Then red did that fake charge. AKIRA bought it, shifted his block, and suddenly he was moving the wrong direction. RYU-X kept pressing into him and shoved the whole exchange toward the right edge. My brother went quiet after that because even he realized AKIRA was being bullied into the corner by a move that barely needed to touch him.

I was joking all night that AKIRA fights like a weather system, and then that moment made the joke feel literal. Near the end, with RYU-X looking sunburnt by damage and stubbornness, blue came barreling in again. AKIRA’s body snapped into a forward stab, the kind of strike that makes the air seem to crease around it. It caught RYU-X before he could rebuild his guard. The red fighter was carried backward toward the right edge, sliding, staggering, trying to keep his dignity in his stance. But the momentum was plain: AKIRA was the storm front, and RYU-X was debris getting pushed downrange.

There is a rhythm in fights where you can hear who owns the next few seconds, and here it belonged to AKIRA. We are still in the opening third, before the big reversals and last-gasp explosions, but the color of the match has already started shifting blue. RYU-X stands there in red with his stance a little too narrow, his elbows a little too honest about the damage he has been taking. AKIRA reads that weakness and bursts forward in a straight, ruthless line. The camera almost loses him, which is the point: one instant he is outside reach, the next he is inside RYU-X’s space and making contact with enough force to move the man, not just hurt him. RYU-X is driven toward the right perimeter, sliding and twisting, his feet stuttering for traction. He does manage to stay upright, and that is worth something, but it is the kind of survival that gives the attacker even more confidence. AKIRA’s posture after impact says he expects the retreat. RYU-X’s posture says he is tired of being made to retreat. That difference is the whole story of the moment.

On the storm-lashed roof, the antenna mast becomes the center of a duel neither fighter intended. Vale has been throwing lightning needles at Yuki all evening, each one forcing her to dodge farther from the roof hatch. Finally he corrals her against the mast’s guy wires and flicks five needles in a spread pattern. Yuki dives through the narrowest gap, cutting her cheek but keeping her footing on the slick tiles. Vale snaps his fingers to call the needles back for a second strike. Yuki was waiting for that. She wraps her scarf around the lowest guy wire and swings her whole body around the mast just as the needles reverse. They chase her curve and bury themselves into the metal pole instead of her back. Vale’s smile vanishes when the mast begins to hum. Yuki kicks off, skids past him on one knee, and clips his ankle with the trailing scarf. The storm answers the charged mast with a single blinding bolt. It does not hit Vale directly; Yuki’s scarf yanks him sideways at the same instant. But the shockwave hurls him into the water tank, and the tank’s painted dragon face caves in around him.

From a neutral view, this is where the match tilts harder toward RYU-X. AKIRA attempts to act during the early phase, but the red fighter intercepts with a slicing counterblow that lands clean and forces him rightward. AKIRA's recovery is shaky, his blue guard closing after the damage is done. RYU-X remains the one advancing, and AKIRA is visibly being worn down before the fight has even reached its later intensity.

A news drone became the strangest weapon of the night when Rika and Voss fought beneath the broken departure board. The drone hovered too close, trying to broadcast their duel, its little camera blinking red. Voss grabbed it by one rotor cage and swung it like a buzzing mace. Rika ducked the first pass, but the propeller wash blew her bangs into her eyes, and the second pass clipped the shoulder of her jacket. She stumbled into the hanging chain that controlled the old station shutters. Instead of pulling away, she wrapped the chain around her forearm and stepped into Voss's next swing. The drone tangled in the links, rotors shrieking. Rika yanked down hard. The shutters behind Voss crashed shut one after another, their metal slats dropping like a drumroll, and the final slam startled him just enough for Rika to palm-strike the drone's off switch against his chest.

I watched it on replay after seeing it live, and it somehow looked worse the second time. RYU-X’s reaction was so delayed. Late fight exhaustion had him a half-step behind, and AKIRA was already in predatory mode. The blue fighter lunged with a straight, penetrating shot that slammed into RYU-X and sent the red warrior sliding to the right side of the stage. There was a tiny moment where RYU-X’s feet scrambled for traction, and that tiny moment told the whole story. He was not countering. He was not setting a trap. He was being forced back by AKIRA’s relentless pressure.

As a longtime RYU-X defender, that sequence hurt to watch. He had not been beaten outright yet, but the fatigue was showing in all the little places: the late guard, the stiff hips, the way his recovery no longer snapped cleanly back into form. Then AKIRA came in wearing that blue light like a warning sign, covering distance in one committed burst. RYU-X saw it, I think, but seeing and stopping were two different things by then. The hit landed square enough to fold his posture and push him toward the right edge of the arena. It was not just loss of space; it was loss of initiative. Earlier, RYU-X could answer fire with fire. Here, he was being forced to accept AKIRA’s pace. The red aura still flared, but it looked defensive, strained, almost stubborn. AKIRA kept his forward line, aggressive and confident, and RYU-X had to give ground in a way that made the middle of the fight feel like the beginning of a downhill slide for him.

Aya’s impossible dodge came when the glass elevator doors opened behind her and revealed nothing but the shaft. The assassin Pelle fired three dart-wires in a triangle pattern, one at her head and two at her ribs, confident she would have to choose which hit to take. Aya stepped backward into the open elevator shaft as if falling by mistake. Pelle actually laughed until the wires jerked taut around empty air. Aya had caught the maintenance ladder inside the shaft with one hand, her body hanging flat against the wall just below the floor line. As Pelle leaned in to confirm the drop, she kicked upward with both heels, striking the underside of the elevator door track. The doors tried to close on Pelle’s extended wires and pinched all three cables together. Aya climbed one rung, wrapped the bundled wires around her forearm, and gave a sharp downward tug. Pelle was yanked forward, forehead stopping a finger’s width from the door frame as the safety sensor reopened with a cheerful chime. Aya popped back onto the platform, dusted her sleeve, and returned the darts to him in a neat little bundle.

Kaito and Rina crashed through the arcade doors at the exact moment Juro tried to reload his gauntlet with spirit cartridges. Kaito did not punch him; he slapped the front panel of a prize machine, making a row of metal capsule toys pop loose. Rina kicked one capsule up like a soccer pass, Kaito caught it between two knuckles, and Juro laughed because it looked harmless. Then Kaito flicked it into the exposed loading slot of the gauntlet. The capsule jammed the mechanism, and Juro’s next blast inflated inside the weapon instead of leaving it. Rina used that half-second to slide beneath the sparking arm and hook both heels behind Juro’s ankles. When Kaito palm-struck the stuck gauntlet upward, Rina scissored her legs sideways, toppling Juro flat into a dancing rhythm game cabinet. The cabinet still registered steps as his armor bounced on the pads.

I was in the crowd on the right side, and this was the moment everybody around me stopped cheering for a second because we all saw AKIRA getting herded our way. Mid-fight, when you expect both of them to have settled into a rhythm, RYU-X suddenly took over like he’d found the lever that moved the whole match. He came forward in red, shoulders set, and sent that cutting burst across AKIRA’s guard. AKIRA’s blue blur jerked back and slid toward the right-side limit, not flying dramatically, just being driven there in the most humiliating way—forced to give ground because he couldn’t hold it. You could tell AKIRA was tired. His defense arrived late, his feet didn’t answer cleanly, and even when he recovered enough to face RYU-X, it looked more like survival than readiness. RYU-X, meanwhile, was still pressing, still advancing, turning the center into his territory and making AKIRA look like someone running out of room and answers.

Kaito and the first masked twin fight inside the abandoned festival bus after the crowd evacuation, swaying between rows of hanging straps. The twin uses the straps like gymnastic rings, swinging from one to another to pepper him with sharp heel kicks. Kaito blocks three and gets driven backward toward the rear door. On the fourth swing, he grabs the strap she just released instead of the leg coming at him. The bus hits a pothole outside, and the strap jerks downward with his weight. The sudden pull opens the overhead luggage rack, dumping someone's packed festival drums into the aisle. The twin lands among them and keeps moving, kicking a drum into Kaito's shins. He jumps, plants both feet on the bus's vertical handrail, and spins around it horizontally. The spin lets the drum pass under him and turns his body into a sweeping kick. The twin ducks, but Kaito's real target is the stop-request cord. His heel snaps it, making every bell in the bus chime at once and masking his landing behind her.

Koji’s attempt to blindside Rika in the arcade corridor failed because of the claw machine glass. He lunged from behind a dancing rhythm cabinet, fist glowing blue, and she only caught his reflection at the last possible instant. Instead of dodging away, she dropped flat and kicked both legs into the base of the claw machine. The cabinet lurched forward on its hidden wheels, the glass front taking Koji’s punch. His energy burst spiderwebbed the pane without breaking it, trapping his hand in a humming crater of cracked safety glass. Rika rolled under the prize chute, popped up on the far side, and hit the machine’s joystick with her elbow. The claw descended, absurdly slow and cheerful, then clamped onto Koji’s ponytail just tightly enough to yank his head back when he tried to free himself.

Mid-fight, and this is where AKIRA began turning control into punishment. RYU-X was already fading, his counters slower, his stance too high. AKIRA slipped into range and drove the heel of his hand straight through him, not a slap, not a shove, a compact, brutal impact. RYU-X was forced across the floor toward the right side, boots scraping, red aura flickering unevenly as he fought to stay upright. The important thing was not just the hit; it was the geography. AKIRA put him closer to having nowhere to retreat. Blue was advancing with purpose, and red was being compressed into a cornered, tired version of himself.

I swear the whole screen snapped when AKIRA hit him. Not with a flashy windup, not some huge dramatic charge, just a sudden open palm that landed like a door slamming in a storm. This was still early, before the fight had settled into its nastier late rhythm, and yet RYU-X already looked like he’d been made to carry too much damage. The red guy got blasted sideways, drifting hard toward the right edge of the stage, arms trying to remember where defense was supposed to be. AKIRA didn’t look surprised at all. That was the scary part. He was hunting, not gambling. RYU-X was being pushed into a smaller and smaller world, and everyone watching could feel the momentum tilt blue.

Tetsu’s floor-slam against Oren was a contest of stubborn giants, and neither won cleanly. Oren charged with both iron boots sparking, planning to tackle Tetsu through the central column. Tetsu crouched, stone aura spreading from his shoulders into his hands, and accepted the impact. Their foreheads nearly touched as they strained, boots carving trenches in the marble. Then Oren shifted tactics, hooking his ankle behind Tetsu’s heel for a reaping trip. Tetsu responded by hardening the floor around his own foot, locking himself in place. That made him immovable but vulnerable. Oren grinned and drove an uppercut toward his chin. Tetsu released the floor at the exact moment of the punch, letting the force lift him. In midair he grabbed Oren’s wrist with both hands, rotated his stone-heavy hips, and came down sideways. The landing drove Oren’s trapped arm into the floor first, not breaking it but numbing it completely. Tetsu rolled away clutching his jaw, while Oren shook fingers that would not obey.

From a coach's angle, AKIRA's problem was his exhausted first reaction. Early on, he might have read the shoulder line and refused to move. Here, in the closing stretch, he was late, overprotective, and too willing to believe the threat. RYU-X exploited that perfectly. He presented the attack, drew AKIRA's guard and weight the wrong way, then advanced through the space AKIRA gave up. No wasted motion. No panic. Just red dominance, forcing blue to surrender ground. The important part was not the contact; it was the real estate. AKIRA got pushed toward the right edge, and once he was there, his options shrank badly.

I’ll be the skeptic and say it wasn’t the end, not by a long shot. RYU-X still had enough threat that AKIRA couldn’t get lazy. But that mid-round collision was a major warning flare. AKIRA had been applying sustained pressure, and RYU-X’s responses were becoming more about damage control than counterattack.
