When AKIRA brought the strike down from the high lane, RYU-X failed to shift out before contact. The impact drove him toward the right edge and robbed him of neutral footing. That is the kind of positional loss that snowballs. Even if RYU-X survived the hit, he came out of it more tired, more confined, and more obviously behind in the momentum race.

It looked like a lie with footsteps. RYU-X, all crimson heat and intent, offered AKIRA a shadow of an attack. AKIRA, pale-blue glow fraying at the edges, believed it because he had been battered into believing anything dangerous. His guard rose like a tired reflex. His heel dragged. The arena seemed to tilt to the right. RYU-X followed, not chasing so much as conducting him, and AKIRA gave up ground he could no longer afford. At that late hour of the fight, the trick felt almost crueler than a wound. Red did not need to break him open; red only had to convince him that the next break was coming.

Vexa corners Rook beneath the ceremonial coin tree, whose golden prayer tokens have been shaken loose by earlier impacts and now litter the floor like bright scales. She raises her magnet gauntlet and the coins leap upward into a spinning halo around her fist. Rook laughs because he expects a simple metal punch and braces with crossed bracers. Vexa feints that punch, then opens the gauntlet's palm to reverse the pull. Every coin slaps away from her at once, not at Rook, but into the wooden pillars around him, pinning dozens of silk streamers across his path. When Rook lunges anyway, the ribbons tighten and twist around his elbows, slowing the arc of his counterpunch. Vexa steps inside the ruined punch, touches two fingers to his chest plate, and activates a tiny magnetic pulse she has hidden there with the first feint. His own armor jerks him backward into the web of streamers, leaving him dangling and furious but unharmed.

I was in AKIRA cosplay at the watch party and still had to admit RYU-X cooked him there. My whole table was chanting for blue to hold center, but he couldn't. RYU-X came forward with that scary almost-attack, the kind that makes you cover before you think. AKIRA did exactly that, and because he was already drained, he couldn't spring back into position. Red flowed around the reaction and kept driving him toward the right side. It felt like watching someone get backed up by a bluff they absolutely could not afford to call.

On the banquet level, Mira turns a spilled tea service into a trap no one sees coming. Saito charges her with his elbow blazing blue, expecting her to retreat down the aisle between overturned tables. Instead, Mira snatches the rolling tea cart by its brass handle and shoves it directly into his path. Saito punches through the top shelf, smashing cups into glittering dust, but the lower kettle survives and erupts a curtain of steam into his face. He swings blind, carving a glowing arc through empty air. Mira ducks under the cart, slides on her back between its wheels, and kicks the brake lever loose as she passes. The cart lurches, catches Saito behind the knees, and folds him onto it. Before he can roll away, Mira pops up on the far side, flips a serving tray like a discus, and smacks the kettle’s lid shut. The trapped steam blasts from the spout, propelling the whole cart backward and ramming Saito through a row of decorative screens.

As someone who had been rooting for RYU-X, that part hurt to watch. The fight had barely gotten into its first act, and already he was being herded to the side instead of setting the pace. AKIRA kept stepping in, cutting off escape angles, making every backward movement cost something. RYU-X tried to brace and fire back, but he was late. AKIRA came rising out of close range with a savage punch that climbed right into him. RYU-X’s body jolted upward and sideways, then he was shoved toward the right limit of the stage like the blue fighter had drawn a line and forced him over it. RYU-X was not finished, but he looked noticeably worn, while AKIRA looked hungry.

Across from the tea stand, Priestess Luma faces two masked twins who move as if sharing one shadow. One twin attacks high with crescent knives while the other stays low, cutting at Luma’s calves whenever she shifts her stance. She cannot block both, so she stops trying. Luma catches the edge of the tea cart with her prayer staff and shoves it into the low twin’s path, wheels squealing over shattered tile. The high twin hops onto the cart to keep his momentum, exactly as she predicts. Luma knocks the boiling kettle’s lid loose with the butt of her staff, releasing a white cloud of steam that hides her next step. Through the steam she switches places with her own hanging sash, leaving the high twin to slash empty cloth. The low twin skids on spilled jasmine tea; the cart spins; the high twin loses balance; and Luma brings the flat of her staff down on the cart handle. The handle flips up and clips both twins under their chins in one absurdly neat double strike.

Okay, I am saying this as the kid in the living room who was literally sitting on the carpet yelling at the TV: Akira was in trouble right there. It was almost over, you could feel it. He tried to go at RYU-X, but RYU-X did this super solid red wall thing and Akira just could not get through. Then RYU-X leaned in and made him slide all the way toward the right side like Akira was being pushed by a truck. Akira looked tired, not normal tired, but hero-at-the-end-of-the-episode tired. RYU-X looked scary because he was not panicking at all. He was the one moving forward, and Akira was the one being forced back.

Taro’s one-off trick with the train doors was messy but effective. The wolf-eared rival, Zed, had him cornered inside the derailed commuter car, slashing so fast the hanging hand straps danced from the wind. Taro kept retreating until his back hit the manual door lever. Zed lunged, claws wide. Taro yanked the lever and jumped upward, grabbing two hand straps. The doors snapped open behind him, and Zed’s lunge carried him out onto the slanted exterior step. Before Zed could spring back in, Taro swung forward from the straps and kicked both feet into the door panels. The doors slammed shut on Zed’s long coat, pinning him by the hem rather than his body. Zed snarled and tried to tear free, but Taro was already running along the seat backs. He vaulted off the fare box, bounced once on a dangling strap, and shoulder-checked Zed through the window beside the door. The coat ripped loose only after Zed had been knocked into a pile of luggage outside.

Okay, I was yelling for AKIRA, so this one hurt. It was still early enough that I kept telling myself he was just downloading RYU-X, just taking notes, you know? But then RYU-X came forward again, red aura flaring, and poked him with this nasty little straight punch that didn’t look huge until AKIRA got shoved back by it. Suddenly my guy was drifting toward the right edge, and it felt like, oh no, this is becoming a pattern. RYU-X wasn’t letting him breathe. Every forward step from red made AKIRA look more cramped, more tired, more stuck defending instead of fighting back. It wasn’t the finishing moment or anything, but it was the kind of early hit that tells you who’s steering the whole round.

The fight briefly entered the arcade, where Byte tried to turn every machine against Arashi. Screens flashed warning-red, joysticks snapped like little fangs, and skee-ball ramps spat wooden balls across the floor. Arashi looked overwhelmed until he noticed the rhythm of the claw machine beside him. Byte had possessed it too, making the claw descend with murderous precision. Arashi deliberately let a skee-ball clip his shin, stumbled into the machine, and smacked the prize button with his elbow. The claw dropped exactly as Byte lunged through the screen in a body made of pixel static. Arashi shoved the machine forward on its casters. The claw closed around Byte’s digital ponytail, not damaging her but anchoring her avatar in place for a crucial second. Arashi then grabbed the joystick, rotated it hard left, and dragged Byte sideways into a row of dancing-game cabinets. The impact made all the machines start playing different songs at once. Byte reformed instantly afterward, furious, but she never gave Arashi another chance near that claw game.

Late fight, momentum red. That is the simplest way to call it. AKIRA is already dulled, his movements heavier than they were at the start, and RYU-X takes advantage with a savage forward punch that lands flush. The impact drives AKIRA toward the right boundary, his blue energy dragging behind him as he stumbles and slides. RYU-X does not back off after contact; he advances into the result, aggressive and confident, while AKIRA looks less like a challenger and more like someone trying to stay upright long enough to find one final answer. The whole exchange says the same thing without narration: RYU-X is forcing the finish, and AKIRA is being worn down step by step.

Kyra’s mirror-step reversal happened beneath the cracked moonroof, where puddles reflected every fighter twice. Juno tried to exploit the reflections by hurling three throwing needles at the images rather than at her body, forcing her to reveal which shimmer was real. Kyra answered by shattering her own left bracer against the floor. The polished fragments scattered into the puddles, multiplying her reflection into a broken constellation. Juno hesitated for half a heartbeat, and that was all she needed. She slid on one knee between two shards, caught a needle between the flat faces of her twin daggers, and snapped it back with a twist. The redirected needle did not fly at Juno’s chest. It struck the buckle of his scarf, pinning the cloth to a tilted telescope stand. When he yanked away, the scarf tightened across his throat. Kyra rose behind the confusion and tapped the back of his neck with the dull side of her dagger, a warning blow that still sent him sprawling.

As an old coach, I winced at AKIRA’s footwork there. Early rounds are where you establish your base, and he let RYU-X crowd him. The red fighter read the retreat, turned his hip, and let a round, slicing leg attack crash through. AKIRA took it while moving backward, which made the shove worse, and he was driven toward the right boundary instead of circling out. That’s not just one hit; that’s a lesson in pressure. RYU-X was the hunter, and AKIRA was burning energy just to stay upright.

As a coach, I would pause the tape right on the entry, because that was where Ryu-X lost the exchange. Early in the contest, he was already conceding initiative: weight high, rear foot too narrow, guard focused on Akira's hands instead of Akira's hips. Akira read all of that. He did not rush upstairs. He changed level and attacked the foundation, a clean low arc that struck through Ryu-X's stance rather than merely tapping the ankle. The red fighter tried to brace, but his balance had been softened by the pressure that came before it. That is why the contact sent him traveling toward the right boundary instead of just making him stumble in place. You could see Ryu-X's body choosing survival over counterattack: arms out, torso twisting, steps getting messy. Meanwhile Akira, in blue, was already moving after him, not admiring the hit, not resetting, just turning a landed low attack into territorial control. In the opening third, that is a brutal message. Akira was not just ahead; he was making Ryu-X fight from bad positions and spend extra effort on every recovery. Red was getting worn down piece by piece, and this was one of the clearest early signs.

The final distinct exchange in the brawl happens under the central bell, after everyone thinks the fight has moved to the platforms. Gant rises one last time and hurls the station’s ceremonial bell clapper like a battering ram at Kael’s back. Kael hears the chain scrape too late to dodge normally, so he drops his shoulder and dives into the circular shadow of the bell itself. The clapper misses him by a finger’s width and smashes into the bell’s inner lip. The impact produces a massive note that ripples through the concourse, rattling glass, armor, and teeth. Kael uses the vibration rather than enduring it: he presses both palms to the bell’s bronze surface, lets the ringing travel through his arms, and kicks off the base as the bell swings back. The rebound launches him feet-first toward Gant. Gant raises his forearms to block, but Kael twists sideways in the air and lands with one heel on the chain above the clapper. His weight yanks the chain down, pulling the clapper back like a pendulum. It bumps Gant gently but decisively in the chest, knocking him into a seated sprawl as the last note fades.

The sound is what stays with me: a sharp crack, then the scrape of RYU-X being driven across the floor. This was late, when both should have been exhausted, except AKIRA somehow still had forward bite while RYU-X looked battered and dulled. AKIRA surged in from blue stance and landed a straight thrust into the red fighter’s body. RYU-X tried to resist, but the force pushed him toward the right boundary, his balance breaking in pieces. It felt like watching a door get kicked open from the inside. AKIRA kept advancing after contact, and RYU-X’s retreat was not strategy anymore; it was damage showing itself.

I was sitting on the right-side stands, so it looked like AKIRA got thrown straight at us. One second he was wobbling but still upright, trying to square up, and the next RYU-X dropped out of the air with that brutal red streak behind him. The collision made everyone around me flinch. AKIRA’s body snapped back and slid toward the edge, almost sideways, like he had lost all say in where he was going. You could tell this was near the finish because the usual clean counters from him just were not there anymore. He reached for balance, missed it, and kept getting pushed. RYU-X looked fresh in comparison, not untouched, but meaner, sharper, hungrier. It felt less like a single hit and more like red physically dragging the match into its last corner.

As someone sitting practically on the right-side rail, I swear the whole floor hummed when AKIRA came in. We were still in the early going, but RYU-X already looked like he had eaten too many small losses. AKIRA’s blue trail snapped across the gap and crashed into him before the red guy’s counter even formed. RYU-X slid my direction, boots kicking dust, one arm pinned in close and the other trying to keep AKIRA off his centerline. It was not a finishing moment, but it was a bullying one. AKIRA was walking him down without walking at all, forcing him closer to the edge and making him burn strength on balance instead of offense.

The important detail is spacing. At the center phase of the fight, RYU-X’s retreat path had already narrowed because AKIRA kept winning the small exchanges. When AKIRA committed to the descending strike, it functioned as both damage and relocation. RYU-X’s guard was high enough to survive but not stable enough to hold position. The blow landed on the upper line, compressed him, and pushed him camera-right, away from neutral space and closer to the perimeter. That is why the moment mattered. AKIRA did not merely score; he converted pressure into arena control. RYU-X, visibly worn, was no longer choosing where to stand. He was being placed there by AKIRA.

From my seat it felt like the whole bout had shifted blue before the strike even landed. We were past the feeling-out stage, and RYU-X was already moving like every block cost rent. AKIRA kept pressing, stepping in with that calm, mean timing, then suddenly came down on him from high guard. The hit cracked onto RYU-X before the red fighter could square up, and it didn’t just stop him; it shoved him backward and sideways until he was skidding toward the far right boundary. You could see the problem instantly: AKIRA had the initiative, the space, and the rhythm, while RYU-X was being squeezed into fewer and fewer choices.

On the pedestrian bridge, Mina tried to end the chase with her ribbon-blade, snapping it around Haru’s neck from ten meters away. Haru did something he had not done in the whole fight: he stopped running straight forward and dropped backward over the railing, one hand still clutching a hanging advertisement banner. Mina yanked, expecting to drag him in, but the banner tore free from its clips and wrapped around the ribbon like a sail. A bus roared underneath, its roof-mounted air conditioner catching the cloth and pulling Mina’s weapon downward. Haru swung below the bridge in a wild arc, planted both sneakers against the side of the bus for one absurd instant, and launched himself back up through the gap. He came over the railing behind Mina and tapped two fingers into the pressure point under her shoulder blade. Her ribbon arm went numb, and the blade clattered harmlessly around her own boots.

From where I was yelling in the cheap seats, this was the moment you could feel the match tilting for good. The red aura surged first, not as a flourish but as a threat, and RYU-X stepped through AKIRA's guard with that awful, compact punch that sounded like a door being kicked off its frame. AKIRA, already looking spent in the late going, folded around the impact and skidded away toward the right boundary. He did not fly like he was surprised; he slid like his legs had finally stopped taking orders. RYU-X kept moving after him, shoulders forward, hungry, while the blue light around AKIRA sputtered and dragged behind him.

The firecracker dragon that looped above the festival stalls was supposed to be decoration, but Kade turned it into a roaring hazard. He snapped his charged gauntlet against the dragon's paper tail, igniting the entire string of fireworks in a rippling chase of red sparks. The dragon frame whipped loose and serpented through the concourse toward Nara. She ran under three explosions, vaulted a takoyaki grill, and grabbed a vendor's water bucket without slowing. Kade expected her to douse the fireworks. Instead, she hurled the bucket at the floor ahead of herself and slid on the spreading water, passing beneath the lowest arc of the burning dragon. As Kade stepped in to catch her, the empty bucket bounced up from the floor and clipped his chin. Nara popped out of the slide behind him and shoved him face-first into a harmless cloud of smoke.

If you freeze the feeling rather than the frame, it is all pressure: red advancing, blue collapsing. RYU-X's strike lands during the closing minutes, when AKIRA's reactions have lost that sharp early-fight snap. The punch buries in, the sound goes flat and savage, and AKIRA is driven across to the right side of the arena as if the floor itself is rejecting him. His aura flickers in torn ribbons behind him. RYU-X follows the path of the hit without overextending, proving he is not just swinging wild; he is forcing geography, making the boundary part of the attack. AKIRA is still there, still conscious, but the fight is being written over him.

Hoshiko faces Tetsu in the umbrella alley, where every festival guest has abandoned bright plastic umbrellas after the first shockwave of the fight. Tetsu snatches a red umbrella and thrusts it like a lance, using its metal tip to keep her outside his boxing range. Hoshiko catches the shaft under her armpit, but he pops it open in her face. The sudden bloom hides his left hook, which thuds into her ribs. She staggers, then answers by grabbing two discarded umbrellas at once and opening them low, like twin shields at knee height. Tetsu laughs and jumps over them for an axe kick. Hoshiko snaps both umbrellas shut around his descending leg, trapping his ankle between the crossed frames. She twists and pulls, turning his graceful kick into an awkward one-legged hop. Tetsu refuses to fall; he balances on his hands and mule-kicks the umbrella handles out of her grip with his free foot. The broken umbrellas spiral away like colorful wheels, and both fighters reset, drenched and furious.

Aya turned a falling chandelier into a weapon without ever touching its chain. The serpent twins had boxed her against the grand staircase, one lashing low with a bladed sash while the other sent a high ribbon looping for her neck. Aya jumped straight up, not away, and the crossed ribbons sliced through the chandelier cable above her. As the crystal mass dropped, she kicked off a stair rail, planted both feet on the chandelier's rim for a single ringing instant, and rode it downward like a descending moon. The twins separated to avoid being crushed, exactly as she wanted. Aya sprang from the chandelier before impact, snapped open her fan, and used the blast of displaced air to shove the low twin into the high twin's path. Their ribbons tangled around each other instead of her. The chandelier exploded between them and the floor, scattering crystals that reflected so many versions of Aya that neither twin knew which silhouette to strike.

I was in the cheap seats screaming for AKIRA to plant his feet, but you could see he didn’t have that kind of strength left. Late fight, shoulders sagging, blue aura flickering like a bad bulb, and RYU-X smelled it. The red guy just came barreling in with that nasty rotating leg strike, his body turning so fast the afterimage looked like a red wheel. It smashed into AKIRA and sent him sliding toward the far right side of the arena. Everybody around me went quiet for half a breath, because it wasn’t just damage, it was position. RYU-X had herded him there. AKIRA was being pushed out of options.

Aki and the white-haired duelist Naru fight behind a row of painted folding screens, so the onlookers see only silhouettes: two blades, a ponytail, a sleeve snapping like a flag. Naru relies on the shadows to disguise his footwork, cutting through the screens one at a time and forcing Aki to retreat into ever smaller panels of painted cranes. Aki notices that the lantern behind her makes her shadow larger than her body. She steps out of her sandals and leaves them planted beneath the oversized silhouette, then crouches and crawls along the bottom rail of the screen. Naru thrusts at the shadow's chest and pierces only paper, triumphant for half a heartbeat. Aki rises behind him with a screen rib in each hand, crossing them over his sword arm in a simple lever. She does not disarm him with strength; she rotates the paper frame so the torn screen wraps his blade like a sleeve, forcing him to let go or spin with it. He chooses the spin and lands dizzy among painted crane feathers.

From a coach’s perspective, RYU-X lost that exchange before the blade even connected. His rear foot was too close to the right side, his hips were squared wrong, and fatigue had made his guard predictable. AKIRA recognized it instantly. In the end phase, when many fighters hesitate, he accelerated. The blue fighter’s cutting motion entered through the weak side of RYU-X’s stance and carried him laterally, forcing him toward the boundary rather than simply knocking him back. That’s high-level pressure: damage plus map control. RYU-X absorbed the blow, but the worse part was where he ended up. AKIRA remained balanced and advancing; RYU-X became a tired target with less space to recover.

From the cheap seats, all I saw was blue commit and red lose ground. AKIRA burst in during the middle of the scrap, when RYU-X was already moving like the fight had started to weigh on him. The contact landed hard enough to force RYU-X backward and sideways, sending him toward the right boundary before he could recover his footing. It was the kind of exchange that makes everyone stop arguing about who has control. AKIRA had it. RYU-X was still fighting, still dangerous, but he was being pressed, battered, and crowded. That forward crash said the whole story in one motion.

The medical crew near my section all leaned forward at once. That tells you how bad it looked. RYU-X had been deteriorating through the late portion, slower to lift his hands, slower to recover his line. AKIRA exploited it immediately. A blue-charged forward drive landed into RYU-X’s center and forced him backward, step after scraping step, toward the right boundary. The hit was not just painful; it displaced him, compressed him, made him fight the floor as much as AKIRA. From that instant, the red fighter seemed less like a challenger and more like someone trying to survive the remaining seconds.

Aya's one-off rescue of Kenji doubled as an attack on the umbrella swordsman. Kenji had been launched across the food court and was about to hit a wall of glass shelves. Aya slid beneath him on a serving tray stolen from a dessert stall, one leg extended like a skater's. She caught Kenji by the back of his jacket without stopping, and their combined weight shot them under the umbrella swordsman's thrust. The swordsman snapped his umbrella open, turning the missed stab into a spinning shield. Aya let go of Kenji and slapped the tray upward with her heel. It ricocheted off the underside of the open umbrella, folding the canopy inside out around the swordsman's head. Kenji, still sliding, kicked a pastry cart into the man's shins. Aya completed the motion by snapping her fan against the umbrella ribs, locking them shut. The swordsman toppled backward, muffled inside his own weapon and sprinkled with powdered sugar.

From where I was sitting, the tide had clearly tipped by then. This wasn’t the opening feeling-out stuff anymore; both of them had marks, but the red fighter was carrying the damage worse. Akira, glowing blue and moving like he’d found the rhythm, stepped in with that heavy downward crash and caught Ryu-X clean. You could see Ryu-X’s stance fold for a second before his whole body was shoved sideways, boots skidding and sparks dragging behind him as he was forced toward the far right side of the arena. It felt less like a single hit and more like Akira announcing, “I’m not letting you breathe.” Ryu-X didn’t go down, but he looked pressured, tired, and badly crowded.

The animation sold the power through displacement rather than gore or overdone sparks, which made it nastier. In the opening third, while both fighters should theoretically have plenty left, AKIRA had already established himself as the one initiating contact. RYU-X’s reactions were increasingly defensive, almost delayed by accumulated pressure. Then came that compact palm strike: AKIRA’s shoulder drove through, his stance stayed rooted, and the blow landed with a concussive snap that sent RYU-X sliding toward the right-hand perimeter. The red fighter’s posture collapsed for a breath, hips behind his feet, guard scattered. It was a clean visual sentence: blue pushes, red yields. What I liked was how it clarified momentum without needing commentary. AKIRA advanced into the space RYU-X lost, so the hit became both a strike and a territorial claim. RYU-X survived it, yes, but he looked less like an equal opponent afterward and more like someone being steadily carved down before the fight had even reached its middle.

Bro, the red side fans got real quiet right there. It was still early, so nobody wanted to admit RYU-X was getting leaned on, but AKIRA made it obvious. Blue boy snapped forward so fast it looked like the animation skipped a few drawings, and RYU-X got caught before he could answer. The hit did not send him flying upward or anything dramatic like that; it was worse, honestly. He got bulldozed sideways-back toward the right edge, struggling to keep his boots under him while AKIRA stayed glued to the advance. You could see RYU-X wearing down in real time: guard high, shoulders tight, reactions a half-step late. AKIRA was the one asking all the questions, and RYU-X was stuck paying for every wrong answer.

As a coach, I hated Ryu-X’s positioning there. Midway through, he was already breathing heavier, and Akira sensed it. Instead of backing off, Akira stepped into range and put his whole base behind one punishing collision. The red fighter’s centerline collapsed; he couldn’t anchor in time, so the force carried him straight toward the right-side perimeter. That’s not just damage, that’s ring control. Akira was dictating distance, direction, and pace. Ryu-X needed a clinch, a pivot, anything—but all he managed was a staggered slide while Akira advanced behind the pressure.

On the service elevator landing, Kenji tried to trap Lio between closing steel doors. He slammed the call button, shoved Lio backward, and drew his baton so the only retreat was into the elevator shaft. Lio took one step back, then another, timing his breathing with the warning chime. When Kenji lunged, Lio hooked his toes under a discarded wet-floor sign and flipped it upward. The yellow triangle snapped open between the doors just as they tried to close, making them bounce apart. Kenji's baton thrust hit the sign and skidded down the slick plastic. Lio used the redirected baton as a handhold, vaulted over Kenji's shoulder, and landed behind him. Before Kenji could turn, Lio kicked the wet-floor sign out from between the doors. They shut on Kenji's cape, pinning him there while Lio saluted from the rising elevator.

From the booth, it felt like RYU-X had seized the script before AKIRA ever found his rhythm. Still early in the match, the red fighter pressed in, hips turning with that sweeping leg, and the strike caught AKIRA clean across the guard and upper body. The blue side didn’t crumble, but he skidded backward in a nasty diagonal, boots scraping as he was shoved toward the right boundary. That was the clearest sign of the opening stretch: RYU-X was dictating distance, and AKIRA was already starting to look sanded down.

There was a cruel elegance to it. RYU-X advanced in scarlet, unhurried but relentless, and his leg traced a bright arc through the space AKIRA thought was safe. The blow found him, bent him, and sent the blue fighter drifting toward the right edge as if the arena had tilted under his feet. In the first third of the duel, that kind of displacement felt ominous. RYU-X was not merely landing attacks; he was herding AKIRA, making exhaustion arrive ahead of schedule.

Inside the department store, the duel reached the bedding section, which should have looked ridiculous but somehow became terrifying. General Mako raised his obsidian spear and stabbed for Tetsu’s ribs. Tetsu jumped onto a display mattress, sank too deep, and seemed trapped. Mako grinned and drove the spear down, but Tetsu grabbed the fitted sheet with both hands and rolled sideways, stripping it off the mattress in one violent corkscrew. The elastic edge snapped around Mako’s spear shaft and wrist. Tetsu kept rolling, dragging the sheet tight until Mako’s arm was pinned across his own chest like a wrapped parcel. Then Tetsu bounced off the mattress springs, tucked his knees, and slammed both feet into the trapped spear. The weapon levered Mako backward into a pyramid of boxed pillows. The boxes burst open on impact, and white feathers exploded around him like a defeated demon shedding fake snow.

Aya avoided a finishing blow by using the parade dragon in the least heroic way possible. Brutus chased her beneath the suspended silk dragon float, swinging a stone hammer that carved sparks from the roof tiles. Aya saw the dragon's belly sagging from its bamboo ribs and sprinted straight toward what looked like a dead end. At the last instant she dropped to her stomach, slid through spilled sesame oil, and vanished under the float's red cloth. Brutus swung anyway. His hammer smashed through the dragon's painted jaw, tangling in streamers, teeth, and bamboo whiskers. Aya popped out through a tear near the tail, hooked one ankle around a support pole, and kicked the pole backward. The float pivoted like a huge lazy fish and wrapped Brutus from shoulder to boot in glittering fabric. He could still roar, but he could not swing, and Aya bowed to the ruined dragon before running on.

Renga tries to overpower Hoshiko at the shrine steps with a straight wrestler's rush, confident that the cramped stone path gives her nowhere to circle. She waits until his hands lock around her waist, then drops a wooden ema prayer plaque between his forearms and twists it sideways. The little plaque becomes a wedge that ruins his grip. Renga growls and lifts anyway, but Hoshiko hooks her knee over the shrine gate's lower beam and refuses to move, hanging almost upside down while his strength works against him. She reaches under his chin with the ribbon of a bell rope, loops it across his shoulder, and uses her hanging weight to drag one of his arms behind his back. It is not a choke, just an ugly improvised shoulder lock that forces him to kneel. Renga solves it brutally by headbutting the gate post, shaking loose a cascade of bells. The ringing startles Hoshiko just enough for him to roll forward, dumping her into a pile of white fortunes tied along the railing.

Venn seized a maintenance ladder from the wall and wielded it like an enormous fork, trying to pin Mira against a departure board. Mira kept slipping through the rungs, frustrating him until he drove the ladder down flat to cage her against the floor. She rolled sideways at the last instant, but deliberately left one arm threaded through a rung. Venn stepped on the ladder to trap her. Mira grinned, twisted her trapped arm, and used the rung as a lever to flip the entire ladder up between his legs. The far end cracked him under the thigh and lifted him awkwardly onto his toes. Before he could regain balance, she scissored both legs around the ladder's side rail and rolled, turning the ladder into a giant wrench around his ankle. Venn dropped his weapon and performed an undignified hop-spin to avoid the takedown becoming a lock. He escaped only by shedding one boot, leaving Mira holding the ladder and his footwear like trophies.

I was watching for RYU-X’s counter timing, because early on he had been punishing straight approaches. That is why this mid-fight sequence stood out. AKIRA attacked anyway. The blue fighter compressed the distance in a single explosive line and struck RYU-X before the red fighter could turn his tired guard into a real answer. The impact did not simply stop on contact; it carried through. RYU-X was driven to the right, his boots sliding, his shoulders twisting as he tried to avoid being completely opened up. The arena position told the story better than any dialogue could. AKIRA had center pressure and forward intent. RYU-X had damage in his posture and less room behind him. It felt like AKIRA had solved the tempo problem: keep forcing RYU-X to react, keep making him spend energy he no longer had, keep pushing him until the boundary becomes another opponent.

Ringside, the sound was the part that got me—the quick tear through the air, then AKIRA’s boots grinding as he was forced sideways. This came during the middle run of the fight, after enough punishment had stacked up that AKIRA’s reactions were starting to fray. RYU-X had become the hunter by then, red closing distance again and again, and this exchange showed it clearly. He sent a sharp cutting wave into AKIRA’s guard, struck him clean enough to bend him off line, and drove him toward the right perimeter. AKIRA stayed upright, but he looked compressed, cornered, and increasingly spent. RYU-X didn’t celebrate; he just kept leaning forward, because he knew the pressure was working.

Okay, so mid-battle, this is the moment I started yelling at my screen like an idiot. Ryu-X had already been losing little pieces of himself in the exchanges, and Akira was absolutely not giving him any space. Blue boy came forward, planted hard, and slammed into him with this brutal, ground-shaking strike that just bullied the red one across the stage. Ryu-X tried to brace, you could tell, but his feet scraped backward and he got launched toward the right boundary like he’d been hit by a moving wall. Akira was all momentum here, all pressure. Ryu-X still had fire in him, sure, but he was being shaved down, and this hit made it obvious who was controlling the fight.

Akira’s hit has that gorgeous early-fight dominance framing: blue surges in from the active side, red gets displaced toward the screen’s right margin. The palm connects with this heavy, spiraling follow-through, and Ryu-X’s body language sells the damage perfectly—head snapping, torso folding, feet scraping for traction. What I love is that the scene does not present it as a random clean strike. It is part of a pattern. Akira has been pressing the tempo from the start, and this shove is him turning pressure into territory. Ryu-X is already getting worn thin, forced to spend his balance just to avoid being cornered. The fight is young, but the direction is obvious: Akira is attacking, Ryu-X is surviving.

People keep talking about the impact, but the footwork before it was the giveaway. RYU-X had already won the argument over space. Late in the fight, AKIRA was circling less and retreating more, which meant his defensive choices were narrowing. RYU-X pressed in, forced the eyes forward, then delivered the high descending hit that punished AKIRA's compromised guard. The collision dragged AKIRA toward the right edge, and that carry was just as important as the damage. Red stayed close enough to threaten after landing; blue was left hunched, displaced, and visibly slower. In momentum terms, there was no ambiguity. RYU-X was surging. AKIRA was being ground down in real time.

Jun's strangest moment occurs in the service elevator shaft after the doors burst open to reveal no elevator, only swaying cables and the glowing kitchen floors far below. The crane-masked bruiser grabs Jun by the front of his jacket and tries to hurl him into the shaft. Jun goes willingly for half a step, then clamps both knees around one dangling cable and twists his body sideways. The bruiser's throw becomes a pivot. Jun swings in a tight arc, still gripping the attacker's sleeve, and plants both feet against the opposite wall. For one frozen second they form a human slingshot: Jun braced on the wall, the cable humming, the bruiser leaning over empty air with stubborn disbelief. Jun releases the sleeve but keeps the cable twisted. It whips back and smacks the bruiser's shoulder, not hard enough to injure him badly, just enough to turn him around. The elevator finally rises from below with a cheerful bell, and its roof bumps the bruiser upward through a laundry chute instead of into the pit.

From the caster desk, that was the instant the whole match tilted almost past recovery. RYU-X, in red, kept walking AKIRA down like he smelled the finish, and AKIRA was already moving like his legs had borrowed time. Then RYU-X rose into that brutal top-down swing and brought it crashing onto AKIRA before blue could guard high enough. The impact shoved AKIRA sideways, boots skidding, shoulders buckling, all the way toward the right-side boundary. You could feel the arena realize this was late in the fight, not a trade or a reset. RYU-X was pressing the advantage, AKIRA was getting sanded down, and the space behind AKIRA was basically disappearing.

The aquarium wall is not part of anyone’s plan until Toma gets desperate. Nari has him pinned against the glass with a spear of frozen light pressed to his throat, the tropical fish scattering behind his head like sparks. She tells him to yield. Toma responds by tapping two fingers against the glass, not hard enough to break it, just hard enough to send a dull note through the tank. Nari frowns, and that hesitation saves him. He repeats the tap in a faster rhythm, matching the pulse of her freezing aura. The frost crawling over the glass turns brittle and white. When Nari thrusts, Toma shifts his chin aside and shoulder-checks the weakened panel. The tank bursts outward in a roaring sheet. Water engulfs them both, knocking Nari off balance and dissolving the spear before it lands. Toma rides the flood on a serving platter, surfs past Nari’s sweeping kick, and slaps a decorative eel charm onto her sleeve. The charm crackles once, not enough to electrocute her, but enough to lock her muscles while the wave dumps her into a heap of flopping fish nets.

I swear the whole crowd felt the ending coming before the impact landed. AKIRA had that forward lean, that nasty calm, like he’d smelled fatigue on RYU-X and decided to stop giving him air. Then the blue blur crossed in, steel flashing in a bright crescent, and RYU-X’s red frame buckled sideways. He didn’t fly back in some dramatic clean line; he got driven, shoved by the cut itself, sliding toward the rightmost side like the stage was rejecting him. Late in the duel, with both of them marked up, AKIRA looked sharpened by the damage while RYU-X looked drained by it. That exchange was basically a statement: blue was pressing, red was surviving.

Kaito’s first clean hit came when the fight spilled under the broken monorail. Renga rushed him head-on, swinging the cracked signal post like a club, expecting Kaito to backpedal again. Instead, Kaito dropped flat onto his shoulder, slid under the horizontal sweep, and kicked both heels into the post from below. The impact popped the metal shaft out of Renga’s grip and sent it spinning straight upward. Before Renga could even look up, Kaito sprang to his feet, caught the falling post by one end, and used its own downward momentum to jab the blunt tip into Renga’s armored stomach. Renga folded around it with a burst of steam from his chest vents, and Kaito let go immediately, leaving the pole wedged there just long enough for Renga’s next step to trip over it. It was not repeated; the signal post snapped in half when Renga crashed through a ticket gate.

The arena lighting made the strike look almost too clean, like a blue comet drawing a pale seam through red smoke. AKIRA came in during the waning moments of the fight, when hesitation usually creeps into everyone’s shoulders, yet his motion had none. RYU-X, meanwhile, wore the match on every part of him: heavy breathing, late hands, legs that answered commands by committee. The cutting blow met him near center-right and dragged the contest further that way, sending him skidding toward the outer limit. It was not just a wound but a direction. AKIRA pointed, and RYU-X went. The audience noise rose because everyone understood the implication. The closer red got to that side, the more the fight belonged to blue.

By the middle stretch, Akira had seized command. He closed the gap before Ryu-X could reset, dropped his weight into a crushing impact, and sent the red-clad warrior reeling to the arena’s right-hand limit. Ryu-X absorbed it badly; his guard sagged, his balance broke, and his retreat wasn’t tactical anymore. Akira, in blue, was driving the action. Ryu-X was surviving it.

Coach brain here: the important part was not power, it was positioning. In the late phase, when both fighters should have been cautious, RYU-X took the center and made Akira pay for being tired. Akira’s entry was predictable, a little too upright, his recovery lagging. RYU-X met him with a compact defensive frame, caught the blue fighter’s force without giving ground, then transferred weight forward through the forearms and hips. That single action changed the geometry of the fight. Akira was driven toward the right side of the arena, where his escape lanes narrowed badly. You could see the fatigue in his footwork; he could not pivot out cleanly. RYU-X was not merely blocking. He was advancing behind the stop, turning Akira’s last push into another retreat.

As a longtime AKIRA defender, this hurt to watch. He had survived so much already, but that late exchange exposed how worn down he was. RYU-X entered like a storm front, red glow burning around his shoulders, and drove a crushing blow into him with enough force to shove him sideways across the stage. AKIRA tried to brace, you could see the attempt in his knees, but the impact overruled it. He was sent sliding toward the right edge, one arm lagging, guard broken open. RYU-X did not look relieved. He looked encouraged, which was worse. The momentum belonged to him completely in that instant.

As a longtime arena photographer, I’d describe that exchange by the footprints. AKIRA’s tracks went forward: decisive, centered, digging in. RYU-X’s went sideways and back, messy streaks toward the right boundary. Late in the match, that told the whole story. The blue combatant launched a slicing blow through the gap in red’s defense, and RYU-X’s torso twisted with it before his feet could catch up. The force carried him across the floor, not into open space but toward the danger line. You could see fatigue in the delay: his guard rose after he’d already been caught, his recovery started after he’d already lost position. AKIRA pressed. RYU-X retreated because his body had no better answer.

The glass bridge fight produced one exchange everyone remembered because it was so quiet. Yori faced the silent swordsman Omen while cracks spread under both of them. Omen attacked with a draw cut too fast to see, aiming to force Yori into a broken pane. Yori did not parry. He tossed his scarf upward. Omen’s blade cut it into two red strips, and for an instant the fluttering cloth hid Yori’s hands. Behind that curtain, Yori unclipped the magnet charm from his belt and slapped it onto the bridge’s steel support cable. When Omen stepped through the scarf pieces for the finishing cut, Yori dropped backward through a hole in the glass. The magnet held him by the belt charm just below the bridge. Omen’s slash passed through empty air, and his forward foot landed on the weakened pane meant for Yori. It shattered. Yori swung beneath the bridge like a pendulum, kicked Omen’s ankle from below through the gap, and sent him sprawling safely onto an intact panel rather than into open air.

The ring-side view made the impact feel less glamorous and more mechanical. RYU-X compressed his stance, transferred all that red-charged mass through his arm, and hit AKIRA at exactly the wrong time for the blue fighter. AKIRA had already been fading by this final stretch, his guard slower to return after every exchange. When the blow connected, it did not just hurt him; it relocated him. He was forced toward the right perimeter, almost scraped along an invisible rail by the force. RYU-X's aggression was unmistakable. He was not responding to AKIRA anymore. He was dictating, stepping into the space Akira had abandoned before Akira even finished sliding.

From the announcer desk, it felt like the whole match tipped on that turn of RYU-X’s hips. We were already deep in the closing stretch, with AKIRA in blue breathing hard and giving ground, and then RYU-X came in red-hot, literally and tactically. He pivoted through a full rotation and snapped his leg across AKIRA’s guard, catching him clean enough to shove his entire frame sideways. AKIRA didn’t fall, but he skidded and stumbled toward the right-hand boundary like he’d lost the floor under him. RYU-X was the one dictating everything here: pressure, angle, pace. AKIRA looked less like he was countering and more like he was surviving the next second.

I do not usually buy into the hype, but that late exchange was genuinely nasty. Akira looked like he had one more surge in him, and for half a second I thought he might actually claw the round back. Then RYU-X just stood his ground in that red, locked-in posture and made Akira’s attempt collapse on contact. The result was ugly for the blue side: Akira got shoved toward the right edge, heels skidding, shoulders folding inward, his momentum stolen and recycled against him. This was deep in the fight, when small mistakes become huge, and RYU-X clearly knew Akira was worn down. He did not rush wildly. He pressed, measured and mean, forcing Akira closer to the boundary while looking like the fresher, crueler fighter.

The exchange at the ticket gate belonged entirely to Hana and Veyl. Veyl had learned to ignore her paper seals, slicing them before they touched him, so Hana baited him with five obvious talismans fluttering in a fan. He cut all five with a contemptuous spin of his glaive. What he missed was the ticket stub she had tucked behind her ear at the start of the brawl. As he finished the spin, Hana flicked the stub under his boot. It stuck to the wet tile and glowed a plain commuter green, not the usual holy silver. The automatic gate beside Veyl chirped, mistaking him for unpaid cargo, and its waist-high bars slammed together around his hips. Veyl snarled and chopped down to break them, but Hana had already slapped both palms onto the gate console. The machine vomited out a hundred rejected tickets, each one folding into a tiny paper hand. They swarmed up his glaive shaft, pried his fingers open, and fed the weapon politely into the validator slot. The gate stamped it void, bent it in half, and spat it back into Veyl's shocked face.

Rina's exchange with the masked archer happened atop the departure board, with letters flipping beneath their feet like black metal scales. The archer loosed three crescent arrows in a vertical line, aiming not for Rina's body but for the hinges above her. She recognized the trick a half-second late as the sign began to fold down. Rather than jump away, she ran toward the collapse, stepped onto the first falling panel, and used it like a descending stair. At the bottom, she snapped her scarf around the archer's bowstring and yanked. The bow did not leave his hand, but it rotated hard enough to fire his next arrow backward into the station clock. Glass rained between them. Rina used that glittering curtain to vanish, then reappeared behind him just long enough to tap the pressure point below his shoulder blade and make his bow arm drop uselessly.

Man, I was yelling at my screen like RYU-X could hear me. He had been tough earlier, no doubt, but by this point he was running on fumes, and AKIRA was absolutely hunting. Blue darted in, blade line snapping across red’s front, and you could see RYU-X’s body fold with it. He got shoved toward the right side, boots dragging, one arm late to cover, face doing that anime grit-teeth thing where you know the tank is empty. AKIRA didn’t stumble after him or look surprised. He just kept moving forward like, yep, that’s mine. Final stretch, momentum all blue. RYU-X wasn’t getting outplayed in theory anymore; he was getting physically herded.

I’m telling you, that hit changed the temperature of the whole match. Not the beginning, not the desperate finale yet—right in that messy middle where fatigue starts telling the truth. Ryu-X had been getting nicked, shoved, and interrupted for a while, and he was starting to look like someone trying to fight underwater. Then Akira pressed in again. No hesitation. Blue aura flaring, shoulders forward, he hammered Ryu-X with a massive body-jarring blow that seemed to make the floor itself complain. The red guy’s frame snapped back, then sideways, and suddenly he was sliding toward the right end with no grace at all, just grit and panic in the way he tried to keep his heels under him. Akira followed the motion like a predator chasing a stumble. He didn’t admire the hit; he used it to take more space. Ryu-X was still upright, still dangerous in theory, but the match at that point belonged to Akira’s tempo. Every step Ryu-X gave up made him look more worn, more boxed in, and less able to answer.

On the rain-slick roof of Kisaragi Station, Rika charged Captain Voss with her red festival umbrella folded like a spear. Voss swung his iron prayer bell in a clean horizontal arc, aiming to smash through the umbrella ribs and her shoulder together. At the last instant, Rika popped the umbrella open, not to block but to catch the bell inside the canopy. The impact snapped two ribs, yet the silk wrapped around the bell just long enough for her to twist. Voss was yanked off balance, boots skidding through a puddle of lantern reflections. Rika released the handle and ducked under him as the tangled bell dragged him sideways into a melon soda vending machine. The machine spat cans like cannon fire, and Voss had to raise both forearms while Rika slid away under the bouncing hail of green metal.

Chat was losing its mind here because RYU-X had fully switched from testing to bullying. This wasn’t early feeling-out stuff anymore; by this point AKIRA was already moving heavier, and RYU-X smelled that weakness. Red dashed in, let that razor-like gust rip across the lane, and blue got tagged before he could properly brace. AKIRA skidded toward the right border, arms coming up too late, and you could almost hear the collective “uh-oh” from everyone watching. It’s the kind of hit that doesn’t end the fight, but it tells you who’s dictating it. RYU-X stayed planted forward, ready to chase. AKIRA was backing up, wearing damage, and running short on space.

From the medic’s corner, that was the kind of impact you mark mentally. AKIRA had already absorbed enough early pressure to look slower on the reset, then RYU-X stepped in and snapped a wide, hooking kick into him. The collision turned AKIRA’s torso and carried him toward the right side, forcing him to recover while moving instead of planting. It happened too early for AKIRA to be this visibly taxed. RYU-X’s tempo was doing exactly what pressure is meant to do: make the opponent tired before the fight is halfway formed.

I swear the air changed color right before it happened. AKIRA was breathing hard, his stance loose in that dangerous way that says the body is negotiating with defeat, and RYU-X saw it. The red fighter closed the gap and dropped a brutal hand into him, not flashy, just heavy and final. AKIRA's head snapped, his whole frame buckled, and the blue trail behind him streaked toward the right-hand limit of the battlefield. This was deep in the fight, past the part where comebacks feel clean. RYU-X had all the forward pressure, stalking after the impact, while AKIRA was being herded like there was nowhere left to retreat except out.

As someone who came in cheering for Ryu-X, this was the first moment that made my stomach drop. We were not deep into the fight yet, not even close to the desperate late-stage chaos, and already Akira was walking him down. Ryu-X tried to square up, but Akira slipped into range and slammed that bare-handed thrust into his body with enough spin behind it to send him reeling toward the right boundary. It looked brutal because Ryu-X didn’t bounce back with his usual snap. He slid, caught himself, and still seemed a step behind. Akira was fresh-looking, hungry, pushing the pace. Ryu-X, meanwhile, was starting to look like every blocked and half-blocked exchange had taken something out of him.

Old arena veterans always talk about the difference between striking an opponent and moving an opponent. AKIRA moved him. At the tail end of the fight, when RYU-X’s red shine had dulled and his defense was starting to sag, AKIRA advanced and punched a thrust straight through the space RYU-X needed. The contact landed solid. RYU-X was driven toward the right-hand edge, dragged by the force of it even as he tried to dig in. That was not a neutral exchange. AKIRA was pushing the pace, deciding the angle, and making RYU-X surrender ground he could not afford to lose.

Kaito is driven into the arcade plaza, where Renga rips a vending machine from its wall bolts with a roar that silences even the game cabinets. He shoves it forward like a refrigerator-sized battering ram. Kaito cannot dodge left because claw machines block the path, so he jumps onto the vending machine's front glass as it slides at him. His boots crack the display but hold. Renga keeps pushing, trying to crush him against a racing game cabinet. Kaito punches the cola selection button with his heel, again and again, until the damaged machine spits cans into Renga's shins like metal hail. Renga powers through the first few, then one rolls under his heel. His push stutters. Kaito seizes that tiny hitch, springs off the glass, and flips over Renga's shoulder. While upside down he hooks two fingers into Renga's belt and tugs, not to throw him, but to turn his hips. Renga's own shove redirects the vending machine into the racing cabinet, triggering a ridiculous burst of digital engine noises.

Mira’s cleanest dodge happens in the station washroom corridor, where the floor is already slick from a toppled mop bucket. Sable fires three needle-thin throwing blades down the narrow passage, each one curving with a faint violet trail. Mira has no room to sidestep and no weapon in hand. She stomps on the edge of the mop bucket, flipping it upright just as the first blade arrives. The blade pings off the bucket’s metal rim. Mira hops inside the bucket with both feet, grabs the mop handle like a ski pole, and shoves backward. The bucket skates down the wet hallway, carrying her under the second blade, which slices a lock of hair from above her ear. The third curves toward her chest, so Mira plants the mop against the wall and vaults, spinning the bucket ninety degrees. The blade pierces the bucket instead of her coat, pinning it to the tile. Mira tumbles out, snatches up the still-spinning bucket, and flings it back down the hall. It ricochets off both walls before cracking Sable squarely on the shoulder.

From where I was yelling in the cheap seats, the finish was already starting to smell like AKIRA’s match. RYU-X had that heavy, punished sway, his red guard coming up a fraction too late, and AKIRA just kept taking ground. Then blue snapped forward with a hard, straight-body drive, not fancy, just brutal and clean. It caught RYU-X square and shoved him backward across the floor, boots skidding toward the right boundary like he was being pushed by a storm door. The crowd knew it too: this was late-fight pressure, not an opening exchange. AKIRA was hunting, and RYU-X looked like he was running out of places to fall.

Old arcade brain speaking: that was pure corner-carry psychology. RYU-X did not spend some flashy all-in attack. He threatened, paused the truth just long enough, and let AKIRA's tired defense do half the work. Late match, when your resources are gone and your hands are twitchy, you bite on that stuff. AKIRA bit. He braced for the obvious lane, RYU-X took the useful lane, and blue lost floor fast. The right side of the stage got closer and closer while red stayed glued to him. If this were on a cabinet, everyone watching would be muttering, don't get trapped, don't get trapped.

At the shrine steps, Aya faced the twins Ren and Rui, who had been mirroring her movements perfectly all night. She finally broke the rhythm by tossing her sword into the air and kneeling as if surrendering. Both twins lunged from opposite sides, blades aimed at her shoulders. Aya clapped her hands once, and the sword she had thrown struck the bronze temple bell overhead, producing a deep vibration that rattled the stone lanterns. The twins flinched at the same time, ruining their symmetry. Aya rolled forward between them, snatched the fallen bell rope, and whipped it around Ren’s ankle. Instead of pulling Ren down, she hauled herself upward with the rope, swung in a tight circle around the bell post, and kicked Rui in the chest as she passed. Ren, still tethered, stumbled into Rui, and the twins collided hard enough to split one wooden sandal clean in half.

Crowd audio probably peaked there, because even through the broadcast compression you could hear the panic. AKIRA's back foot had been betraying him for several exchanges, and RYU-X finally cashed in. He threw that crushing straight-in blow and it connected with a nasty thud, snapping AKIRA out of whatever defensive rhythm he had left. The blue fighter went sliding to the right side, arms loose for a second, like his guard had been unplugged. This was not early-match testing. This was endgame bullying. RYU-X kept his red shoulders squared and advanced behind the hit, making AKIRA cover distance he clearly did not want to give up. You could feel the finish getting closer.

Rika and Goro collide under the cracked festival bell while everyone else is still trading sparks across the shrine roof. Goro tries to end it with brute force, grabbing Rika by the sash and hoisting her overhead for a backbreaker against the bronze rim. Rika hooks one ankle around the bell rope at the last instant, letting her body swing behind him instead of falling where he wants. The rope yanks taut, the bell tilts, and Goro suddenly finds himself fighting the weight of both Rika and the bell. She twists her sash free, plants both feet against the bell’s side, and kicks off. The bell booms once, loud enough to flatten the paper lanterns, and the recoil whips the rope around Goro’s wrists. Rika lands in a crouch, gives the rope a sharp tug, and Goro is spun like a tied hammer into the stone offering box, scattering coins and charm slips everywhere.

Kyra’s blade catch against Rika was a silent, nasty moment amid all the thunder. Rika had stolen one of Juno’s knives and hidden it in her sleeve, waiting until Kyra committed to a high kick near the cracked moonroof. When the kick came, Rika stepped under it and thrust upward toward the unarmored gap beneath Kyra’s ribs. Kyra did not parry with her daggers. She folded her raised leg tighter, catching Rika’s wrist behind her knee while balancing on one foot. At the same time, she pressed the flat of one mirror dagger against Rika’s knuckles, trapping the stolen knife without cutting her fingers. Rika tried to twist free, but Kyra leaned backward into a dancer’s bridge, dragging Rika forward and forcing her shoulder joint to rotate. The stolen knife clattered down. Rika avoided the full dislocation only by headbutting Kyra’s supporting knee, making them both collapse in an ungainly heap that scattered mirror fragments like silver petals.

Kaito's clash with the horned giant on the luggage conveyor had its own rhythm, separate from the rest of the brawl. The giant grabbed two suitcases by their handles and swung them like meteor hammers, forcing Kaito to hop backward along the moving belt. Kaito parried the first suitcase with his forearm guard, but the second burst open and sprayed folded shirts into his face. Blind, he dropped flat and let the belt carry him under the next swing. His hand found a travel pillow, which seemed useless until he jammed it between the conveyor's rollers. The belt stuttered, then jerked backward. The giant, mid-swing, lost his footing and slid toward Kaito. Kaito rose on one knee, caught the giant's nearest horn with both hands, and performed a sharp seated twist that redirected the fall into the oversized baggage scanner. The machine lit up around the giant's skull, displaying a perfect X-ray of his stunned expression.

From the commentator desk, that was the first real statement from RYU-X. Still early in the fight, with neither fighter fully settled, the red blur stepped in and snapped a compact punch straight into AKIRA’s guard line before the blue fighter could reset. It wasn’t a huge haymaker, but it landed clean enough to make AKIRA’s whole stance skid backward. You could see the pressure building: RYU-X was marching forward, shoulders square, claiming space, while AKIRA was getting shaved down little by little and forced toward the right boundary. At this stage, RYU-X looked like the one dictating the pace, and AKIRA was already reacting instead of answering.

I know people online are going to argue that AKIRA “blocked most of it,” but come on. Watch his feet. Watch the slide. This is not a neutral trade. By the middle of the fight, AKIRA’s defense had already started looking more like damage control than confidence, and RYU-X was the one walking him down. The red guy turns through with that sweeping kick, catches AKIRA while he’s bracing, and the whole blue silhouette gets shoved toward the right edge of the screen. That’s the giveaway. Even if AKIRA’s arms are up, his position gets wrecked. RYU-X ends the exchange closer, balanced, ready to pile on. AKIRA ends it nearer the boundary, shoulders tight, posture tired. So no, it wasn’t just a flashy spin; it was RYU-X taking territory from a worn-down opponent.

Toma's drum-shield exchange began when Brutus hurled a broken roof tile at his head like a discus. Toma ducked into the music platform and came up with the huge festival taiko strapped to his back, its painted hide facing outward. The tile struck the drum with a thunderclap that made everyone within ten paces flinch. Brutus charged through the echo, expecting the drum to slow Toma down. Instead, Toma planted one foot on a fallen cymbal and slid backward, using the drum's round shell as a shield and sled at once. Brutus's next hammer swing hit the drum rim and rebounded awkwardly. Toma twisted with the impact, letting the drum roll off his shoulders and around his hip. As it spun past Brutus's knee, Toma jabbed the drumstick through a lacing hole and yanked. The drum stopped dead; Brutus's shin did not. He toppled over it like a felled tower.

On the broadcast tower roof, Sadao tries to end the brawl by forcing Kaito toward the humming antenna array. Rain lashes sideways, and every strike throws sparks from the wet metal grating. Sadao flicks his iron fan open and channels a thin arc of static along its ribs, daring Kaito to block. Kaito backs up until his heel touches the warning stripe around the antenna base. When Sadao thrusts, Kaito raises both hands as if surrendering, then drops his head under the fan and bites the end of his own scarf. With the scarf held taut between teeth and hand, he catches the fan's edge in the cloth and turns his neck with the motion, guiding the charged strike into a grounded maintenance pole. The shock flashes blue, numbing both fighters' arms. Kaito cannot punch, so he headbutts Sadao's sternum. Sadao staggers, laughs despite the pain, and sweeps Kaito's legs with the closed fan, sending him skidding dangerously close to the antenna's crackling base.

Blue nation, that was the one where I stood up. AKIRA had RYU-X softened, no question. The fight was in that grinding middle stretch where pride starts turning into bad footwork, and red was already backing up more than he wanted to admit. AKIRA saw the shell, jumped the line, and hammered straight down onto him. Not a clean little tap either; it hit with weight, enough to drive RYU-X across the floor toward the right edge. The best part was AKIRA’s body language afterward. No panic, no celebration, just forward pressure like the next answer had already been solved. RYU-X was still dangerous, sure, but he was being worn into a corner one forced step at a time.

The chef assassin attacked Goro in the banquet car while the monorail lurched over a gap in the track. Cleavers flashed between hanging pans, and every swing rang like a cymbal. Goro backed into the dessert table, palms sticky with syrup, and the assassin grinned as if the fight had become ridiculous. When the next cleaver came down, Goro grabbed a spun-sugar centerpiece shaped like a phoenix and raised it like a shield. The blade sliced through the sugar bird, but the syrupy strands clung to the cleaver and the assassin's wrist. Goro twisted the sticky mess around a chandelier chain, then kicked the table's rolling brake loose. The whole dessert table slid with the train's tilt, dragging the tangled assassin off balance. Goro hopped onto the table, rode it past him, and bumped him through a curtain into the pantry shelves.

Kaito's duel with the tea master assassin is quiet for the first ten seconds, almost polite. The assassin slides a boiling iron kettle across the floor with his foot, making Kaito hop over the handle, then darts in with two finger strikes aimed at pressure points under the ribs. Kaito blocks the wrists but cannot stop the kettle from spinning back behind his ankle on its curved bail. The assassin smiles, expecting a trapped stance. Kaito answers by stomping the kettle lid open. A vertical plume of steam erupts between their faces, turning both fighters into pale silhouettes. The assassin's fingers stab through the cloud and touch only Kaito's discarded headband, held out like bait. Kaito has dropped flat, hooked the kettle's handle with the end of his scarf, and swung it in a tight circle around the assassin's lead foot. The iron is too hot to grab and too awkward to kick away; when the assassin shifts weight, the handle drags his ankle sideways. Kaito rises with one palm under the man's elbow and gently tips him into a rolling fall across the tatami.

I am not saying RYU-X was being nice before, but this was the moment he got downright disrespectful. AKIRA is barely keeping the blue fire together, final stretch tension everywhere, and red decides to scare him into moving. Not smash him, not overpower him directly, just make him flinch. He flashes in like the attack is obvious, AKIRA covers, and whoops, wrong answer. RYU-X has already taken the space and is crowding him toward the right edge. It was bully-ball with a magician's grin. AKIRA looked like he wanted to plant his feet, but his body was too worn out to argue.

Okay, chat, I know people are going to argue about whether AKIRA could have blocked that, but come on. At that point he was cooked. Not finished, not giving up, but cooked. RYU-X had been mauling him through the final stretch, and blue was stuck guessing. Red steps in, makes it feel like another forward rush, and then bam, the strike comes down from the sky angle. AKIRA gets clipped hard and shoved toward the right wall, and you can see the panic in the movement afterward. He is not resetting; he is surviving. RYU-X is all gas, all pressure, and AKIRA is just trying not to get swallowed by the corner.

The exchange has a very clear tactical reading: AKIRA wins the entry. At the middle phase, with RYU-X already carrying accumulated wear, AKIRA chooses a direct acceleration rather than another feint or ranged probe. The blue fighter penetrates RYU-X’s guard and transfers momentum through the torso, causing lateral displacement toward the right boundary. RYU-X’s response is delayed and incomplete. His feet attempt to catch, but the pressure has already broken his balance. This matters because ring position changes the entire fight. AKIRA is not merely landing damage; he is converting offense into territory. RYU-X, in red, is forced from contesting center space into absorbing contact while retreating. The sequence shows AKIRA as the active decision-maker and RYU-X as the increasingly depleted defender.

Vexa and the calligrapher monk clash in the archive balcony, where hundred-foot paper scrolls hang from rafters and black ink bowls wobble on low stands. The monk fights with a staff that paints symbols in midair, each stroke hardening briefly into a barrier. Vexa's magnet gauntlet is useless against wood and paper, so she improvises with the iron-rich ink. She lets him drive her backward until her heel touches a bowl, then kicks it upward without looking. The monk sweeps his staff to block her face, but the ink arcs over the barrier and splashes across the hanging scroll behind him. Vexa flicks her gauntlet fingers, pulling the wet black line sideways. The scroll jerks like a sail caught by wind, wrapping around the monk's staff and pinning it to the balcony rail. He releases one hand and starts a palm strike. Vexa ducks, grabs a brush as long as her forearm, and paints a messy circle on the floor around his feet. It has no magic at all, but he hesitates, expecting a trap, and that pause lets her hip-check him into a cushioned reading alcove.

The brawl’s final side exchange erupts inside the cracked bell itself, where Daigo and Iori tumble after a blast knocks the bronze shell onto its side. The interior rings with every scrape. Iori crawls up the curved wall and kicks off, spinning with both green-flamed blades aimed at Daigo below. Daigo cannot dodge far; the bell’s curve keeps sliding him back to center. He grabs a loose incense burner that rolled in with them and hurls its ash straight upward. Iori cuts through the cloud, but the ash coats his flames, turning them into choking green smoke. His spin falters. Daigo plants both feet against the bell wall and punches the bronze beside him, not Iori. The bell answers with a deafening pulse that rattles Iori midair and cancels his balance. As Iori drops, Daigo catches one wrist, pivots in the cramped space, and drives him shoulder-first into the bell’s inner lip, making the entire courtyard hear a single terrible gong.

From the stands it felt like Akira had already decided where Ryu-X was allowed to stand: nowhere comfortable. Still early in the fight, the blue fighter stepped in first, beat Ryu-X to the space, and smashed an open-hand strike into him with that sudden twisting force. Ryu-X didn’t just flinch; he got carried sideways, boots skidding toward the far right boundary like the floor had tilted under him. You could see the red fighter trying to brace, but he was already getting softened up by Akira’s constant pressure. This was not a comeback moment. This was Akira setting the rhythm and shoving Ryu-X closer to trouble.

At the central fountain, Renga finally catches Mira by the collar and hurls her toward the marble basin. She twists midair to land on the rim, but the fountain has been flash-chilled by Hoshiko's earlier charm, leaving the stone glazed with ice. Mira's foot shoots out from under her. Renga charges, expecting an easy finish. Instead of fighting the slide, Mira drops into a seated skid and uses the basin rim like a circular track. She whips around the fountain once, gathering speed while Renga tries to follow on the slippery edge. As she comes around the second time, she snatches a bronze fish statue by the mouth and pivots around it, converting the slide into a spinning kick. Her heel catches Renga behind the knee. The big fighter does not fall into the water; he slams both palms down and bridges over the basin, stubbornly suspended above the icy spray. Mira's momentum carries her past, and Renga retaliates by kicking a sheet of ice up like a broken mirror between them.

Nix tried to end the rooftop segment with style, freezing a patch of rainwater into a glassy ramp and launching himself upward with both boots. He came down toward Hana with an overhead ice spear, glittering against the moonlit station dome. Hana did not dodge left or right. She flipped open a paper umbrella that looked absurdly delicate, spun it once, and let the spear punch into the oiled paper. The ribs of the umbrella were actually lacquered steel; they flexed around the spearhead and trapped it. With a sharp turn of her wrist, Hana redirected the descent so Nix's own force hauled him past her shoulder. As he flew by, she hooked the umbrella handle behind his knee and tugged. Nix hit the roof on his back, sliding across wet tiles in a spray of chipped frost. He recovered by freezing the umbrella shut around her hand, trapping her fingers to the handle. Hana stared at the ice for one calm second, then snapped the umbrella's secret spring release, leaving Nix holding the frozen shell while she stepped away with only the bare steel cane.

Under the shattered skylight, the floor became a glittering field of broken glass. Venn charged across it anyway, expecting Sera to retreat, but she lowered her center of gravity and skated backward on two serving trays she had stolen from the station cafe. Every slash he made carved sparks from the trays instead of flesh. When he thrust low, she split her feet, letting the blade pass between the trays, then snapped them together around his sword with a metallic clap. Venn tried to wrench the blade free. Sera let the trays go, grabbed his sleeve, and used his own tug to spin him in a half circle. He did not fall; he adapted, planting one boot on a large pane of glass and sliding past her in turn. For one absurd second they crossed paths like duelists on ice. Then the trapped sword popped loose and both skidded into opposite benches, each blaming the floor rather than admitting the other had improvised well.

Kaito and Rook collide on the lacquered bridge above the banquet hall just as the temple bell begins swinging from a snapped ceiling chain. Rook tries to shoulder-charge him into the rail, but Kaito plants one sandal on the bell's bronze rim as it sweeps past, rides it sideways like a pendulum, and lets the momentum pull him out of reach. On the backswing he hooks his scarf around Rook's raised forearm, not to choke or bind him, but to yank Rook a half-step forward at the exact moment the bell returns. Rook ducks the bronze mass by sheer reflex, grinning as if he has solved it, only for Kaito to release the scarf and drop behind him. The bell misses Rook's head, smashes the bridge post instead, and the collapsing railing funnels Rook into a rolling tumble down a banner-draped staircase. It is not a knockout, just a humiliating forced descent that removes him from the bridge for a few crucial seconds.

The aquarium wall in the station restaurant becomes the center of a strange, luminous exchange between Kael and the water mage Iri. Iri draws thin whips of water out of the tank without breaking the glass, lashing Kael’s ankles and wrists with glowing blue arcs. Kael cannot get close without being snared. He backs into the sushi counter, grabs a rolling pin meant for noodle dough, and bats away two whips, but the third wraps his forearm and yanks him toward the aquarium. Instead of resisting, he runs with the pull, jumps onto the counter, and plants both feet on the glass. Iri smiles, expecting him to crack it and flood himself. Kael angles the rolling pin sideways between two decorative metal fish mounted on the frame, creating a temporary rung. He vaults over Iri’s water line, somersaults above her head, and flicks the restaurant’s soy sauce dispenser open as he passes. The dark spray hits the water whips, making them visible and heavy. Iri hesitates in surprise, and Kael lands behind her with the rolling pin braced across her elbows in a quick standing arm lock.

The smallest fighter in the brawl, Niko, survives his first clash with the iron-masked giant by noticing the giant’s habit of lowering his shoulder before every charge. Niko backs toward the station’s lost-and-found counter, where a jar of ornate hairpins has been knocked over during the chaos. When the giant thunders in, Niko grabs three pins between his fingers and dives straight toward the charge instead of away. The giant’s fist crashes through the counter behind him, showering the floor with claim tags. Niko slides under the punch, pops up beside the giant’s elbow, and taps the pins into three pressure points along the exposed inner arm, each one shallow but perfectly placed. The giant’s hand opens involuntarily, dropping the iron hammer he has been dragging all fight. Niko catches the hammer’s handle for only half a heartbeat, unable to lift it, but that is enough to swing its heavy head into the giant’s ankle. The giant’s own weapon sweeps his feet out, and he falls like a collapsing bell tower.

Seen through noir-tinted eyes, it was a simple crime of momentum. AKIRA came forward in blue while the fight was still young, all intent and sharp edges, and buried a knee into RYU-X before the red fighter could rewrite the scene. The force sent RYU-X drifting hard toward the right boundary, not with elegance, but with that staggered honesty fighters hate to show. AKIRA kept the pressure like a debt collector.
