RYU-X, proud as ever, stayed on his feet, yet the wear was beginning to leak through his posture. Too early for a verdict, maybe, but not too early to know who was making whom suffer.

Man, I was yelling before the hit even landed because you could feel AKIRA hunting. It was still early, but RYU-X already looked like he’d been shoved into a bad rhythm: block, stumble, reset, block again. Then blue just burst in from underneath him. AKIRA’s fist came up like a piston, clean and nasty, and RYU-X got popped backward toward the right edge with his red aura wobbling all over the place. The crowd went insane because it wasn’t just damage, it was a message. AKIRA wasn’t waiting, wasn’t measuring forever, wasn’t letting RYU-X breathe. He was the one pushing the story, and RYU-X was getting scraped away one exchange at a time.

Rika’s duel with Tetsu inside the mirror maze turned on one broken reflection. Tetsu moved carefully, spear held short, refusing to chase her false images. Rika realized he was tracking her by the squeak of her left boot on the polished floor. She stopped, peeled the loose rubber sole off that boot, and slapped it onto a mirror panel at waist height. Then she sprinted silently barefoot across the opposite lane. The next squeak came from the mirror when the sole slid downward under its own weight. Tetsu stabbed at the sound and punched his spear through the glass, trapping the blade in a glittering web. Rika burst from the real side, grabbed the spear’s tassel, and tied it around his wrist in one quick knot before vaulting over his shoulder, leaving him attached to his own mistaken reflection.

You could feel the middle of the fight tilting before it happened, and then AKIRA made it undeniable. Blue came in stalking, shoulders low, not giving RYU-X a breath, and RYU-X was already backing up like every exchange had sanded a little more off him. Then AKIRA rose and brought that attack down from above, clean through RYU-X's guard. Red snapped under it, not flattened, but shoved hard enough that his boots skidded toward the far right side. The crowd noise jumped because it was not just damage, it was position. AKIRA had the initiative, the space, the rhythm. RYU-X looked like he was still standing mostly out of stubbornness, and the wall was suddenly way too close.

No joke, that single punch changed the geometry of the fight. Before it, AKIRA still had some room to pretend he could circle out. After it, he was being carried toward the right boundary with RYU-X bearing down on him. This is early action, too, not some late exhausted scramble, which makes AKIRA’s condition more worrying. RYU-X is the aggressor in red, tight and decisive. He drives his fist through the lane in front of him, catches AKIRA clean, and forces blue to skid backward. AKIRA’s guard doesn’t fully save him; it just keeps him from folding completely. The momentum arrow is bright red.

Suzu's scuffle with the crow-helmeted courier burst through the paper umbrella shop. The courier was faster, bouncing from counter to counter with bladed boots that shredded the displays. Suzu ducked beneath a kick, grabbed a bundle of unopened umbrellas, and hurled them straight up instead of at him. The courier laughed and launched himself over her head, aiming to rake her back. Suzu stomped the shop's floor pedal, the one used to rotate the ceiling rack, and every tossed umbrella snapped open at once as it hit the spinning hooks. A sudden canopy of painted circles filled the air. The courier's boot blades caught in three different umbrella skins, halting him mid-flip. Suzu slid underneath, seized his trailing sash, and pulled him down through the spinning colors so he landed seated in the merchant's ink tray, perfectly marked with a black crow-shaped splash.

Nami got her revenge at the capsule-toy machines, where the floor was littered with plastic prize shells. Bront, twice her size and wearing an armored jaw guard, tried to body-check her into the row of machines. Nami kicked one capsule under his leading foot and another under his trailing foot, but he was too heavy to slip; the capsules simply cracked. So she changed the plan mid-charge. She jumped, planted both boots against his chest plate, and let him continue pushing her backward until her shoulders hit the glass of the biggest machine. The impact triggered the prize coil inside. A jumbo plush dragon dropped into the retrieval chute behind Bront’s calves. Nami released her grip at once, slid down, and hooked her arm through the dragon’s soft looped tail. When Bront took his next step, the plush wedged between his legs like a cheerful anchor. Nami yanked the tail, swept his feet with the toy’s stuffed body, and sent him toppling into a shower of bouncing capsules that all opened to reveal tiny versions of his own scowling face.

Mako’s improvised counter in the parking level began with him losing his footing on a trail of leaking motor oil. Juno lunged to exploit it, blades flashing toward Mako’s ribs. Instead of fighting the slide, Mako sat into it, grabbed the handle of an abandoned scooter, and let the oil carry both him and the scooter sideways. The blades struck sparks from the concrete pillar where he had been. Mako popped the scooter’s kickstand with his heel, turning the little vehicle into a metal hook. It caught Juno’s ankle as Mako spun past. Juno tried to hop free, but the scooter’s front wheel clipped a speed bump, sprang upright, and dumped him over the handlebars in a graceless half-somersault. Mako ended the exchange still seated on the slick floor, one hand raised as if he had meant to park there.

Sora’s exchange with the wolf-masked twins was all balance and timing. The twins had cornered him on the narrow maintenance bridge above Platform Seven, attacking in a rhythm meant to pinch him between mirrored crescent kicks. Sora backed up until his shoulders touched the signal-light pole. When the left twin swept low and the right twin spun high, Sora jumped straight up, not away, pressing both palms against the pole and tucking his knees. Their kicks passed under and over the empty space he had occupied, striking the pole together. The signal light shuddered, flickering from red to green to red again. Sora used that vibration to twist around the pole like a gymnast and drop behind the right twin. He did not kick him; instead, he unclipped the twin’s decorative tail sash and looped it around the left twin’s ankle as the two tried to reset. One tug sent both masks knocking together. By the time they looked up, Sora was sitting cross-legged atop the signal box, asking whether their pack had a leader or just matching accessories.

Mira disarmed a magnetic gauntlet in a way that depended on one spilled box of sewing needles. The gauntlet-wearing enforcer, Pell, kept catching her hairpins before they reached him, the device whining as it pulled metal toward his fist. Mira retreated to a costume stall and slashed open a drawer with her fan. Hundreds of needles scattered across the wet tiles. Pell laughed and raised the gauntlet, expecting to yank them all into a storm. Mira snapped her fan shut and kicked the drawer itself toward him. He magnetized the needles just as the wooden drawer slid under his leading foot. The needles flew upward, not at Mira, but into the gauntlet's exposed cooling vents. The magnet choked, sparked, and locked his arm straight above his head. Mira stepped in close, plucked one harmless ribbon pin from his collar, and used it to fasten his raised sleeve to an overhead clothesline. Pell dangled there, furious and decorative.

There was a beautiful brutality to it, if you like your anime fights with consequences. Mid-battle, with the glow of blue pressing into the heat of red, AKIRA descended into RYU-X’s space and struck him down along the crown of his defense. RYU-X had already been dulled by the chase, his counters coming later, his stance less proud than stubborn. The blow did not simply hurt him; it carried him, scraping his balance toward the rightmost side, where escape starts to feel imaginary. AKIRA followed as if gravity itself had taken his side. RYU-X remained upright, but the scene made him look smaller, worn thinner, and trapped inside AKIRA’s momentum.

I swear the whole arena tilted blue for a second. We were still in the early stretch, not even deep enough for anyone to call it a comeback situation, and AKIRA was already walking RYU-X down like he owned the floor. RYU-X tried to plant his feet in red and answer, but AKIRA slipped in tight and ripped a punch straight up through the guard. It caught RYU-X under the jaw and sent him skidding and lifting toward the right boundary. That was the moment you could see the wear starting to show: RYU-X drifting backward, shoulders loose, balance broken, while AKIRA kept moving forward like the fight had only just opened for him.

At the mooncake stall, Juno turned a cooking prop into a weapon without ever breaking the vendor’s display. Kuro lunged at him with a hooked saber, forcing Juno backward until his heel hit the iron griddle. Rather than dodge wide, Juno snatched up the long-handled spatula used for flipping festival cakes. He parried the saber once, twice, then let the third strike slide down the spatula’s edge until Kuro’s blade wedged against the handle guard. With his free hand, Juno flipped a steaming mooncake straight up. Kuro instinctively looked at it, expecting a distraction to the face, but Juno had aimed for the sign rope above him. The cake slapped the rope, powdered sugar burst like smoke, and the hanging menu board swung down behind Kuro’s knees. Juno shoved the locked saber and spatula forward at the same time, tripping Kuro neatly over the board. Kuro crashed into a stack of empty flour sacks, while the single mooncake landed back on the griddle, somehow browned perfectly on both sides.

Hoshiko's glass-floor moment silenced the whole rooftop for a breath. She and Sable had reached the observation bridge, a transparent walkway over the lower market. Sable tried to frighten her by stamping cracks into the glass with his iron-heeled boots, each spiderweb fracture glowing underfoot. Hoshiko noticed the cracks formed a jagged circle around him, but not around her. When he dashed forward for a low sweep, she did not jump. She tapped her prayer staff once on the exact intersection of three cracks and whispered a calming chant. The glass pane under Sable did not explode; it simply dropped an inch out of its frame. That tiny fall stole his balance. His sweep slid beneath Hoshiko's robes, missing by a finger's width, and his other leg plunged through the loosened pane up to the thigh. Hoshiko caught him by the scarf before he could fall farther, then tied the scarf around the bridge rail and walked away while he complained about mercy.

The animator in me noticed the weight of it more than the flash. Early on, when the combatants still should have been testing each other, RYU-X was already taking command. His red silhouette narrows, shoots forward, and the contact point lands hard enough that AKIRA’s blue outline compresses before sliding away. The motion pulls the eye toward the right margin: AKIRA is forced back there by the force of the hit, not by choice. It’s a very clean piece of visual storytelling. RYU-X’s body language says pursuit; AKIRA’s says absorption. He’s still upright, still fighting, but the fatigue is starting to show in how late his recovery is.

Listen, as a RYU-X fan, that was delicious. Not because it was flashy in the usual overdone way, but because it showed control. Halfway through, Akira was still dangerous, sure, but he was getting sanded down. RYU-X had him reacting, flinching, stepping where he did not want to step. Then red slipped in and cracked him with that curved icy punch, the kind that comes around the guard instead of politely meeting it. Akira got shoved toward the far right, and you could almost see the panic calculation start: less room, heavier legs, RYU-X still coming.

That was the kind of contact you feel in your teeth. Akira came forward in blue, calm but mean, and put his hand through Ryu-X’s defense like he was pushing open a stuck door. Ryu-X, all red and stubborn, got blasted sideways toward the right-hand border, and for a second his resistance looked purely mechanical—feet catching, knees locking, body trying not to give up more ground. This is still the front portion of the match, which makes it worse for him. You do not want to be visibly fading this early. Akira is the one choosing when the clash happens, where it moves, and how hard Ryu-X has to work afterward. Ryu-X is being shaved down exchange by exchange.

The exchange at the broken aquarium was uniquely cruel to Sable's composure. He cornered little Kenji beside the cracked glass tank, confident his gravity gauntlet would make the boy's jumping style useless. Sable punched downward, and every loose pebble in the hall slammed flat. Kenji did not jump; he dove into the shallow flood spreading from the aquarium, sliding on his stomach beneath the heavy field. Sable tried to stomp him, but Kenji caught a floating decorative castle, flipped it upright, and wedged it under the heel before the boot landed. The sudden height difference pitched Sable forward. Kenji popped up behind him with a koi net, hooked the gauntlet's exposed wrist cable, and pulled as if ringing a bell. The gravity field inverted for one ridiculous heartbeat. Sable rose two feet into the air, arms windmilling, while every rescued goldfish bounced gently upward around him like orange lanterns.

Poor RYU-X, man. You could see he wanted to reset. This wasn’t the opening rush anymore; they were deep enough into the battle that every breath looked heavy, and red was carrying the bruises of all those earlier exchanges. Then AKIRA came in again, relentless, and struck down from above like he was punishing RYU-X for even thinking about lifting his eyes. The hit snapped RYU-X out of his attempted recovery and sent him stumbling toward the right-hand limit. It felt cruel because it wasn’t reckless. AKIRA looked fresh enough to keep forcing decisions, while RYU-X looked like he was borrowing time from the next mistake.

My photographer brain remembers it as a diagonal smear of color. AKIRA’s blue shape leaned forward, arm extended, the whole body behind one narrow line of force. RYU-X’s red silhouette buckled at the point of contact, knees bent wrong, heels scraping as he was pushed toward the right-hand border. The late-battle wear showed everywhere: the loosened guard, the slower recovery, the way RYU-X’s head snapped after the strike instead of rolling with it. AKIRA was not waiting for mistakes anymore. AKIRA was creating them, step by step, and that thrust was the clearest frame of the pressure turning into displacement.

An old dojo instructor would point to that exchange and say the match was won before the contact. AKIRA had made RYU-X carry tension in the legs and shoulders through the middle portion of the duel. By the time the blue fighter launched that high-to-low attack, RYU-X’s base was compromised. The red fighter met the strike too upright, absorbed it badly, and was driven toward the right-side boundary. It was a lesson in initiative: the attacker chose height, timing, and direction; the defender merely received consequences. RYU-X was not broken yet, but he was being shaved down. AKIRA, meanwhile, kept advancing like pressure was a craft, not an emotion.

Let me tell you, that was the point where I started smiling because RYU-X had him. Not finished, sure, but handled. Midway through, AKIRA was no longer moving like the confident blue menace from the start. He was a step slow, a little hunched, and RYU-X just marched into that weakness. The red fighter whipped out a clean cutting strike, caught AKIRA across his attempt to guard, and sent him sliding toward the right edge of the field. Beautiful pressure. No wasted motion. No hesitation. AKIRA got pushed back into bad geography while RYU-X stayed on offense, and that’s when you knew the fight’s rhythm belonged to him.

Goro and the porcelain-faced monk collided beside the noodle cart, and for a moment the brawl turned absurdly domestic. The monk caught Goro's first hammer punch in a prayer clasp and redirected it into a pot of broth, scalding steam bursting up to blind them both. Goro roared and grabbed the entire cart axle instead of retreating. The monk expected a swing, so he ducked early, but Goro only lifted one side of the cart and let the wheels spin. The hanging ladles became a rattling curtain, striking the monk's mask at irregular beats. When the monk finally stepped through the clatter, Goro abandoned the axle, seized a bundle of uncooked noodles, and slapped them across the monk's wrists. It was not damaging, just sticky enough to ruin the monk's next hand seal. Goro then shouldered him into the broth barrel, where the monk surfaced wearing a cabbage leaf like a crown.

From a coach’s eye, the important part was not the flash, it was the positioning. Early in the match, AKIRA had already forced RYU-X to respect the center. RYU-X was giving ground in small, ugly pieces, and then AKIRA punished that retreat perfectly. He dipped under the red fighter’s response, drove upward from his legs, and the blow rose clean through RYU-X’s middle line. RYU-X’s head snapped, his frame came unglued, and he was carried toward the right side of the arena. That was not a desperate swing. That was pressure converted into elevation. AKIRA was dictating, and RYU-X was starting to look chipped down.

Kaito survived the incense-smoke ambush by dodging something he could not see. Near the shrine brazier, Veyra extinguished every lantern with a wind cut and tossed a fistful of powdered incense into the coals. Sweet smoke boiled outward, thick enough to erase hands and feet. Kaito heard her sandals circle him, then heard three false footfalls made by thrown pebbles. Rather than guess, he flipped his own scarf into the smoke and watched the fabric's edge twitch in the disturbed air. A narrow ripple sliced toward his ribs. Kaito folded backward so far his knuckles brushed the tiles, letting Veyra's invisible blade pass over his stomach. He then kicked straight up, not at her body, but at the little bell tied to her sword hilt. The bell rang once inside the smoke. Kaito spun toward the sound and shoulder-checked her out of the cloud, both fighters emerging like ghosts from a burst of gold ash.

In the library archive, Professor Haze floated above the floor on pages torn from forbidden books, dodging Rei’s short sword with lazy contempt. Rei sheathed the sword and climbed the rolling ladder instead, which made Haze laugh even harder. The professor sent a cyclone of pages to shred the ladder’s wheels. Rei jumped at the last second, not toward Haze but toward the towering card catalog. She kicked one drawer open, used it as a foothold, and sprang again as dozens of index cards erupted behind her. Haze’s paper cyclone swallowed the cards, suddenly clogged with alphabetical dividers and brass labels. Its rotation stuttered. Rei landed on the top rail of the moving ladder, which was still rolling from her first push, and rode it like a jousting horse. She unsheathed the sword only at the end, slicing the strap that held Haze’s book satchel. Without the satchel, his floating pages dropped him into the reading table.

Chat lost it when that quick red-hand check landed. We were only in the first chunk of the match, but RYU-X was already playing like he owned center screen. AKIRA tried to hold ground, maybe angle out, but the timing was rough: RYU-X darted in and popped him with a tight forward strike, just enough snap to make the blue side stutter and slide toward the right wall. It was such a momentum swing without being a giant explosion. You could see AKIRA getting bullied backward, posture less confident, options narrowing. RYU-X, meanwhile, looked fresh, mean, and completely in control of the pace. Early fight, yes, but the story was obvious: red advancing, blue deteriorating, and the boundary getting way too close.

Okay, casual viewer here, but even I could tell who was running the match. This was still early, the sort of phase where both fighters are supposed to be testing each other, yet RYU-X had already turned it into a chase. AKIRA was backing up, breathing heavier, and looking like every contact was costing him more than it should. Then RYU-X came in from the left side of the pressure, cocked his arm just enough, and drove a direct punch into him. No fancy spiral, no long windup, just a burning red line forward. AKIRA got sent sliding toward the right edge, boots scraping, balance half-broken. It felt like the first clear sign that blue was in trouble.

I was watching with my little brother, and even he could tell who was in control. This was late, when both fighters should have been cautious, but AKIRA wasn’t cautious at all. He advanced like he had plenty left, cutting across RYU-X’s front with a fast, brutal sweep. RYU-X tried to block, or maybe just flinched into something that looked like a block, but he was too worn down to make it matter. The red fighter got pushed hard toward the right edge, stumbling in that panicked way characters do when the wall is suddenly a character too. My brother just whispered, ‘He’s trapped,’ and honestly, yes. AKIRA wasn’t merely scoring a hit. He was compressing the battlefield around a tired opponent.

Early on, before the clash had reached its heated middle, RYU-X caught AKIRA trying to reset. A red streak ripped across the blue fighter's front and shoved him back toward the right edge. AKIRA didn't collapse, but you could see the toll in the way he stumbled and guarded late. RYU-X stayed on offense, pressing forward without giving him room.

I swear the crowd made one sound when it landed, like everyone inhaled at once. This was not the opening scramble anymore; they were deep enough in that Akira's movements had started to lose their brightness. RYU-X had been pressing him for a while, red streaking forward again and again, and then he finally slipped into range with that bent-arm smash from the side. Akira tried to brace, but it still cracked across him and sent him skidding toward the right edge of the arena. The worst part was how RYU-X followed immediately, like he smelled that Akira was fading.

At the taiko platform, Oren turns sound into a weapon, but only after pretending to lose the rhythm. Kage darts around him in a blur, striking the drumheads with kunai so every boom masks his footsteps. Oren’s staff keeps arriving a fraction late, gouging wood where Kage had just been. Then Kage vanishes behind the largest drum and stabs through its skin, aiming for Oren’s ribs. Oren catches the kunai point between two fingers, but Kage uses the grip to yank him forward. It looks like the assassin has the perfect opening. Oren headbutts the drum instead of Kage. The impact sends a deep, warped note through the torn hide, and the broken drum amplifies it unevenly, making the whole platform buck. Kage’s balance falters for the first time. Oren releases the kunai, spins his staff under one arm, and strikes three smaller drums in sequence: left, right, center. Each beat kicks up a visible ring of pressure. Kage dodges the first two, but the third catches the smoke bombs on his belt and detonates them all at once, wrapping him in his own blinding cloud while Oren calmly sweeps his legs.

From where I was yelling in the cheap seats, this was the moment the end started feeling real. AKIRA, still glowing blue and still moving first, slipped in close and popped RYU-X with that tiny, nasty lead-hand strike—not huge, not flashy, but it landed clean. RYU-X’s red frame jolted backward like his feet had forgotten the floor was there, and he got shoved farther toward the right boundary. You could tell he was already fraying by then: shoulders stiff, guard late, reactions half a breath behind. AKIRA wasn’t chasing anymore; he was herding. This late in the fight, that little hit carried the weight of everything before it, and RYU-X looked like he knew he was being pushed into a corner he might not escape.

Kanna uses the broken bell clapper as an anchor in her clash with Venn. The iron clapper lies across the floor, chained to the fallen bell rope, too heavy for most fighters to move. Venn steps over it confidently and thrusts his palm toward Kanna’s sternum. She retreats one pace, luring him until his rear foot is inside the loop of chain. With a quick toe flick, she flips the loop up around his ankle. Venn notices and tries to jump away, but Kanna drives her heel into the clapper’s round end. It rolls half a turn, tightening the chain and yanking his leg backward. His palm strike falls short by a finger’s width. Kanna rotates under his extended arm and applies a shoulder lock, but Venn drops his trapped knee hard onto the clapper. The shock travels through the chain, jarring her grip loose. He tears free, yet the escape leaves him hopping on one foot, and Kanna calmly sweeps the other with the bell rope.

Tetsu chases Hoshiko through the bakery stalls, snapping short punches that explode trays of sweet buns around her head. She ducks behind a stack of flour sacks, and he drives a fist through the top bag, creating a white burst that blinds them both. Tetsu expects panic and swings by memory at where her face was. Hoshiko has already dropped to the floor, sweeping a rolling pin across the tiles. The pin clips his front foot, but he hops over it and brings his heel down like a hammer. Hoshiko uses the rolling pin as an axle, sliding her body around it just outside the stomp. She kicks the leg of a cooling rack, sending rows of custard tarts skidding between them. Tetsu steps on one, loses traction, and windmills his arms. Hoshiko rises inside the flour cloud with a baker's peel, the flat wooden paddle used for ovens, and smacks him squarely on the backside. The hit is more humiliating than damaging, launching him headfirst into a curtain of hanging pretzels.

Mina tries to end the rooftop side of the brawl with a single talisman arrow aimed at Kuro’s chest. Kuro waits until the glowing paper fins are close enough to light his mask, then raises a broken roof tile like a shield. The arrow pierces the tile and detonates, but instead of being blown back, Kuro twists with the blast and lets the tile shatter into a fan of ceramic shards. He snatches one shard from the air between two fingers and skips it across the sloped tiles like a flat stone on water. Mina expects a direct shot and leans away; the shard ricochets off a copper rain gutter behind her, clips the bowstring at her knuckles, and pins the severed string to a wooden spirit charm. Her bow whips uselessly open. Kuro lunges to capitalize, but Mina kicks the pinned charm free, snapping the loose bow limbs together against his nose with a sharp crack.

At the city fountain, the final exchange before the villains regrouped belonged to little Toma, who had been dismissed as a tagalong. The assassin Selene lunged at his sister with a needle hidden in her sleeve. Toma threw his backpack at Selene’s face, and she sliced it open without slowing down. Notebooks, candy wrappers, and a tin pencil case scattered into the fountain spray. Selene stepped through them, but Toma had already kicked the pencil case lid into the water jet. The jet flipped the shiny lid upward like a tiny mirror. Sunlight flashed off it into Selene’s eyes at the exact instant she aimed the needle. Her thrust went wide, pricking only the strap of Toma’s backpack as it fell. Toma grabbed the dangling strap with both hands and swung around Selene’s extended arm, wrapping it once, then twice. His sister finished the moment by tapping Selene’s wrist with a wooden practice sword, making the hidden needle drop into the fountain drain.

Jax's aura flared red as he charged straight through a curtain of paper talismans Kuro had scattered across the concourse. Everyone expected explosions, bindings, or ghostly chains. Nothing happened. Jax laughed, believing Kuro had bluffed, and swung a hook the size of a mallet. Kuro leaned back just far enough that the punch grazed his chin, then tapped two fingers to the floor. The talismans were not traps for Jax; they were markers for the tiles. Every tile beneath Jax popped upward by an inch in a zigzag path, throwing off his stance one foot at a time. His second punch fired into empty air. Kuro stepped along the rising tiles as if climbing stairs, reached Jax's shoulder, and chopped at the pressure point near his collarbone. Jax grimaced but refused to fall. He headbutted the last raised tile with such force that it flipped up and smacked Kuro in the back as he landed.

The chandelier exchange belongs entirely to Mira and the armored captain Boru. He swings a slab-like shield in a horizontal arc that clears three tables and would have flattened Mira against the orchestra pit. She leaps, catches one of the crystal chandelier ropes, and lets the shield pass beneath her bare feet close enough to ring the metal anklets. Boru yanks the rope's loose end, thinking he can bring her down, but Mira had already hooked her heel around a second rope hidden among the dangling prisms. The pull tilts the whole chandelier like a ship's wheel. Crystal droplets rain down, not sharp enough to wound, but bright enough to fill Boru's visor with fractured reflections. Mira releases at the top of the tilt, flips once, and lands on the back of his shield while he is still looking upward. Rather than striking him, she taps the shield's release latch with her toe. The shield face drops open like a drawbridge, and Boru charges straight into the soft pile of velvet chair cushions behind it.

Oro's most elegant escape was from Juno's water-chain technique near the fountain memorial. Juno had finally caught him: three streams wrapped Oro's wrists and throat, dragging him toward the fountain basin where a sealing circle glowed under the water. Oro went limp, letting the chains pull him faster. Juno tightened his stance, expecting a last-second knife trick. Instead, Oro opened his mouth and bit the stream at his throat. His golden aura turned his teeth into a tuning fork; the bitten water vibrated, and that vibration traveled back along the chains into Juno's fingers. Juno's hands numbed instantly. Oro used the slack to fold backward, plant both boots on the fountain statue's face, and push off. He shot toward Juno headfirst, wrists still bound, and used the water chains like reins to steer himself around a marble pillar. The chains wrapped the pillar twice, yanking Juno off his feet. Oro landed behind him, flicked his bound wrists apart, and made the water snap like wet rope against Juno's back. The sealing circle in the basin activated on empty air, trapping only Oro's reflection for a few glittering seconds.

The strangest exchange erupted when every fighter converged near the fallen chandelier, its crystal strands scattered like glittering vines. Tetsu tried to seize control of the battlefield by magnetizing the chandelier's iron core, lifting the whole broken fixture into a spinning overhead hazard. Juno immediately threaded wires through the crystal loops, turning his weapon into her puppet. Tetsu pulled left, Juno pulled right, and the chandelier began wobbling above them like a drunken moon. Rook saw the shadow pass over Mira and shoved her aside with one shoulder, taking the first falling strand across his back. Mira, annoyed at being rescued, punched upward with a gravity burst that made half the crystals shoot toward the ceiling instead of down. Selene used those rising crystals as stepping stones, skipping across them to reach Tetsu's blind side. Hana noticed the attack first and flicked her umbrella open in Selene's path, not to block her body but to hide the crystal she was about to step on. Selene's foot found empty air. She dropped, slashed the umbrella canopy to ribbons on the way down, and landed in a crouch just as the chandelier core finally tore free and embedded itself in the floor between all six fighters.

If you chart the momentum, that late sequence is the clearest red spike. Akira was already on diminishing returns: slower entries, weaker stance recovery, and less lateral control. RYU-X exploited exactly that. He met Akira’s advance with a firm defensive check, stopped the blue fighter’s offense cold, then converted the stopped force into territorial gain. The result was Akira being funneled toward the right boundary, which is a terrible position at that point in the match. RYU-X was the aggressor even though the contact began defensively, because he gained ground, dictated direction, and forced Akira to respond under pressure. Akira’s body language said survival. RYU-X’s said closing procedure.

As someone watching from the lower rows, the sound is what I remember first. Not a dramatic explosion, just that ugly, heavy thud when AKIRA’s bent leg crashed into RYU-X and made the red guy buckle backward. This was still near the beginning, so nobody expected RYU-X to look that bothered yet, but he did. He went sliding toward the far right side, trying to plant his feet while AKIRA kept leaning into the attack. Blue had this look like he smelled weakness. Red had the look of someone realizing the match was already becoming more expensive than planned.

Mako and Tetsu collided beside the giant taiko drum displayed in the cultural wing, and for a moment it looked like a simple test of strength. Tetsu slammed the spear shaft across Mako’s forearms, forcing him down toward one knee. Mako stopped resisting all at once. The sudden slack made Tetsu overcommit, and Mako ducked beneath the shaft, ramming his shoulder into the taiko’s stretched hide. The drum boomed so loudly that everyone on the floor flinched. More importantly, the rebound threw Mako back into Tetsu from an unexpected angle. He used the bounce to clamp Tetsu around the waist and lift just enough to turn him, not throw him. Tetsu’s boots landed inside the huge drum’s wooden stand, wedged between two carved supports. Mako released him and backed off while Tetsu chopped at the stand, furious and stuck.

Rina's most elegant counter happened in the rain beyond the station doors, where the plaza tiles were painted with neon reflections. A swordswoman in a white coat pressed her with a draw-cut so fast that the blade seemed to skip frames. Rina tossed a handful of paper talismans upward, but the swordswoman sliced them before they could ignite. That was the feint. The cut created dozens of fluttering halves, and each half drank the rain until it became heavy enough to fall in a ring around the swordswoman's boots. Rina stamped once. The wet paper snapped taut into a low binding circle. The swordswoman tried to step out and found her ankles cinched by paper cords. She still managed a final horizontal slash. Rina leaned backward just enough that the blade skimmed a single raindrop off her nose, then answered by flicking that same droplet from her fingertip into the swordswoman's eye.

Man, the crowd noise would have swallowed the room right there. AKIRA tried to sneak something in during the early run of the fight, and RYU-X just shut the door on him. Red blade, sharp sweep, blue body jolting backward. AKIRA got forced toward the right border with that ragged slide that says he absorbed more than he wanted to admit. RYU-X was all forward pressure; AKIRA was starting to look like he was carrying the whole match on bruised legs.

The strangest moment belonged to Old Man Sazan, who had spent most of the brawl pretending to be too frail to join in. When Goro the Stoneback charged him near the souvenir kiosks, everyone expected Sazan to vanish or counter with some secret blade. He did neither. He opened an umbrella. Goro’s fist struck the black fabric with enough force to bend the steel ribs backward, but Sazan rotated the handle with two fingers at the instant of contact. The umbrella caught the punch, folded around Goro’s forearm, and locked the big man’s wrist inside a cage of bent spokes. Sazan then stepped in close, tapped Goro’s elbow with the lacquered handle, and made the entire arm lever sideways. The joint-lock was tiny, almost polite, but Goro’s knees buckled as if the floor had betrayed him. Sazan guided him face-first into a postcard rack, apologized to the rack, and abandoned the ruined umbrella because the trick could never work with that mangled frame again.

Daichi’s clash with the clockwork monk took place beneath the giant station clock, whose minute hand had frozen during the chaos. The monk’s metal sleeves extended on springs, punching from impossible distances. Daichi kept getting tagged until he noticed each sleeve retracted with a ticking delay. He baited a left punch toward his face, ducked, and slapped a baggage claim sticker onto the sleeve as it shot past. The sleeve retracted into the monk’s robe, sticker and all. Daichi then ran straight for the clock’s maintenance chain. The monk fired both sleeves to stop him, but Daichi jumped and caught the chain, swinging just above the punches. One sleeve struck the frozen minute hand, jarring it loose. The clock boomed, and the hand dropped from twelve to six in a rapid sweep. Daichi released the chain, landed behind the monk, and tugged the baggage sticker’s long paper backing, which still trailed from the left sleeve. The monk turned to punch, but the paper had wrapped around the descending minute hand. His own sleeve was pulled upward, lifting him onto his toes in a ridiculous half-salute as the clock finally resumed ticking.

The judging note is simple: clean offense, positional gain, visible effect. RYU-X initiated during the early portion, landed a pronounced curved kick, and forced AKIRA toward the right perimeter. AKIRA did not answer immediately; he absorbed and retreated, which made the exchange read decisively in RYU-X’s favor. More importantly, AKIRA appeared to be wearing down under sustained pressure already. For scoring the flow of the fight, this moment strongly reinforced red’s command of pace.

Forum take, posted immediately after rewatching it three times: that late push was not just a block, it was a statement. Akira had been fading for a while, and RYU-X finally turned that fatigue into map control. Blue goes in, red braces, contact gets swallowed, and suddenly Akira is being forced toward the rightmost lane with no clean reset. The direction matters. If Akira had space behind him, maybe he could roll out or circle. Instead, RYU-X keeps him traveling sideways into the danger zone, making every step look more desperate. This is why I say RYU-X was fully on offense even while using a defensive shape. He wins the exchange because Akira loses territory, balance, and composure all at once.

I watched it like a boxing coach and winced before it even landed. AKIRA’s weight was too high, his exit was predictable, and RYU-X was reading him early. We’re still in the first third of the battle, yet blue is already taking the kind of pressure that makes your guard heavy. RYU-X steps into range and fires a straight-line punch with red heat behind it. It connects square, and AKIRA is driven toward the right edge, not by choice but by impact. His feet try to reset, but his upper body is shoved back first, which is always ugly. RYU-X keeps the forward posture after contact, which tells you he’s not relieved he landed; he expected to. AKIRA, on the other hand, looks like he’s losing comfort by the second.

Okay, so from my seat it looked less like a flashy strike and more like RYU-X just imposed himself. The red guy came in guarded, shoulders tight, forearms up, and when AKIRA tried to check him, the whole clash buckled in RYU-X’s favor. AKIRA slid sideways, boots dragging, blue aura flickering like it was struggling to keep the outline together. They were already well into the match by then, past the feeling-out part, and you could see AKIRA had been softened up. He didn’t crumble, but he lost the patch of ground he was trying to defend. RYU-X kept advancing and made him retreat toward the far-right edge, which had the crowd around me making that low “oh no” sound because everyone knew what corner pressure meant. This was RYU-X taking command without needing a huge windup.

Juno tried to end the fight on the glass skybridge by turning retreat into a trap. He sprinted away from the Oni Twins, letting his long white scarf stream behind him as if he had simply forgotten it. Mako, the larger twin, stomped after him and swung a concrete breaker overhand. Juno hopped onto the bridge railing, wrapped the scarf around a hanging maintenance hook, and dropped backward. The scarf went taut across ankle height just as Mako lunged. Instead of tripping forward, Mako planted the breaker and vaulted, almost avoiding it completely. Juno grinned, flicked his wrist, and the scarf's hidden clasp released from his collar, whipping around Mako's raised knee. Mako spun in midair and crashed through a row of holographic train ads, landing in a shower of flickering cherry blossoms.

As a shameless RYU-X fan, this was delicious. We were barely into the match and he was already bullying the blue guy like rent was due. He darts in, red flare cutting across the space, and plants that long forward strike right into AKIRA’s defense—except the defense basically folds. AKIRA gets shoved toward the right edge, boots skidding, shoulders turning like he’s trying to catch himself and failing. That’s the part I loved: RYU-X didn’t overextend or celebrate, he just kept advancing, like this was exactly the pace he planned. AKIRA looked annoyed, sure, but more than that he looked worn, already getting trimmed down by pressure before the fight had even reached its middle stretch.

From the press row, the decisive image was Akira's body angling away after impact. The bout had settled into its central stretch, and the initiative belonged increasingly to RYU-X. He advanced in red with no hesitation, while Akira's blue silhouette looked slower, more reactive, worn by the previous exchanges. RYU-X delivered a tight, curving punch from close range that landed cleanly and drove Akira laterally across the floor. The push carried him toward the right edge, changing the geography of the fight. RYU-X remained the pursuer; Akira became the fighter being moved.

As a play-by-play guy, I swear this was the point where the finish started to feel inevitable. RYU-X was already walking AKIRA down, red aura eating up the space, and then he sold that sudden entry like he was going to crash straight in. AKIRA bit hard. His guard lifted, his feet stuttered, and RYU-X slid into the opening without ever giving him the strike he expected. It was not a huge blast, just a cruel little misdirection that stole the last safe patch of floor. AKIRA skidded backward toward the right boundary, shoulders tight, clearly tired. Late in the fight, with blue fading and red pressing, that fake-out felt heavier than any clean punch.

Okay, I screamed. I admit it. Because that palm strike was nasty. RYU-X had been getting chipped down for a while, and you could see him doing that anime thing where he’s still pretending he’s fine even though his breathing is uneven and his guard keeps drooping. Then AKIRA just says, basically, no more breathing room. He steps in, blue aura popping, and plants his hand right into RYU-X’s chest or ribs, somewhere that made the whole red side of the screen jolt. RYU-X gets shoved hard to the right, stumbling backward with his arms half-open like he didn’t expect that much force. This was not early nerves anymore; this was mid-fight momentum, and AKIRA was absolutely driving it.

The kid beside me had been cheering for the red guy all night, and even he went quiet there. It was the final stretch, the part where every breath looks expensive, and RYU-X was paying too much for every step. AKIRA, in blue, pressed in with no hesitation. One compact, stabbing surge landed flush, and RYU-X was driven across the floor toward the right margin. It wasn’t a dramatic toss or a wild blast; it was a clean connection that kept moving after it hit. AKIRA looked fresh enough to chase. RYU-X looked like he was being filed down into nothing.

Mako’s most embarrassing dodge happened when Oren tried to finish her with the heavy ceremonial bell. He had torn it from the upper balcony and swung it by its rope, timing the arc so it would catch her as she leapt over a fissure in the floor. Mako saw the bronze mouth widening toward her and, instead of blocking, she deliberately killed her own flame aura. The sudden loss of lift dropped her straight down into the gap. Oren’s bell whooshed over the opening, clipped the balcony rail, and rang so loudly that everyone in the brawl flinched. From inside the crack, Mako jammed both palms against opposite stone faces, halted her fall, and exhaled a thin spark upward. The spark shot into the bell’s hollow interior, igniting the dust and bat guano caked inside. The bell coughed a cone of dirty fire back at Oren’s face, forcing him to release the rope and stagger away blind.

Old fan here, and that moment reminded me of classic corner-carry punishment. None of the flashy nonsense matters if one fighter is tired and the other keeps taking ground. RYU-X had the initiative late, plain as day. AKIRA was backing off, shoulders tense, guard not quite where it needed to be. RYU-X hammered him from the high line, and the blow sent him scooting toward the right side. That is veteran cruelty: do not just land something big, land it in a way that puts the opponent closer to the trap. AKIRA in blue was still brave, sure, but bravery was not stopping the red machine from marching him down.

If you want the honest streamer's take, this was the moment the matchup started looking grim for Ryu-X. We're in the middle phase, resources visibly spent, and Akira is the one pressing buttons first, so to speak. He darts forward and lands that straight-line impaling strike before Ryu-X can stuff it. Boom, red gets shoved toward the right edge, sliding back with the kind of stagger that says, 'I blocked too much earlier and now my reactions are cooked.' Akira keeps the initiative after contact, not giving him room to reset. It is not a flashy explosion moment; it is worse for Ryu-X, because it is controlled. Blue is taking space, red is losing it.

As someone who coaches fundamentals, I hated and admired that exchange. AKIRA had his back-line awareness failing because fatigue was taking over. In the last phase of the contest, once a fighter starts conceding steps without re-centering, the opponent can choose the finishing geometry. RYU-X did exactly that. He stayed on offense, made AKIRA respect the forward threat, then struck from above the guard. The hit forced AKIRA toward the right boundary and turned a bad defensive position into a worse one. AKIRA did not simply get hit; he lost territory at the same time. That is the kind of late-match pressure that breaks disciplined fighters. RYU-X was accelerating, while AKIRA was shrinking.

From the press row, it looked like the closing paragraph writing itself. RYU-X maintained forward pressure through the late stage, refusing to let AKIRA reset to center. AKIRA, visibly depleted, tried to hold his ground for a fraction too long. The red fighter's attack descended over the top and struck cleanly, breaking through the defensive posture and carrying AKIRA toward the right boundary. The crowd reaction shifted from excitement to recognition: this was not an even exchange. It was the aggressor extending control. AKIRA lost both stability and space, while RYU-X emerged from the contact still advancing, still imposing the rhythm, and clearly pushing the match toward its conclusion.

As a coach, I hated what RYU-X did there. He gave AKIRA the lane. Early in the contest, when legs should still be fresh, the red fighter was already reacting late, and AKIRA punished that hesitation with a brutal heel-of-the-hand blow straight through the guard. The impact folded RYU-X just enough to break his stance, then sent him sliding toward the right-side limit of the arena. AKIRA followed with that forward lean that says, I am not letting you breathe. RYU-X was not finished, but he was losing the small battles: balance, room, timing, confidence. That single palm strike told the whole story of the opening third: blue advancing, red deteriorating.

When the shrine bell crashed down in the center of the concourse, everyone scattered except Ayu and the spear saint Renka. Renka used the bell as cover, stabbing around its bronze curve with impossible accuracy. Ayu circled, unable to get close, until she noticed the bell still humming from its fall. She flicked two prayer coins into the hollow underside. The coins ricocheted inside, making the bell’s vibration wobble. Renka thrust again, but the distorted resonance bent the spear tip’s sound-tracking enchantment. It skewed left by a handspan. Ayu let the blade tear a ribbon from her sleeve, then stomped the bell’s rim with both feet. The bell tipped just enough for Renka’s spear shaft to wedge under it. Ayu vaulted onto the bronze surface, ran up the curve, and slid down the other side like a ramp, heel-first. Her sliding kick struck Renka’s chest exactly as the bell finished tipping back, pinning the spear flat beneath it. Renka went down coughing, not beaten for long, but completely disarmed for that one ringing, embarrassing beat.

The moment reads like a predator finally getting the angle. Earlier, RYU-X had space to flare up, answer, and make AKIRA respect him. By the middle stretch, that space was disappearing. AKIRA came in blue-fast, body lowered, intent absolutely clear, and smashed into RYU-X before the red fighter could regain a stable base. The force dragged RYU-X toward the right side, his feet scraping backward in a way that made the whole crowd groan. You could tell he tried to harden his stance, but his body had already absorbed too much from the exchanges before it. AKIRA stayed in control of the line, pushing the fight where he wanted it to go. That is the scary part: RYU-X was not just hit; he was relocated. The right edge became a threat because AKIRA made it one, and RYU-X looked like he was running out of clean answers.

From the couch, I could feel the match tilting completely toward AKIRA by then. It was late, both fighters already looked scraped up, but RYU-X was the one whose guard had started to sag. AKIRA in blue didn’t give him room to breathe. He stepped in and fired one clean, direct punch right down the middle, no flourish, just pressure and timing. It cracked into RYU-X in red before he could reset his feet, and the impact shoved him backward toward the right side like the arena itself was running out of space for him. That was the moment where it stopped feeling even. AKIRA was hunting; RYU-X was surviving.

The snack-cart joint lock began with Mina apparently surrendering. Ozu had seized her wrist in a crushing grip beside the rolling cart full of bottled ramune, and he twisted her arm behind her back while bragging that no one escaped his bear hold. Mina winced, nodded, and reached with her free hand for a bottle as though she needed a drink. Ozu laughed and tightened the hold. Mina used the marble-stopper bottle as a tiny lever, wedging its neck between his thumb and her trapped wrist. Then she pressed the marble cap against the cart’s opener with her hip. The bottle popped open explosively, fizz spraying across Ozu’s knuckles. His grip loosened for exactly one breath. Mina rotated toward the thumb, slid under his arm, and kept the bottle trapped against his wrist as she turned. The motion folded his elbow over the cart’s push handle, locking his forearm between metal rail and glass. He was not hurt, just immobilized and furious, while Mina calmly took a sip from the still-fizzing bottle and asked if he preferred melon or original before she called for help.

Bro, the arena might as well have tilted to the right. RYU-X hit AKIRA so clean that blue just got relocated. This was not late-match desperation either; it was during the first chunk, when you’re still expecting rhythm checks and cautious pokes. Instead, RYU-X is already all offense. He pushes in, throws a hard, flaming-looking punch right through AKIRA’s front, and AKIRA stumbles back across the screen toward the right wall. The man is trying to stay upright, but he’s clearly getting softened up. Red didn’t win the whole fight there, obviously, but that one impact screamed, “I’m deciding where you stand.”

If you freeze the memory, it is all posture. AKIRA is tilted forward, hips committed, blue energy tucked into a precise line. RYU-X is late, chest open, red guard collapsing inward. The hit lands as a thrust, and the result is immediate: RYU-X gets driven toward the right boundary while AKIRA keeps bearing down. By this late stage, RYU-X no longer has the spring to turn the pressure aside. He absorbs it, loses ground, and looks smaller with every slide. AKIRA is the aggressor in the purest sense here, not just attacking but deciding where the fight will exist.

There’s a version of this scene that people will remember as just the big spinning impact, but the heartbreak is in the three seconds around it. AKIRA, in blue, has already spent too much of himself by the final stretch. Earlier he had answers, little bursts of footwork, counters that made RYU-X respect him. Here, though, he’s late. His guard is there, but tired. His feet are under him, but barely. RYU-X, burning red and pressing like the match clock personally insulted him, rushes into that weakness. He turns through the strike, leg sweeping across with enough force to shove AKIRA sideways rather than simply sting him. AKIRA is driven toward the right edge of the arena, scraping for balance, shoulders folding as he tries not to give up even more ground. The visual is brutal because RYU-X keeps coming after contact. He doesn’t admire the hit. He doesn’t pause for drama. He lands, advances, and makes AKIRA’s world smaller. By then, the fight has stopped feeling even. AKIRA is still brave, still dangerous in theory, but he’s being worn down in public, and RYU-X is the one deciding where the next collision happens.

Mira’s exchange with the masked twins happened on the station stairs, and it was all timing. The twins attacked from different heights: one vaulted down with twin knives, the other crawled low along the railing with a hooked chain aimed at Mira’s ankle. Mira did not try to block either. She kicked a loose soda can into the air, struck it with her palm, and made it burst against the overhead light. The spray and glittering glass flashed between all three fighters. In that half-second of blinking confusion, Mira twisted backward over the chain, planted one hand on the stair edge, and scissored her legs around the descending twin’s wrist. She used his fall to yank him sideways into his own brother’s path. Their weapons clanged together, chain wrapping knife, knife pinning sleeve, and both twins tumbled down the stairs in a ridiculous knot. Mira landed on the railing with one foot and flicked the last drop of soda from her cheek like she had planned the mess exactly.

I was there with a camera, and the shutter missed the start but caught the consequence. RYU-X’s red outline was arcing toward the right edge, his mouth open, his guard no longer protecting anything. AKIRA was underneath him, blue light still gathered around the arm that had just blasted upward. This was not late-fight desperation; this was in the first third, when endurance should still be intact. Yet RYU-X looked rattled and sanded down already, like AKIRA’s pressure had been chewing at him since the bell. The movement told the truth better than any crowd reaction: AKIRA had stepped into command, struck from below, and physically moved RYU-X out of the center.

Journalist’s note: the early narrative of the fight sharpened in one violent push. Akira, representing blue, seized the initiative and drove a palm strike into Ryu-X with enough force to carry the red fighter toward the right edge of the battleground. The sequence showed more than impact; it showed control. Akira remained balanced and advancing after contact, while Ryu-X was forced into a retreating skid, visibly losing composure and stamina. At this stage of the contest, the damage is cumulative rather than decisive, but the trend is unmistakable. Akira is applying steady forward pressure, and Ryu-X is already beginning to erode under it.

I was sitting on the right side of the venue, so this one felt like it was coming straight at me. Around the midpoint, RYU-X had that awful look fighters get when they are still dangerous but tired of answering questions. AKIRA kept asking anyway. He crowded him, blue aura flickering like a warning light, and when RYU-X tried to brace for another forward rush, AKIRA changed the angle and smashed down from above. It caught red high and ugly, folding him just enough to ruin his stance. The impact sent him stumbling in my direction, closer and closer to the right boundary, while AKIRA landed balanced and already hungry for the next chase. That was the moment I stopped thinking this was even. RYU-X was not out, but he was being whittled, and AKIRA was clearly the one deciding where the fight happened.

Mira and Venn collided inside the ruined tea kiosk, where neither had room to swing properly. Venn used the cramped space first, slamming a drawer with his knee so it spat spoons at her face. Mira blocked with a tray, then noticed the copper kettle screaming on the stove. She tipped it with two fingers, sending a white jet of steam between them. Venn flinched back from the heat, and Mira vanished into the cloud. He anticipated a strike from his right and raised his guard there, but she slid low through spilled tea and struck the kettle itself with her elbow. The kettle spun off the stove, handle-first, and hooked Venn behind the knee. Mira pulled it like a grappling hook, making him stumble forward into the remaining steam. When he swung blindly, she was already standing on the counter behind him. She tapped the back of his head with a porcelain cup, more insulting than damaging, before springing away as the kiosk collapsed.

RYU-X fans probably loved this part because it was pure control. No wasted flourish, no big dramatic leap—just red armor-forward pressure at exactly the right time. The match had reached its center stretch, and AKIRA was already breathing harder, his counters a fraction slower than before. RYU-X caught him with a hard braced entry, smothering the blue fighter’s attempt to regain space. The impact turned into a shove that carried AKIRA across the stage toward the right border. What impressed me was how RYU-X stayed glued to him. He didn’t let AKIRA bounce away or reset; he kept the line closed and made the retreat look mandatory. AKIRA’s body language said he wanted to pivot out, but his legs were behind the decision. RYU-X was the one writing the sentence, and AKIRA was just being pushed to the punctuation mark at the side of the screen.

On the rain-slick rooftop, Kenji faced Lady Mirei beside a forest of television antennas. Mirei’s fan blades kept slicing every lightning-charged punch before it reached her. Kenji stopped aiming at her and drove his fist into a rusted satellite dish. The dish bent inward, gathering rainwater in its bowl. Mirei mocked him, then slashed horizontally. Kenji lifted the dish like a shield at the exact angle of her cut. Her fan blade skipped off the curved metal, shaved through the puddle, and sent a crescent of water into the air. Kenji punched the water itself with a crackling knuckle. The droplets lit up into a brief electric veil, not strong enough to injure but bright enough to blind. Through the flash, he vaulted off a bent antenna, landed behind Mirei, and used the broken satellite arm to hook both of her fan handles together. Her next flourish locked her own weapons closed.

My little brother called it a trip, my dad called it bad footwork, and I called it Akira being a menace. The fight was still early, but Akira was already the one moving like he owned the stage. Ryu-X in red tried to hold his ground, maybe throw something back, but he looked softened up from the constant pressure. Akira suddenly went low and slashed across Ryu-X's stance. Red lost his footing and got knocked sideways, sliding toward the right boundary while trying not to fall apart completely. Blue followed right after him, which made it feel less like a single landed attack and more like a chase. Ryu-X was surviving; Akira was winning the moment.

On the mall's second-floor aquarium bridge, Juno charges the masked twin with a spear made from a broken parade banner pole. The twin does not meet the thrust directly; she taps the pole aside with the heel of her palm and slaps a sticky festival prize octopus onto Juno's visor. Juno flails blind for half a second, long enough for the twin to step onto the railing and bounce off it in a narrow flip. She lands behind him and kicks the banner pole's tail end, driving its blunt tip forward into the aquarium glass. A white crack spreads across the giant tank. Juno rips off the toy octopus and realizes too late that she has positioned him exactly where she wants him. When the tank bursts, the wave does the real hit, smashing Juno through a sunglass kiosk while carp and colored pebbles scatter across the tile. He recovers by grabbing a sliding shark-shaped sign, rides it like a shield down the flood, and clips the twin's ankles in return.

From where the medical crew waits, you read bodies more than fireworks. AKIRA’s was telling a bad story by then. His stance had narrowed, his breath was sharp, and he was bracing after attacks instead of before them. RYU-X came forward during that final run with no hesitation, rotating through a powerful kick that struck AKIRA hard enough to displace him across the mat. The blue fighter was forced toward the right boundary, trying to catch himself with a dragging step that looked painful even before the dust cleared. RYU-X did not overextend, which made it worse for AKIRA. He landed the blow and stayed in pursuit range, calm and aggressive, while AKIRA looked increasingly worn down.

From where I was sitting, the late-fight balance had already tipped blue, and this was the proof. AKIRA stepped in first, not waiting, shoulders low and blade hand snapping across RYU-X’s guard. The red fighter tried to brace, but he looked hollowed out by then, too slow to plant his feet. The hit carved through his defense and sent him skidding sideways toward the right boundary, heels scraping, sparks kicking up behind him. It wasn’t a clean reset or a lucky exchange; it was AKIRA walking him down and making the arena smaller. RYU-X was still upright, but every inch he gave up said the same thing: he was running out of fight.

Live from the stands, the noise changed right then. Earlier, people were reacting to every feint, every clash, all that back-and-forth excitement. By now, though, it had become tense because AKIRA was visibly wearing down and RYU-X was getting bolder with every step. Red rushed in, turned his body all the way through, and cracked AKIRA with that spinning sweep. I swear the impact looked like it moved the floor under him. AKIRA didn’t fly straight back; he was forced sideways, dragged by the force toward the right edge, arms still trying to guard while his legs struggled to catch up. RYU-X came out of the rotation looking sharp, like he knew he’d just taken another chunk of control. AKIRA stayed upright, yes, but upright in the worst spot: closer to being cornered, breathing heavier, with less room to make RYU-X miss. That was the middle of the fight turning uglier for blue.

Mira's gravity gauntlet flared purple when Rook came barreling through the smoke, and she chose not to meet his stone-armored punch head-on. She slapped both palms onto the wet floor, increasing gravity in a perfect circle beneath his front foot. Rook's heel sank through the tiles as if the station had turned to mud, but he drove his trapped leg deeper and used it as an anchor, swinging his upper body around like a fortress door on a hinge. The back of his fist caught Mira across both raised gauntlets and sent her skidding into a stack of vending machines. Before the machines could topple, Mira reversed the field around only the loose cans inside. They burst from the dispensing slots in a glittering wave, peppering Rook's chest with enough force to make him stumble. One can lodged between two stone plates on his shoulder, hissing soda foam into his ear. Rook grimaced, grabbed the can, and crushed it without looking, but Mira had already used his blink to vault onto the machine roof.

In sportswriter terms, RYU-X converted pressure into territory. The exchange occurred late, with AKIRA visibly diminished and operating mostly on defensive instinct. RYU-X, controlling tempo, presented a credible forward attack that drew a commitment from AKIRA's guard. Once AKIRA reacted, the promised line of attack vanished. RYU-X stepped into the hesitation and continued to advance, forcing AKIRA toward the right boundary. It was a subtle but decisive moment because it showed the difference between an aggressor choosing the pace and a defender merely surviving it. AKIRA was not just losing exchanges; he was being positioned for the endgame.

Veteran fighting-game brain here: that was corner carry, plain and simple. RYU-X already had advantage in the midsection of the fight, and Akira was showing the classic signs of a player forced into defense too long. Red dashed into striking range, used a tight looping fist from the side, and clipped blue hard enough to send him sliding toward the right wall. The hit itself looked brutal, sure, with that freezing visual crack at contact, but the position was the real disaster. Akira did not just lose a trade; he lost the middle of the stage.

I hate admitting it because I was rooting for Akira, but that was the moment my stomach dropped. We were already in the final stretch, and Akira looked scraped raw from everything before it. He still tried to stand up to RYU-X, still threw himself forward with that blue flare, but RYU-X just caught him in a hardened stance and pressed through. Akira did not get knocked dramatically into the sky or anything. Worse, he was marched backward toward the right side, losing space in plain sight. His knees looked late, his shoulders were sagging, and every little correction came a fraction too slow. RYU-X looked like he knew it. He kept crowding him, not giving Akira a breath, turning defense into another way to grind him down.

Juno's most theatrical move happened beside the giant brass station clock, whose hands had frozen at midnight after the first explosion. Hana lunged with the steel cane hidden inside her umbrella, aiming for Juno's sternum. Juno caught the cane with two crossed wires, but Hana twisted, winding the wires around the shaft until both fighters were tied to the same weapon. For a second they stood nose to nose, arms trembling, neither able to free the cane without giving the other a clear shot. Juno solved it by kicking the clock's maintenance latch open. The enormous minute hand dropped a few degrees with a thunderous tick, and Juno looped one wire around it. As the hand fell, it hauled Hana's cane arm upward. Hana went with the pull rather than resist, running up the clock face in three quick steps. At the top, she flipped over the falling hand and stomped down on Juno's wire spool. The spool cracked, spraying springs across the floor, but Juno used the final length of wire to yank Hana's ankle and slam her into the clock's padded velvet casing.

I was yelling at AKIRA to move left before the punch even came. RYU-X had him lined up. Early in the contest, red was already marching forward while blue looked like he’d been made to block too much. Then RYU-X threw that hot, direct hand and it thudded into AKIRA. The result was immediate: AKIRA got shoved toward the right edge, scrambling for balance, with no counter coming back. It felt like RYU-X was saying, “You don’t get center stage anymore.”

Beneath the stadium, Akio fought the masked wrestler Garan in the equipment tunnel. Garan had already thrown him through two lockers, so Akio stopped resisting the next grapple. When Garan grabbed his belt for a suplex, Akio hooked one finger through the pull-ring of a rolling chalk-line cart used for marking the field. As Garan lifted him upside down, the cart rolled underneath them, spilling a perfect white line across the concrete. Akio twisted midair and slapped the chalk cord around Garan’s neck like a loose scarf. When they landed, Akio hit first but kept rolling, using the cord to pull the cart around Garan’s ankles. The wrestler tried to stand for a finishing stomp and discovered his legs laced to the cart axle. Akio sprang up, yanked the handle, and the cart zipped forward. Garan toppled face-first, leaving a chalk outline of his own slide all the way to the tunnel door.

That was the first moment I really thought, oh, AKIRA is in trouble. RYU-X did not just hit him; he interrupted him. AKIRA's blue form started to shift forward, and then the red arc came across and knocked him off-line, sliding him toward the right side like the stage itself was tilting against him. Still early, but the wear was visible already. RYU-X had the initiative and wasn't giving it back.

Riku and Sable met at the noodle stall just as the hanging lanterns snapped loose in the wind. Sable lunged with a lacquered spear, aiming for Riku's ribs, but Riku kicked the stall's brass soup urn sideways instead of retreating. The urn skidded between them, spilling a ribbon of steaming broth across the polished deck. Sable planted his spear to vault over the hazard, and that was the instant Riku wanted: he slid under the spear shaft on one shoulder, caught Sable's airborne ankle with both hands, and twisted his body like a thrown wrench. Sable's vault became a lopsided spin. He slammed back-first into the paper menu wall, noodles raining over his armor, while Riku rolled through the broth and came up with one singed sleeve and a grin.

Rika’s opening feint looked like another headlong charge across the rain-slick tiles of the clocktower observatory, but she cut left at the last instant and planted one boot on the brass rim of the fallen astrolabe. When Sable lunged with his hooked chain, Rika let it skim past her cheek, caught the trailing links under her armpit, and spun once around the astrolabe like a gymnast. The momentum yanked Sable off balance just as Tetsu tried to cover him with a stone-fisted punch. Rika released the chain only halfway, causing Sable to stumble directly into Tetsu’s swing. The punch missed his jaw but crushed the chain’s anchor weight against the floor, pinning it. Rika landed in a crouch, flicked rainwater from her glove, and used Sable’s trapped weapon as a tightrope, sprinting along it to knee him under the chin before he could unhook himself.

There’s a moment in a fight when pressure stops being abstract. This was it. AKIRA, wearing blue, had been taking the initiative through the opening portion, and RYU-X was already showing the little signs of strain: slower shoulders, less spring, guard not quite sealing in time. Then AKIRA stepped inside and drove a flat-handed strike into him with such clean timing that it turned defense into travel. RYU-X’s body lurched to the viewer’s right, skidding back toward the outer edge instead of answering. No reversal, no trade, no clever counter. Just red being displaced. The exchange made the geography of the fight obvious: AKIRA owned the center and was using every hit to herd RYU-X away from safety. For something happening this early, it felt ominous. RYU-X was not broken yet, but he was already being worn into a shape AKIRA wanted.

There is a brutal elegance to the way AKIRA seizes that moment. The bout is in its middle passage, the early testing gone, the final desperation not yet arrived. RYU-X is already frayed, red aura flickering around a body that has taken too many forced defenses. AKIRA, blue and sharpened by momentum, suddenly commits to a piercing advance. He strikes into RYU-X and continues through the line of contact, converting speed into a shove that sends RYU-X sliding toward the right edge. The important thing is RYU-X’s lack of choice. He is not retreating strategically. He is being displaced. AKIRA’s aggression fills the screen, while RYU-X’s resistance looks increasingly expensive.

Sable and Tetsu’s brief struggle in the bookstore became a joint-lock nobody could repeat on purpose. He grabbed her sleeve and twisted for a shoulder throw, but she let the fabric tear halfway instead of resisting. The dangling strip whipped across a spinning display of travel guides, snagging the wire rack. As Tetsu pulled, the rack rotated, wrapping the torn sleeve around his forearm. Sable stepped into the wrap, pressed a hardcover atlas under his elbow, and levered upward with the book’s spine. His spear clattered from suddenly numb fingers. She finished by kicking the base of the display so it spun one last time, binding his wrist against a row of glossy maps. Tetsu stood there furious, technically defeated by geography, while Sable tore the rest of the sleeve free and vanished between the shelves.

From the medical table, fatigue was the loudest part of it. AKIRA's shoulders had been dropping between exchanges, and his recovery after each motion was slower. RYU-X recognized that and forced a decision at the worst possible time. He suggested an incoming hit, abrupt enough to trigger AKIRA's survival response. AKIRA tightened up, shifted backward and right, and then realized too late that the danger had been a lure. RYU-X advanced immediately, keeping the initiative and denying him time to breathe. By the time AKIRA corrected his posture, he was closer to the right boundary and visibly more spent. That sort of deception is damaging because it makes a tired fighter waste energy on fear.

RYU-X's timing there was disgusting in the best way. AKIRA started to commit, shoulders turning, blue aura lifting, and RYU-X cut right through the gap before the action could fully form. The hit carried AKIRA across the screen toward the right side, not a clean launch but a brutal forced drift, like he was being herded into a corner. Since this was still in the first phase, it made the imbalance stand out even more: RYU-X fresh, sharp, advancing; AKIRA already losing ground and getting worn down.

Daichi and the spearwoman Ibara fought up the moving escalator while civilians fled down the other side. Ibara had the reach advantage and kept stabbing at his shoes to force him backward. Daichi suddenly stepped onto the rubber handrail instead of the metal stairs. It carried his right foot upward faster than his left, twisting his body sideways in a move that looked accidental until he dropped into a split. Ibara’s spear thrust passed over his shoulder and wedged between two escalator panels. Daichi slapped the red emergency stop button with his elbow. The escalator froze, locking Ibara’s spear in place. She tried to abandon it, but Daichi grabbed the tassel near the blade, looped it around her glove, and let himself slide down the smooth center divider. His weight pulled her off balance and spun her around the stuck spear shaft. She landed on the step above him, sitting perfectly upright, furious and disarmed.

As someone who has been in rings, that moment hurt to watch. Late in a fight, when your legs are dead, being walked down is worse than being hit clean. Akira still had spirit, but his base was gone. RYU-X read the incoming pressure, sealed himself behind a tight guard, and let Akira crash into something immovable. Then came the real damage: red advanced through the collision. Not a reckless shove, not a wild counter, just controlled pressure that made Akira give up ground step by step until he was near the right edge. You could see Akira trying to recover posture, but fatigue delayed everything. RYU-X was dictating the terms now. The blue fighter was no longer choosing where to stand; he was being placed there.

The brawl briefly turns supernatural when the masked twins summon a paper dragon from the storm of torn tickets littering the floor. The dragon is not large, but it is fast, folding and unfolding through the air with a thousand sharp edges. Luma stands alone in the center of the concourse as it dives at her throat. She does not swing her staff. Instead, she breaks the string of prayer beads around her wrist and tosses the beads upward in a loose spiral. Each bead catches one ticket scrap for a heartbeat, weighing down the dragon’s body in scattered points. The creature wobbles but keeps coming. Luma then stamps her staff into the floor mosaic, exactly on the painted compass rose, and spins the staff with both palms. The prayer beads orbit the staff like tiny moons, dragging the ticket dragon into a tightening helix. The twins try to pull their spell free, but the dragon is now wrapped around the staff from tip to base. Luma bows once, yanks a single bead loose, and the whole paper beast unravels into harmless ticket confetti that rains over the twins’ masks.

By the time this exchange happened, the contest had moved beyond measurement and into attrition. Akira had accumulated pressure through forward movement, forcing Ryu-X to spend energy defending rather than initiating. The decisive action came when Akira committed to a linear body attack, a compact forward drive that penetrated Ryu-X's guard before the red fighter could reset his feet. Impact transferred cleanly. Ryu-X was displaced to his right, losing ground toward the edge of the arena, and his posture after contact showed fatigue more than surprise. He was not outclassed in a single instant; he had been softened up first. Akira's aggression made the moment inevitable.

Rika's first clean answer to Veyl came when the fight spilled across Platform Nine's rain-slick departure tiles. Veyl lunged with his crescent glaive held low, trying to sweep both her ankles and herd her toward the electrified rail. Instead of jumping back like she had all episode, Rika stepped onto the flat of the blade for half a heartbeat. The metal skidded under her sandal, but she used the slip as a launch, driving her knee into the underside of Veyl's chin. The impact snapped his head up and knocked loose one of the glowing bead charms in his braid. Before he could recover, she hooked two fingers through his scarf, twisted in midair, and yanked herself behind him. Veyl's own forward momentum dragged him down into a clumsy kneel. Rika landed perched on his shoulder for a blink, palm blazing blue, then shoved off with a heel to the back of his neck, sending him face-first through a paper map kiosk that exploded into fluttering route diagrams.

Toma climbed the central clocktower rope to escape Jax's barrage, but Jax grabbed the other end and yanked, ringing the station bell so hard pigeons burst from the rafters. The rope whipped upward, lifting Toma with it. Instead of panicking, Toma tucked into a ball around the rope, swung in a huge pendulum arc, and came back heel-first.
