Jax crossed his forearms to block, but the kick drove him across the floor and into a stack of ceremonial drums. The drums boomed one after another as he crashed through them. Toma landed proudly, only to realize the bell rope had looped around his ankle during the swing. Jax emerged from the wreckage, grabbed the dangling rope, and gave it a sharp sideways pull. Toma was yanked off his feet and swung horizontally into a soft wall of parade banners. The exchange ended with him wrapped like a festival dumpling, still trying to claim he had meant to do that.

Okay, listen, I replayed that moment way too many times, and it gets better every time. AKIRA had been bullying the space from the start, not recklessly, but with that cold blue confidence where every step makes the other guy answer first. RYU-X was already backing up more than he wanted to admit. You could see it in how his feet kept sliding toward the right side, how his counters were coming out a fraction late. Then AKIRA ducked into the pocket, planted hard, and launched an upward knuckle strike that caught RYU-X flush. It did not just knock him back; it lifted him, folded his rhythm in half, and sent him drifting toward the edge like he had been hooked by a crane. Since it was so early, the hit felt even more brutal. RYU-X should have been fresh enough to hold center, but he was already being eroded. AKIRA, meanwhile, looked like he had found the exact seam in the red defense and planned to keep tearing at it.

The moment had the shape of a closing door. AKIRA, all blue pressure and cold intent, crossed the gap while RYU-X stood too near exhaustion to answer properly. A silver arc opened between them, brief and bright, and the red fighter was swept toward the right margin as if the floor tilted under him. Earlier he might have caught it, rolled with it, even countered. Not now. His limbs lagged behind the impact, his guard folding after the fact. AKIRA remained the one choosing distance, rhythm, direction. RYU-X was being written into the edge of the battlefield, line by line, until there was barely any page left.

Rook's rematch with Boru happens beside the enormous festival drum, a red-lacquered thing taller than both of them and strapped to a wheeled frame. Boru believes he has the advantage in raw force and drives Rook backward with shieldless body blows, each one making the drum tremble when Rook's back bumps it. On the fourth impact Rook notices the stretched hide rebounding like a spring. He lets Boru hit him again, but this time he rolls with the punch and slaps both palms against the drumhead behind him. The drum booms so loudly that everyone nearby flinches. Boru does not, because his helmet muffles the sound, and he steps in for the clinch. Rook grins, hops onto the lower rim, and kicks the drumhead with both heels. The rebound launches him forward chest-first into Boru, turning what looked like retreat into a battering-ram tackle. Boru skids backward in a perfectly straight line, plowing through a neat row of ceremonial gongs that chime one after another like a comic countdown.

Across the half-built skyscraper, Bora swung a crane hook the size of a motorcycle at Jun. The hook carved sparks from steel beams and forced Jun toward an unfinished elevator shaft. Jun waited until the hook came around again, then ran at it instead of away. He planted one foot on the curved metal, rode it for a quarter-turn, and slapped a magnetic talisman onto its underside. Bora tried to yank the hook back, but the talisman pulled every loose bolt, washer, and nail in the area into a rattling cloud around the hook. The sudden extra weight ruined the swing’s timing. Jun leapt from the hook to a dangling safety net, bounced once, and came down with both knees on the crane cable. The cable dipped, the overloaded hook swung low, and Bora had to dive to avoid his own weapon. Jun landed beside the control box and hit the release lever, dropping the hook gently but decisively through the floor grating.

There was a brutal little poem in that instant: blue advancing, red retreating, the arena’s right edge waiting like punctuation. AKIRA’s knee rose with no mercy and met RYU-X in the middle of his resistance, snapping the red fighter’s posture out of shape. They were not deep into the battle yet; the fight still had that early heat, that sharp unfinished feeling. But the momentum had already chosen a side. AKIRA was moving like a storm front, compact and forward, while RYU-X was made to slide, to give ground, to look suddenly less certain. It was one of those hits that says the damage is starting before the finish is even in sight.

From my seat it felt like the whole match had shifted from feeling-out to punishment. AKIRA, glowing in that cool blue aura, suddenly crossed the gap before RYU-X could reset his stance. It was not a cautious advance; it was a shoulder-first surge that caught the red fighter clean and shoved him across the floor. RYU-X tried to brace, heels scraping, but he was already looking tired by this point, his guard half a breath late. The impact carried him toward the far-right boundary, and you could feel the crowd recognize it: AKIRA had taken command. This was the middle stretch, when both fighters should still have options, yet RYU-X was getting compressed, forced back, and made to defend while AKIRA kept pressing forward.

I keep replaying that tiny instant because it had more menace than the huge attacks. The fight was already old by then, the air full of dust and leftover light, and RYU-X looked like a flame that had been burning too hot for too long. AKIRA came forward in blue, calm in that scary way, and put a quick fist into him before red could breathe. It wasn’t beautiful in a graceful sense; it was efficient, almost rude. RYU-X’s head and guard snapped with the contact, and his whole body gave ground toward the right lip of the screen. That movement told you everything. He wasn’t being allowed to recover. He wasn’t setting traps. He was being driven. AKIRA had become the pressure, step after step, hit after hit, and this late exchange made RYU-X look painfully mortal. The edge was getting closer, the options fewer, and the blue fighter’s confidence sharper with every forced retreat.

Reporting from ringside, the decisive exchange came before the match had reached its middle rhythm. AKIRA, wearing blue, advanced behind sustained pressure and drove a knee into RYU-X with enough force to propel the red-clad fighter toward the right boundary. RYU-X remained standing, but the retreat was involuntary and telling. His guard tightened afterward, his movement looked more labored, and he appeared to be absorbing the cost of AKIRA’s pace. AKIRA, meanwhile, continued forward without hesitation. The sequence confirmed the early trend: AKIRA was the aggressor, and RYU-X was being steadily worn down.

The kite-line trip was so specific that even the announcer could not name it. During the brawl's drift toward the fireworks terrace, a child-sized attack drone shaped like a hawk harried Aya from above, forcing her into short, ugly dodges. She spotted a vendor's giant fish kite lying half-unfurled, its spool still tied to a sandbag. Instead of cutting the drone down, Aya grabbed the spool and ran a tight spiral around a bronze incense burner. The hawk drone pursued exactly, following her heat signature. On the third loop, Aya dove flat and yanked the spool over her shoulder. The nearly invisible kite line snapped up across the drone's wings. The machine did not crash immediately; it dragged the fish kite into the air, fought the line, and then slingshotted itself around the incense burner like a tetherball. It smashed beak-first into the sandbag, and the fish kite settled over it like a smug, painted blanket.

Rakka corners Luma inside the ticket booth, where the glass partitions make every movement feel boxed and echoing. He presses two hook swords through the service window, trapping her staff between them like a wishbone. Rather than pull back, Luma leans forward and breathes on the glass. The fog from her breath catches the glow of the warning lamps, giving her a blurry double in the reflection. Rakka strikes at the clearer silhouette. Luma has already slid sideways beneath the counter, leaving only her reflection to take the blow. His swords punch through the glass partition and cross on the far side, locking together at their hooked tips. Luma emerges behind him through the staff door, stamps on the booth’s fallen microphone cable, and jerks it around his ankle. Then she rings the ticket clerk’s little brass service bell with the end of her staff. The sound is harmless, but it makes Rakka turn his head; that turn is enough for Luma to pull the cable tight and send him crashing shoulder-first into the revolving ticket stamp machine.

Taro’s umbrella duel with Madame Shizu lasted only one exchange, but everyone on Platform Four stopped to watch it. Shizu snapped open a lacquered parasol painted with storm clouds, and each rib fired a needle of blue spirit light. Taro had no shield, only a cheap paper umbrella he had bought to hide from the station sprinklers. He opened it late, after the needles were already streaking toward him, and angled it not to block but to catch the wind from their passage. The flimsy umbrella inverted with a pop, becoming a bowl. The spirit needles skimmed around its curve and carved circles in the air behind him. Shizu smiled, thinking his defense had failed. Taro then spun the inverted umbrella by its handle, gathering the remaining sparks along the wet paper. He stepped forward and closed it with a snap, trapping the glow inside for half a second. When he tapped the parasol’s tip against Shizu’s parasol, the stored sparks jumped into her painted storm clouds, making them flash bright pink. Shizu sneezed from the sudden burst of cherry-blossom smoke, and Taro used that polite opening to bow and hook her parasol out of her hands.

Listen to that moment with your eyes closed and you still know who is winning. The late-fight audio drops into a harsh scrape when Akira’s boots start sliding right. Before that, there is the thick thud of blue force meeting RYU-X’s braced red defense, not a clean strike landing, more like someone slamming into a steel door. Then the mix shifts forward: RYU-X’s steps are heavy, regular, advancing. Akira’s are broken and skittering, trying to catch up with the shove. The crowd noise dips because it is obvious he is being crowded to the side. It is a pressure sound, not a knockout sound. RYU-X has become the engine, and Akira is the thing being dragged along by it.

There’s a very old lesson in that exchange: the fighter who yields the middle too early invites the sky to fall. RYU-X had begun yielding, little by little, in the opening third. AKIRA sensed it. He did not chase with anger; he advanced with certainty. When the red warrior’s balance thinned, AKIRA bent his knees and sent his fist upward along a short, punishing path. The contact lifted RYU-X’s head and carried his body toward the right edge, not as a grand explosion but as the result of structure failing. RYU-X was being worn down before the battle had matured. AKIRA was fresh in intention, forward in spirit, and utterly in charge of that instant.

Okay, so this was the part where I stopped pretending the fight was even. Midway through, Akira was still standing, sure, but you could tell he was absorbing too much. His guard kept coming up a little late, his shoulders were tight, and he was drifting instead of choosing where to go. RYU-X, in red, smelled that weakness like a shark. He crowded in with that ugly forward pressure, then snapped his arm across with the point of the elbow leading, catching Akira hard enough that the blue fighter’s whole frame jolted sideways. It didn’t just hurt him; it relocated him. Akira got bullied across the screen toward the right border, and the scary part was how intentional it looked. RYU-X wasn’t swinging wild. He was herding him. Every step Akira lost narrowed his options, and this strike made the center belong completely to RYU-X. By then the match had that middle-round grind to it, where the stronger pace-setter starts turning damage into territory. Akira tried to brace, but his balance was already compromised, and the impact sent him sliding into exactly the direction RYU-X wanted. Red was pressing. Blue was fading.

The final one-off exchange erupts when all the scattered fireworks stored for the closing ceremony ignite in a chain of colored sparks along the garden balcony. Aki faces the masked twins again, but this time she has no weapon except a broken parasol frame. The twins split to flank her, fans flashing red on one side and blue on the other as rockets hiss along the floor between them. Aki opens the skeletal parasol, catches a sputtering pinwheel firework in its ribs, and spins it above her head. The pinwheel's sparks make a circle of light wide enough to hide her exact footwork. The twins attack through opposite gaps, perfectly timed. Aki collapses the parasol frame flat, and the pinwheel drops straight down, bouncing off the polished floor between all three fighters. Both twins flinch away from the sparks, breaking their symmetry for the first time. Aki steps onto the parasol handle, vaults over the blue-fan twin's shoulder, and uses the frame's hooked ribs to tug the red-fan twin's sash. The two spin into each other, wrapped together by the sash as the pinwheel fizzles out like punctuation.

Kei and the shrine guard fought along the clock tower stairs, their boots ringing on copper steps. The guard carried a crescent halberd and used it to keep Kei below him, stabbing down whenever Kei tried to climb. Kei noticed the tower's huge pendulum swinging through the open center shaft, its brass weight passing every four seconds. He feinted left, took a shallow cut across his shoulder, and grabbed the halberd's wooden haft with both hands. The guard braced, expecting a tug-of-war. Kei pulled only enough to lock the weapon between them, then stepped backward off the stairwell into empty air. The guard instinctively leaned after him, and the pendulum swept between them. Kei caught the pendulum chain with one hand, swung behind the guard, and kicked the back of his knee, sending him sliding down the stairs on his own halberd shaft.

From my seat it looked less like a hit and more like a red warning flare with a fist inside it. Early going, not even close to the desperate final stretch, and AKIRA is already being made to retreat. RYU-X plants forward, fires a narrow punch straight through the middle, and AKIRA takes it badly. Blue gets knocked backward with no clean answer, sliding toward the right-side limit as if the stage is shrinking behind him. The scary part is the timing: RYU-X isn’t catching a mistake after a long exchange, he’s dictating before AKIRA has settled. AKIRA’s guard holds for a blink, then his body gives ground. Momentum is fully red.

Juno and Sadao tumble into the glass elevator shaft of the department store after a missed fan slash cuts the call button panel in half. The elevator car is one floor below them, rising slowly with its doors open, full of terrified mannequins from a display spill. Sadao kicks off the shaft wall and tries to pin Juno against the cables with both feet. Juno grabs a hanging inspection chain and lets the kick pass under him, but Sadao snaps his fan shut on Juno's sleeve, anchoring him in midair. The elevator roof comes up beneath them fast. Juno tears free by ripping his own sleeve, lands on the roof, and immediately stomps the emergency hatch. It flips open behind Sadao. Sadao lands where the roof should be and drops waist-deep into the elevator among plastic mannequins. Before he can climb out, Juno kicks a mannequin arm upward through the hatch like a lever, catching Sadao under the ribs and popping him back onto the roof in a graceless sprawl.

Near the vaulted ceiling, Sable tries to finish Jun by driving him onto the face of the giant station clock, whose glass has already been smashed out. The clock’s minute hand juts like a silver bridge over the concourse. Jun scrambles onto it, but Sable follows with catlike balance, sword tip scraping sparks from the metal. She thrusts; he hops back; the hand groans under their combined weight. Jun notices that the second hand, bent during an earlier explosion, still ticks in erratic jumps beneath them. He times Sable’s next lunge to one of those violent ticks and drops flat. The second hand snaps upward through the broken clock face, striking the underside of the minute hand and bouncing Sable’s footing. She sails over Jun, but catches his collar on the way. Jun rolls with the pull, plants both feet against the Roman numeral eleven, and kicks off. The movement spins them around the central pinion, turning Sable’s own grip into a throw that flings her into a curtain of hanging timetable banners.

There is a nasty elegance to how RYU-X takes control here. AKIRA, glowing blue and already under pressure far earlier than he would like, tries to break the pattern with a forward motion. RYU-X has been the aggressor up to this point, so AKIRA's choice makes sense: do something, or get walked down forever. But the red fighter anticipates it. His weapon whips across in a bright, brutal line, meeting AKIRA at the exact moment he is vulnerable. The impact sends AKIRA sliding toward the right flank of the battlefield, and suddenly the geography matters. He is not just hurt; he is being placed somewhere worse. This is still the first part of the duel, but RYU-X is already stacking pressure, position, and fatigue together. AKIRA survives the exchange, sure, but he looks less like a rival trading evenly and more like someone being gradually cornered.

Kazuo's brief fight with the storm-haired rival ended at the edge of the rooftop garden, where rainwater streamed through bonsai trays and over white gravel. The rival hurled lightning-charged punches, each miss bursting a miniature pine into steam. Kazuo kept one hand behind his back, guarding a cracked ceramic watering can he had picked up earlier. When the rival finally rushed with both fists blazing, Kazuo tossed the watering can upward, not at him but into the rain gutter above. The can jammed the gutter's mouth, forcing a sudden sheet of collected water to pour over the rival's shoulders. His lightning aura sputtered for one breath. Kazuo stepped into that breath, caught one wrist, turned under the arm, and used a precise shoulder throw that sent the rival sliding across the soaked gravel in a perfect arc, stopping just before the roof's broken edge.

As an AKIRA fan, I loved how businesslike it was. No grand pose, no waiting for permission. The fight was still in the early third, and AKIRA just stepped in blue-first and put his knee straight into RYU-X’s path. Red got knocked back toward the right side, boots dragging, guard rattled, pride clearly dented. The best part was that AKIRA did not overextend. He hit, advanced, and made RYU-X keep carrying the pressure. You could tell the wearing-down process had started. RYU-X was still dangerous, obviously, but AKIRA was the one making him move, making him react, making him give up ground.

I was watching half-hidden behind a cushion because the middle of this fight was getting stressful, and then AKIRA did that terrifying falling attack. RYU-X had been looking rough for a while, not defeated, but like his armor was made of tired decisions. He raised himself to answer the pressure, and AKIRA came down over him with perfect timing. The impact made RYU-X lurch to the right, closer to the side of the arena, and I remember thinking he didn’t go there because he wanted to. AKIRA was pushing the story forward. RYU-X was still fighting back, but he was starting to look like someone trying to survive a storm rather than stop it.

Rook attempted a clean grapple on Mira after the gauntlet blasts became too unpredictable, lunging low to wrap both arms around her waist. Mira struck downward at his neck, but his stone shoulders absorbed it, and he lifted her clean off the ground for a crushing bear hug. She wheezed, boots kicking, then pressed one gauntlet to his temple and the other to his hip. Instead of blasting him away, she reversed gravity between those two points. Rook's upper body lurched sideways while his lower body tried to fall the opposite direction, ruining his balance without breaking his grip. He staggered three steps into the food court, smashed through a noodle stall curtain, and fell backward onto the chef's broad wooden prep table. Mira landed on top of him and immediately tried to roll free, but Rook clamped one huge hand around her wrist. With his other hand he grabbed a bundle of uncooked noodles and flung them into her face. The ridiculous slap blinded her long enough for him to sit up, still holding her wrist, and transition the failed bear hug into a wrist lock against the table edge.

Sera's scarf had been fluttering uselessly all fight, until Venn grabbed it and tried to yank her off balance. She let him have the pull, spinning into it so fast that the embroidered end wrapped twice around his wrist. Venn laughed and braced for a throw, but Sera slid under his elbow, locked his arm across the back of her neck, and dropped to one knee. The scarf tightened into a sudden joint-lock, forcing Venn onto his toes with his sword arm stretched like a bowstring. He tried to roll through, but Sera pinned his hand with her heel and used her free hand to flick a paper charm onto his knuckles. The charm popped with a tiny burst of blue light, numbing his fingers just long enough for his blade to clatter away. She released him before the lock could become a break, and he staggered off shaking his hand as if it had been bitten.

The clean contact is what sold it. RYU-X did not chase a fancy angle, did not waste motion, just planted himself and rammed his knuckles straight into AKIRA's midline. By this late phase, AKIRA had been giving ground for a while, and this hit made it official. His blue silhouette was shoved across the arena toward the far right side, boots scraping sparks, torso bent from the force. RYU-X, in red, stayed upright and balanced after the blow, which is the scary part. He looked less like someone gambling on a finish and more like someone continuing a punishment he already knew was working.

Rika and Mako had a brief accidental team-up around the monorail doors, and it looked choreographed only because both of them were reckless. Veyl tried to split them by kicking a rolling snack freezer between them, its lid broken and dry ice fog pouring out. Mako punched at the freezer, but Rika shouted for him to wait. She dove onto the lid, palms freezing the hinges solid, while Mako redirected his punch into the floor. The impact popped a row of tiles upward like piano keys. Veyl jumped over the first three tiles, exactly as Rika expected, and landed on the frozen freezer lid. She kicked the lid's side latch. It snapped open under him, releasing a dense burst of white vapor and a cascade of frozen melon bars. Veyl's boots skidded on the bars. Mako came up through the fog with one of the popped tiles in each hand and clapped them together against Veyl's staff, trapping it between ceramic slabs. Rika used the staff as a handhold, swung around it, and planted both heels into Veyl's chest, knocking him backward into the monorail doors just as they opened and announced a delay.

Forum post energy: this is the exchange people are underrating. Everyone remembers the bigger fireworks after, but this little late-fight deception is why AKIRA ended up in such a bad place. RYU-X had momentum, AKIRA was worn thin, and the right edge was becoming a problem. Red faked the direct burst, blue flinched, and that flinch surrendered the lane. RYU-X did not need to overextend; he just stepped into the space AKIRA abandoned and kept the pressure glued to him. The camera even sells it by letting the boundary loom closer while AKIRA's stance looks uglier and uglier. That was not filler movement. That was RYU-X taking command of the map when AKIRA had almost nothing left to give.

As a strategy nerd, I loved how economical RYU-X was there. We were still in the opening portion, so this wasn’t a desperate exchange; it was territory management. RYU-X closed the gap first, fired a short linear strike, and caught AKIRA during the instant his weight was between steps. The result mattered more than the damage itself: AKIRA was nudged hard toward the right margin, where his evasive routes would start disappearing. Red was not chasing wildly; he was herding. Blue, meanwhile, looked like he was already absorbing too many small losses. That single fast contact confirmed the current shape of the fight: RYU-X pressing, AKIRA yielding, the arena space shrinking for him much earlier than he wanted.

The dragon puppet from the festival parade reenters the brawl in the most humiliating way possible. Ryo has been chasing Min through the storage balcony, firing explosive finger snaps that burst crates into confetti. Min ducks behind the abandoned puppet head, a huge lacquered dragon with jeweled eyes and a jaw on ropes. Ryo fires again, blowing half the whiskers off, and shouts for her to stop hiding behind props. Min answers by climbing inside the head. Ryo rushes forward, grabs the upper jaw, and tries to rip it open. That is when Min bites him with the puppet. The wooden jaw clamps over his forearm, not hard enough to break bone, but hard enough to trap his hand and ruin his snap technique. Ryo lifts the entire puppet head with his stuck arm and swings it around, slamming Min into a rack of banners. She rolls deeper inside instead of falling out, pulling the internal control bar with her feet. The dragon’s eyes flare from old fireworks packed in the sockets. Ryo freezes for half a heartbeat. Min uses that blink to launch the puppet head forward on its parade wheels, dragging him across the balcony and into a pile of ceremonial drums.

There was a blue blade of motion and a red figure bent beneath it, and that is the image I cannot shake. The duel had passed its early testing phase; now it was a question of whose will would keep shaping the battlefield. AKIRA's answer came first. He advanced with that cold, rising confidence, refusing to let RYU-X breathe between exchanges. RYU-X, crimson and stubborn, had begun to fade around the edges, his responses a fraction duller, his retreats a fraction longer. Then AKIRA struck from above, a descending arc that split RYU-X's guard and sent him reeling toward the right-hand limit. For a second, the whole arena seemed to lean with him. The momentum was unmistakable: blue pressing forward, red being carved backward, the fight narrowing around RYU-X like a closing door.

Near the aquarium entrance, Shiori fought Koga beside a waist-high touch tank full of harmless rays. Koga kept using his shadow step to vanish whenever she aimed a clean strike. Shiori noticed he always reappeared on the darkest side of an object, so she punched the emergency exhibit lamp instead of him. Bright blue-white light flooded the entire room, erasing most of the shadows. Koga flickered into view halfway through a teleport, his outline stretched like wet ink. Before he could stabilize, Shiori scooped a plastic bucket from the staff shelf and flung seawater across the polished floor. Koga’s foot hit the puddle, and his unfinished shadow step turned into an ungainly skid. Shiori slid after him on one knee, grabbed the strap of his chest armor, and redirected his fall into the acrylic wall of the jellyfish tank. The tank held, but the jellyfish drifted behind his stunned face like glowing punctuation marks.

Near the subway entrance, Tetsu comes sliding down the escalator handrail with both boots aimed at Kaito's chest. Kaito sidesteps onto the turnstile bar, but Tetsu catches his scarf in midair and drags him off balance. For a heartbeat it looks like Kaito will be spun face-first into the fare gate. Instead, he commits to the spin, tucking his knees and letting the turnstile rotate him around like a carnival ride. On the second rotation he snaps one leg out, not at Tetsu's head, but at the plastic emergency cover behind him. The cover pops free and the alarm screams, startling Tetsu's timing. Kaito uses the noise and his own momentum to kick Tetsu's wrist, freeing the scarf, then vaults over the gate. Tetsu answers by kicking a ticket machine panel loose and hurling it flat like a shield. Kaito ducks under it, but the panel smashes the turnstile behind him, removing his escape route and trapping both fighters inside the buzzing gate lane.

The brawl spilled into a ramen alley where steam poured from three portable carts. Soga, the huge monk with iron prayer beads, charged straight at Yumi, shrugging off every normal strike. Yumi grabbed the nearest cook’s bamboo noodle strainer instead of retreating. She dipped it into a bubbling pot, came up with a dripping nest of noodles, and flung them not at Soga’s face but at the ground just before his lead foot landed. The noodles became a slick yellow snare. Soga’s heel skidded forward, but his momentum kept the rest of him coming, so Yumi spun the bamboo strainer like a shield and caught his descending forearm through the hoop. She twisted, using the strainer’s rim as a lever against his wrist. Soga’s own weight completed the throw: he cartwheeled over the cart, landed seated in an empty broth barrel, and the lid dropped on his head with a hollow wooden thunk.

Rin's clash with the glass swordswoman took place in the mirror maze, where every reflection made a false attack appear half a heartbeat early. The swordswoman used a transparent blade that vanished whenever it crossed a bright reflection. Rin stopped trying to track the weapon and focused on the sound of her opponent's anklet bells. She deliberately punched a mirror panel beside her, cutting her knuckles but showering the floor with glittering fragments. The swordswoman advanced, certain Rin had panicked. Rin kicked the broken frame, sending a narrow mirror strip sliding across the floor. It reflected the blade from below, revealing its exact angle as it descended. Rin pivoted inside the cut, trapped the swordswoman's wrist between her forearm and shoulder, and shoved her backward into an intact mirror that did not break, leaving the stunned attacker staring at her own defeated reflection.

Mako’s most humiliating save came when she was trapped between two charging bruisers on the luggage carousel. Both wore brass gauntlets, and they timed their approach so she could not jump left or right without meeting a fist. Mako noticed the carousel’s rubber belt was carrying a lonely blue suitcase toward her, its handle extended. At the last heartbeat, she planted one foot on the suitcase, grabbed the handle, and let the moving belt yank her backward under the first swing. The two bruisers collided gauntlet to gauntlet so hard that their arm guards locked together with a magnetic clack. Mako, still riding the suitcase like a sled, spun around the carousel’s curve and came up behind them. She popped the suitcase open with her heel; a cloud of souvenir scarves exploded out and wrapped around their stuck wrists. She gave the scarf bundle one tidy knot, saluted the bewildered pair, and rolled away before either could agree on which direction to chase.

Chat was screaming before AKIRA even hit the edge. RYU-X dashed in, red aura and all, and clipped him with that curved leg swing so clean it looked unfair. AKIRA’s sprite basically got shoved right, like the stage itself was running out from under him. And this was still the early chunk of the fight! Nobody could pretend blue was saving some big plan yet, because he looked worn already. Red was mashing forward pressure in the smartest, nastiest way.

The final distinct exchange came when villainous Maestro Cael raised his baton and made the rubble itself move in orchestra formation. Chunks of concrete lifted like obedient instruments, circling Hana in a tightening ring. She had no weapon left except a cracked school chair from the evacuation area. Cael laughed at it. Hana threw the chair straight up, not at him. The floating rubble adjusted to intercept anything descending toward its conductor, so three concrete chunks rose to smash the chair overhead. Hana sprinted beneath them during that upward shift, entering the gap they left in the ring. Cael flicked his baton down, trying to crush her, but she slid on her knees through powdered plaster and grabbed the baton hand with both of hers. Rather than wrestle it away, she clapped his palm around the baton and forced him to complete one exaggerated conducting flourish. The rubble obeyed the accidental cue, sweeping outward in a grand finale instead of inward. As Cael stared at his own miscommand, Hana headbutted the knot of his cravat and knocked the wind out of him.

As someone who watches these fights for footwork more than fireworks, this exchange was brutal because of the positioning. In the middle phase, RYU-X had already forced Akira into a defensive rhythm. Akira wasn’t collapsing yet, but he was clearly losing sharpness. Then RYU-X closed the gap on a hard angle and used his elbow like a wedge, smashing through Akira’s attempt to hold ground. The contact folded Akira’s stance and pushed him toward the right boundary. That’s the important part: it wasn’t just damage, it was map control. RYU-X advanced behind the blow, keeping pressure high, while Akira got dragged closer to being trapped with less room to reset.

I swear the red guy had all the traffic lights green at this point. It’s still in the front part of the fight, and RYU-X is already the one choosing the pace, walking AKIRA down like he paid rent on the whole arena. AKIRA, in blue, tries to brace and slide away, but RYU-X steps in with that dead-center driving punch and catches him clean in the torso/guard line. The impact doesn’t just stop AKIRA; it shoves him across the floor toward the far right boundary. You can see AKIRA’s feet skidding, shoulders folding, the wear starting to show way too early. RYU-X looks fresh, angry, and in command.

Mira's fight against the ink sorcerer became a contest over one calligraphy brush. He painted a black tiger across the floor, and the ink beast lunged from the tiles with wet jaws. Mira vaulted over it, but the tiger splashed apart and reformed behind her, driving her toward a wall of festival posters. She grabbed a poster pole, spun around it, and let the tiger bite the wooden shaft. While the beast worried the pole like prey, Mira kicked the ink sorcerer's brush hand. He saved the brush by tossing it to his other hand, exactly as she anticipated. Her second kick struck not him but the poster wall, releasing a cascade of old paper sheets. The falling posters stuck to the wet tiger, giving its liquid body edges and weight. Mira then ripped the brush from the sorcerer's surprised fingers and drew a single sloppy cage bar across the posters, pinning the tiger in place as an accidental mural.

The momentum was red from the start, and this exchange proved it. AKIRA twitched forward as if to steal a turn, only for RYU-X to punish him with a clean diagonal carve that cracked through the blue guard and sent him skidding toward the right boundary. It was the opening stretch of the match, but AKIRA's posture had already started to sag. RYU-X wasn't chasing wildly; he was dictating, forcing AKIRA to retreat and absorb damage before he could find any rhythm.

I was yelling at my screen because Akira really looked like he needed one clean pause, just one second to breathe, and RYU-X absolutely refused to give it to him. This wasn’t the opening anymore; they were deep enough into the fight that all those earlier clashes had started showing on Akira. His blue aura didn’t have that snap, and even his recovery looked heavier. RYU-X came barreling in, red streaking forward, and buried an elbow into him with this nasty, shoulder-driven shove behind it. Akira got knocked off his line and sent skidding rightward, closer to the edge of the battlefield. It felt less like a single hit and more like a statement: “You don’t get the center back.” RYU-X was dictating the pace, walking him down, and Akira was being worn into a smaller and smaller corner of the fight.

Bro, the whole room saw the momentum barometer swing even without any numbers on screen. This was mid-fight, when you expect both sides to be warmed up and scary, but RYU-X looked like he had been blocking with his bones for too long. AKIRA was all forward intent, blue flashing in close, refusing to let red reset. Then he comes in high and drops the hit downward, right onto RYU-X's attempted defense. It lands so clean that RYU-X gets shoved back toward the right side, heels scraping like he suddenly remembered the stage has an end. AKIRA sticks the landing and keeps facing him down, totally the hunter in that moment. RYU-X is tough, no doubt, but that was the kind of impact that makes a comeback feel farther away.

Jun fought Vex beside the monorail turntable, where sparks spat from the exposed magnetic ring. Vex had the advantage in reach, whipping a chain-blade in wide silver loops that carved grooves into the deck. Jun kept backing up until his heels touched the yellow caution stripe. When Vex sent the chain screaming toward his throat, Jun dropped flat, pressed both palms to the magnetized rail, and let the weapon wrap around the steel post behind him. Vex yanked, expecting to drag Jun into the blade, but the turntable powered on with a bass hum. The trapped chain jerked tight and spun Vex halfway around the platform. Jun rose into the rotation, timed one compact elbow strike into Vex's sternum, and stepped away as the chain unwound in a useless spiral.

From my seat it looked like the blue side decided the match was going to be fought on his terms right from the early stretch. AKIRA stepped in before RYU-X could reset, planted that open-hand smash clean into the red fighter’s front, and the sound alone made the crowd flinch. RYU-X didn’t just stagger; he got shoved across the floor toward the far right boundary like his boots had lost their grip. You could tell this was still the beginning phase of the fight, but the pattern was already forming: AKIRA pressing, cutting off space, making every exchange cost something. RYU-X stayed upright, barely, but he was already looking sanded down.

That blue blur was all AKIRA. Halfway in, when RYU-X should have been finding answers, he instead got caught standing in the path of a full-body rush. AKIRA crashed into him and kept traveling, making the red fighter slide backward toward the rightmost side. RYU-X looked drained there, like the earlier exchanges had finally taken the spring out of his legs. He tried to hold shape, but he was being moved against his will. The message was simple: AKIRA was attacking, RYU-X was surviving.

Mira’s duel with the tall umbrella assassin shifts onto the row of waist-high turnstiles near Platform Seven. The assassin jabs with the umbrella tip in a pattern that keeps forcing Mira’s hips backward, trying to line her up for a stab through the ribs. Mira pretends to stumble over a dropped commuter bag and lets one leg swing through the turnstile gap. When the assassin steps in to finish her, she hooks her ankle behind his knee, grabs the rotating steel bar with both hands, and uses the turnstile like the crank of a catapult. Her body spins low and fast under his center of gravity. The assassin is flipped sideways, but not simply thrown; his open umbrella catches the artificial wind from a passing ghost train, drags him into a ridiculous half-glide, and slams him back-first into a map kiosk. Mira lands seated on the turnstile bar, brushes dust from her sleeve, and snaps the umbrella shut on his fingers before he can pull away.

My notes from that exchange are basically underlined in panic: AKIRA in control, RYU-X getting bullied toward the side. We were still in the first part of the fight, but the red fighter had that look where every block is a fraction too late and every retreat costs more than it saves. AKIRA closed the gap and cracked him with a palm-first blast that landed square enough to shove him off his line. RYU-X went careening toward the right boundary, not theatrically flying, more like he’d been forced backward by a shockwave through his ribs. AKIRA immediately claimed the space he gave up. That’s the important bit. It wasn’t just damage; it was positioning. Blue was dictating distance, pace, direction, everything. RYU-X was still on his feet, but the fight was already chewing him down.

I was sitting on the right side of the venue, so I could actually feel everybody around me tense when RYU-X got driven our way. This was still pretty early, before either fighter had emptied the tank, but AKIRA already looked like the one setting the pace. He came in blue and mean, tucked his weight behind a rising knee, and smashed it into RYU-X so hard that red got pushed almost straight toward the edge nearest us. RYU-X’s stance broke for a second. Not a total collapse, but enough to show the pressure was piling up. AKIRA didn’t look reckless; he looked like he had decided RYU-X was going to spend the opening phase backing up.

Look, I love AKIRA, so this hurt. He had been hanging on for so long, and you could tell his legs were starting to answer a half-second late. Then RYU-X did that nasty little phantom rush, the one where your heart jumps because you think the blow is already coming. AKIRA raised his arms, braced, and leaned away. But RYU-X had not committed the way it seemed. He used AKIRA's fear against him and crowded him toward the right side of the arena. It was such a small humiliation, honestly: not a dramatic explosion, not a giant finisher, just AKIRA being made to retreat because he believed the lie. By then red was dictating everything, and blue looked painfully worn down.

As a medic watching from the sidelines, I remember that exchange because Akira's recovery footwork looked late before the punch even connected. Middle phase of the match, fatigue already showing in the blue corner, RYU-X refusing to give him room. Red closed the gap, rotated through his torso, and delivered a short arcing strike that landed flush near Akira's upper body. Akira was shoved sideways, boots scraping toward the right-side limit, and his posture dipped afterward. That was the kind of impact that does not just hurt; it tells the opponent he is being herded.

There was a bleak beauty to it, if you like your anime fights cruel. The endgame had narrowed the world down to red pressure and blue exhaustion. Akira moved as though trying to summon one final answer, but RYU-X became a barricade with a heartbeat. The impact landed into that closed frame, and instead of breaking it, Akira was folded backward by it. The floor lines streamed toward the right as he was driven across them, his aura thinning around the edges. RYU-X did not explode; he compressed. He made every inch feel owned. Akira, once sharp and bright, looked weathered, pushed toward the margin of the battlefield while the red fighter advanced like dusk swallowing the last light.

Security report, if anyone wants the boring version: the red fighter increased forward pressure near the right-side perimeter late in the contest. The blue fighter appeared fatigued and reacted to a deceptive motion that did not develop as first indicated. This caused him to shift his guard and lose balance laterally. The red fighter then occupied the vacated space and continued advancing, compressing the blue fighter's room to maneuver. Crowd volume rose sharply because the blue fighter was driven closer to the edge. From my post, it was clear the red fighter had control of the exchange and was forcing the direction of travel.

Chat was going insane at that moment. Everyone had just been saying RYU-X needed space, because AKIRA had been in his face for the whole middle stretch, making him block, duck, guess, repeat. Then boom, blue comes crashing down from the upper angle and catches him clean enough to send him sliding right. RYU-X tried to plant, but his feet betrayed him, and he got pushed closer to the edge where nobody wants to defend. That was the shift from competitive to uh-oh. AKIRA wasn’t just winning an exchange; he was making the arena smaller for RYU-X. Red still had fire, but he was burning it defensively.

From my couch, it felt like the whole middle stretch of the fight tilted blue in a single breath. AKIRA had already been pressing forward, not wild, just relentless, and RYU-X looked like he was starting to carry every previous exchange in his legs. Then AKIRA stepped in close enough that there was no room for a flashy windup and smashed an open-hand strike into RYU-X’s front. Red buckled, skidding sideways and backward toward the far right boundary like the arena itself was rejecting him. You could see RYU-X try to plant and answer, but his guard came up late, his shoulders sagging. AKIRA didn’t chase recklessly; he stalked, knowing the pressure was working.

Mako got his distinct moment near the luggage carousel, where Hana's paper talismans had transformed abandoned suitcases into snapping crocodile trunks. One of them clamped onto Mako's sleeve, another on his boot, and a third launched itself at his throat. Instead of tearing free, he let all three bite. His aura flared orange and made the suitcase locks pop open. Clothing, scrolls, and someone's ceremonial drums burst into the air around him. Hana flicked a new talisman to bind the mess into a cage, but Mako seized the falling drumsticks with his teeth and both hands. He kicked the boot-trunk into the sleeve-trunk, bounced off their collision, and beat a frantic rhythm on the suspended drums. Each strike made a sound-wave hoop that blasted Hana's talismans out of formation. The last hoop caught the third suitcase mid-leap, flipped it end over end, and sent it snapping shut around Hana's own sash. Mako spat one drumstick into his hand, pointed it at her like a sword, and grinned while the carousel carried her helplessly past a row of stunned commuters.

Tetsu cornered Sable by the mall fountain and drew his short spear in a low sweeping arc meant to cut off both routes around the water. She gave him the retreat he wanted, hopping onto the fountain rim, but she had already palmed three coins from the donation basin. When his spear rose for the follow-up thrust, she flicked the coins one by one into the stream of water spraying from a cherub statue. The jets deflected them into tiny silver ricochets: one pinged off Tetsu’s knuckles, the second nicked the spear shaft, and the third struck the release clasp on his forearm bracer. The bracer sprang open and slid down over his wrist, locking his grip at a useless angle. Sable stepped past the spear point and tapped his chest with two fingers, claiming the exchange without wasting a full strike.

Okay, I need people to understand how oppressive this looked in motion, because a still frame will not do it justice. By this point, AKIRA had already been chipped, shoved, checked, and interrupted so many times that every breath he took seemed expensive. He was still trying to look defiant, because of course he was, that is AKIRA, but the blue around him had that tired, broken-lantern quality. Then RYU-X rose and came crashing down at him with this predator confidence, not rushing in panic, not gambling, just certain. The angle was nasty: high to low, forward through the torso, with enough carry that AKIRA did not simply take the strike and fall where he stood. He was driven across the ground toward the rightmost danger zone, heels dragging for purchase, one arm trying to shield his chest while the rest of him got bullied backward. The crowd noise in my head went from excitement to that low oh no sound, because nobody watching could pretend the flow was even anymore. RYU-X had become the one asking every question. AKIRA, who earlier had been answering with counters and bursts of speed, was now late to everything. Late to guard, late to plant, late to breathe. And RYU-X stayed glued to him after landing, posture forward, red energy still flaring like he wanted the wall, the edge, the whole stage to help finish the job. That sequence screamed final stretch: not flashy for the sake of flash, but cruelly practical. Push the exhausted guy where he cannot retreat, keep him there, make him spend whatever is left.

No fancy analysis needed: AKIRA hit him clean and bullied him rightward. That’s it. The fight was deep into its last stretch, and RYU-X looked cooked. Blue came forward, red tried to hold, the blade flashed, and suddenly RYU-X was sliding toward the edge with his stance broken. AKIRA had the initiative before the strike and even more of it afterward. RYU-X wasn’t choosing distance anymore. He was being moved.

Kuro's black flame slash carved a crescent through the station smoke, aimed at Mira's ribs. She answered with something nobody expected: she snatched the conductor's silver whistle from the floor and blew into it as she spun. The whistle did not make a normal sound. It released a needle-thin pulse that bent the flame crescent just enough for it to miss her by a finger's width and shear the top off a ticket booth instead. Kuro narrowed his eyes, realizing the cheap station whistle was enchanted for crowd control. Mira used his surprise to step inside his guard, tap the whistle against his sternum, and blow again. The pulse launched him backward without burning him, folding his coat around him like a collapsing umbrella. He slid across the marble, stopped himself with his sword point, and looked personally offended that civic safety equipment had outdueled his ancestral technique.

Juno's cleanest rescue exchange happened on the stairway between platforms, where Rika was sliding backward under pressure from Oro's twin knives. Oro had forced her onto a step slick with spilled engine oil, and one more feint would have put a blade under her guard. Juno was three landings below with no line for a normal strike. He grabbed the handrail, swung his legs up, and hooked his knees around it, turning himself upside down. Then he slapped the underside of the rail with both palms, sending a vibration up the metal. The tremor rattled the screws out of the bracket beside Oro's foot. Oro noticed the loose bracket but not the rail itself dropping half an inch. When he lunged, his rear heel caught under the sagging rail. Rika saw the hitch and ducked. Oro's stab went over her head, and Juno, still hanging upside down, slid down the rail like a human pulley. He collided shoulder-first with Oro's trapped leg, sweeping it high. Rika finished the exchange by rising into a palm strike to Oro's ribs, while Juno kept sliding past and crashed harmlessly into a heap of travel pillows.

CHAT, that was the first real blue takeover moment. We’re still early, right, nobody’s supposed to be cooked yet, but RYU-X is already getting walked to the right like he forgot rent was due. AKIRA keeps crowding him, keeps making him block awkward, and then boom, he sneaks under and launches that rising punch straight into him. RYU-X gets popped up and shoved sideways, red effects scattering, no clean answer at all. The wild thing is AKIRA doesn’t even look surprised. He knew it was there. RYU-X looks like he’s absorbing too much too soon, and AKIRA is absolutely the one driving the fight.

Mira's exchange with Sable happens inside the shattered moon-aquarium, where floating lanternfish spill through the air in globes of water held together by stray magic. Sable flicks three needle-thin shadow knives at Mira's face, expecting her to dodge backward into the jagged glass wall. Instead, Mira dives forward onto her knees, slides under the knives, and slaps both palms against a drifting water globe. The globe bursts flat into a rippling shield, catching the knives and magnifying Sable's surprised expression through the sheet of water. Mira twists the wet sash around her waist and snaps it like a towel, sending the captured knives back embedded in harmless bubbles. Sable cuts through the bubbles easily, but the distraction hides Mira's actual move: a low sweep with a broken aquarium rim. Sable hops over it, only to land on a puddled lanternfish membrane that skids like ice, carrying her into a coral display with a bright, indignant splash.

Sable used the fireworks cart only once because it nearly took her with it. Koji had her boxed in against a shuttered toy store, both hands charged for a point-blank blast. She kicked the brake off the festival fireworks cart beside her and dove underneath it. Koji’s blast hit the stacked launch tubes, not hard enough to ignite them but enough to send the whole cart skidding backward. Sable clung to the underside crossbar, boots scraping sparks from the tile. As the cart rolled between Koji’s legs, she hooked one ankle behind his knee and pulled. He toppled onto the cart’s top rack just as the emergency sprinklers finally triggered a row of harmless smoke fountains. The cart continued rolling in a majestic cloud of pink smoke, carrying Koji away like an angry parade float while Sable coughed beneath it.

I was yelling before my brain caught up. Still in the first stretch of the fight, AKIRA in blue just vanished forward, not gone exactly, more like the space between him and RYU-X got deleted. RYU-X had barely reset his stance from the last exchange, and then boom: blue shoulder, blue afterimage, all pressure. The red fighter skidded backward toward the far side on the right, heels scraping like he was trying to argue with gravity and losing. You could tell AKIRA had the tempo completely now. RYU-X was not broken yet, but he was starting to look bothered, arms late, guard dented, breath heavier. It felt less like one hit and more like AKIRA announcing, “You’re fighting my pace now.”

I’m not even an AKIRA fan like that, but that mid-fight drop-in was filthy. RYU-X had been eating pressure for a while, you could tell by how late his reactions were getting, and then AKIRA just rose into that nasty high angle and brought the attack down on him. Red tried to brace, but it was too much leverage coming from too awkward a place. He got forced back hard, sliding toward the right edge of the stage with that little stumble that screams, yeah, I’m still up, but I’m not okay. The crowd noise changed too. Before, people were arguing about momentum. After that, it was obvious: blue was walking him down.

Okay, as someone who rewatches these fights way too much, this exchange is a perfect example of pressure converting into positioning. We’re not at the opening anymore; both fighters have taken their measure of each other, and AKIRA is visibly losing efficiency. RYU-X recognizes that and attacks not just the body but the space around him. He drives a sharp air-shearing strike through AKIRA’s line, catches him while his stance is a fraction too narrow, and the impact sends AKIRA retreating toward the right side. That’s the important part: RYU-X doesn’t merely score contact, he changes the map. AKIRA ends the moment closer to being trapped, worn down, and reacting. RYU-X ends it moving forward.

Mira's duel with Jax moved through the spice stall, where jars had shattered and colored powders painted the floor. Jax stomped down, sending a cloud of saffron and pepper into the air to blind her. Mira shut her eyes before the cloud hit and listened for the scrape of his boots. He faked left with a noisy step, then came silently from the right, but he forgot the cracked jar of star anise stuck to his heel. It clicked once on the tile. Mira ducked under his grab, scooped a handful of cinnamon from a broken sack, and clapped it against his forearm. The powder stuck to his sweat, revealing the outline of his next punch through the haze like a moving shadow. She parried the visible arm and elbowed his ribs. Jax sneezed so explosively that the spice cloud blasted outward, clearing the air and knocking loose every hanging lantern in the stall. Mira blinked at the accidental counterattack and barely rolled away from the falling lights.

As someone who has watched too many arena matches frame by frame, this was classic ring control. Akira had Ryu-X fatigued and backing up during the central phase of the bout. Instead of overcommitting with a wide attack, Akira used a tight forward pierce, entering on a straight line and catching Ryu-X as he tried to stabilize. The red fighter's base broke immediately. He was carried backward toward the right perimeter, not by drama alone but by the direction of Akira's weight and follow-through. Ryu-X's hands came up after the damage was already done. That tells the whole story: Akira was ahead in tempo, Ryu-X was behind in recovery.

I swear this was the point where the middle of the fight stopped feeling even. RYU-X, all red pressure and no hesitation, stepped into AKIRA’s space with that tight defensive crash, like he was using his own protection as a battering ram. AKIRA had the blue glow up, but it looked tired, thin, almost late to respond. The contact didn’t launch him clean away; it bullied him. His feet scraped sideways and he kept giving ground until the whole exchange was sliding toward the right boundary. RYU-X wasn’t just surviving there—he was dictating. AKIRA’s stance held for a second, but you could tell the damage from earlier was stacking up, because he couldn’t plant himself and answer back.

If you freeze the memory of the fight there, it tells the whole story of that middle stretch. AKIRA is moving forward; RYU-X is retreating even before he wants to admit it. The blue fighter takes the inside lane and drives a flat palm into red’s guard line, catching him with enough force to send him sliding toward the right-side limit. RYU-X’s knees dip, his upper body twists, and his recovery step is more survival than strategy. That matters because earlier he had been meeting AKIRA head-on. Now he is being moved. AKIRA’s pressure has become directional, purposeful, almost surgical. RYU-X is not finished, but he is visibly being sanded down.

RYU-X fans ate good in that moment. That was predator stuff. Final stretch, AKIRA looking chipped and slowed, and RYU-X still moving like he had another gear hidden away. He threw the promise of a frontal smash, got AKIRA to lock up, then slipped the real pressure in after the reaction. AKIRA drifted right, then stumbled right, then suddenly the whole fight was leaning that way. The red side was not merely attacking; he was steering. AKIRA's back was being escorted toward the boundary, and the scary part was how casual RYU-X made it seem.

There is a point in a fight when the older masters say the legs confess before the mouth does. Ryu-X's legs confessed here. Midway through the duel, Akira advanced with disciplined pressure and sent a straight penetrating blow into the red fighter's centerline. The contact drove Ryu-X back toward the right boundary, but the important detail was how he yielded: no spring, no immediate answer, only a dragged recovery and a guard that re-formed too slowly. Akira was not merely landing a hit; he was harvesting the fatigue he had created. Ryu-X's spirit remained, but his structure was being worn away, and Akira knew it.

During the fight’s spill into the noodle court, Juno tried to pin Mako with a chair to the throat, driving him backward toward the boiling ramen vat. Mako grabbed the chair legs, not to push them away, but to twist them inward until the folding hinges snapped over Juno’s wrists. For one sharp second, the chair became a crude set of wooden handcuffs. Juno snarled and kicked, so Mako stamped on the pedal that lifted the vat lid. A sheet of steam roared between them. Hidden by it, Mako shoved the trapped chair sideways and ducked. Juno’s own kick missed high, hit the suspended menu board, and brought down a rain of plastic noodle models that bounced harmlessly off his head while Mako used the distraction to rip free the chair back and retreat.

The thing I noticed first was Akira's footwork. In the opening portion, he was not waiting for Ryu-X to swing himself open; he was stealing space one shuffle at a time. Ryu-X, in red, had the look of a fighter who had blocked too much too soon, shoulders tight, guard late, heels drifting. Then Akira dropped his weight and sent a low horizontal strike through Ryu-X's base. It clipped him perfectly, not flashy at the top but vicious where it mattered. Ryu-X's legs went out of rhythm and the force carried him to the right, almost like the floor had tilted that way. Akira followed with that cold, forward-moving confidence, blue aura pressing into red territory. Since this was still early in the fight, it mattered more than a simple knockdown attempt. It showed the direction of the whole exchange: Akira advancing, Akira dictating, Akira making Ryu-X spend energy just to stay upright. Ryu-X did not look beaten yet, but he absolutely looked worn down before the battle had any business getting that ugly.

I swear the blue guy smelled blood there. Not literally, obviously, but you know what I mean. RYU-X had been slipping out of trouble earlier, doing that red flash counter-pressure thing, but by the middle of the fight his movements were getting heavier. Then AKIRA just blasted in, low and fast, and slammed into him like he had decided the entire arena was too big and needed to be shortened. RYU-X got carried sideways, skidding toward the right side, arms folding in too late to stop the hit. It was one of those moments where the advantage is not subtle anymore. AKIRA was walking him down without walking at all, turning speed into force. RYU-X did not collapse, but he looked dented, like every previous exchange had finally made this one stick harder.

The noodle stall exchange starts as slapstick and ends with Nessa proving she has been tracking every spill on the floor. Brann corners her between two toppled counters, swinging a cleaver too heavy to be kitchenware. Nessa blocks with a ladle, which bends instantly, and ducks behind a hanging curtain of uncooked noodles. Brann slices through the noodles and the curtain rod together, expecting her to be hiding there. She is already crouched at his feet, tying the sliced noodles around his bootlaces with a chef’s speed. He notices only when he tries to step and nearly pitches forward. Furious, Brann rips one foot free and kicks a boiling stockpot toward her. Nessa hops onto the lid, rides the sliding pot like a shield, and uses the bent ladle as a paddle to steer. Brann raises the cleaver for a downward chop. Nessa tilts the lid at the last moment, letting the cleaver bite into the iron rim. The trapped blade drags Brann off balance. Nessa springs up, flips the ladle around his wrist, and pours an entire basket of pepper powder into the steam between them. Brann sneezes so violently he headbutts the counter and knocks himself under the soup sign.

If I had to sum it up: RYU-X turned height into pressure and pressure into territory. AKIRA was fading in the final stretch, his blue silhouette no longer springing back after contact. RYU-X, still aggressive, attacked from above and landed hard enough to force AKIRA across toward the right edge. The hit mattered because it came when AKIRA could least afford to surrender position. He was already worn down, already being chased, and now he had less room to escape. RYU-X did not just win that moment; he made the next moment worse for AKIRA too. That is why everyone felt the finish getting closer.

I was yelling for Ryu-X, so trust me, this hurt to watch. The fight was still in its early phase, and red should have been fresh enough to answer back, but Akira had him backing up already. Akira slid in low, almost under the line of sight, and hooked out Ryu-X's footing with a sharp leg attack. It landed with that nasty anime snap where you know the balance is gone before the body catches up. Ryu-X lurched rightward, boots scraping and arms flaring just to keep from eating the ground. Akira stayed on him immediately, blue outfit cutting forward like he had decided the edge of the stage was where this would continue. Momentum was completely on Akira's side there.

Calling it from ringside, I’d say this was the clearest sign that the finish was approaching. AKIRA had become the forward force, and RYU-X was no longer contesting territory so much as surrendering it under fire. In the late exchanges, fatigue had visibly settled on RYU-X: slower pivots, heavier blocks, less bite on the return threats. AKIRA recognized it immediately. He closed the gap and drove a compact, straight-ahead punch into him, the kind that doesn’t need decoration because the placement does the talking. The contact snapped RYU-X backward and carried him toward the right-side boundary, where every retreat feels dangerous. AKIRA’s blue silhouette stayed balanced after the strike, ready to continue pressing. RYU-X’s red frame, meanwhile, looked like it was being forced into the corner of the story itself. The momentum was unmistakable: AKIRA pushing, RYU-X enduring, and the match entering its last harsh downhill slide.

Sable's flashiest one-time dodge happened because of a vending machine that should not have been on a rooftop. Mira fired three silver hairpins at him, each trailing a tiny arc of white energy. Sable ducked the first two, but the third was aimed for where his dodge would end. He solved it by diving backward into the vending machine's cracked plastic window. His shoulders hit, the glass flexed, and the machine's internal spring rack snapped loose with a ridiculous metallic twang. A row of melon sodas shot out like green cannonballs. One can intercepted the hairpin midflight and burst into mist; two more pelted Mira's feet and made her hop back. Sable slid down the machine, drenched and laughing, then kicked the return slot. The last can rolled out. He scooped it up, popped the tab with his thumb, and sprayed foam across Mira's eyes before disappearing behind the snack banners.

Bro, chat would have exploded at that one. Middle of the fight, AKIRA is already in pressure-monster mode, and RYU-X is looking like he’s been downloading pain for ten minutes straight. Red tries to hold mid-screen, probably thinking he can swing back, but AKIRA just darts in and pops him with this savage open-hand body check. Not a fancy spin, not some giant beam, just hand to torso and boom, RYU-X gets shoved toward the right boundary like the stage got tilted. The best part is AKIRA doesn’t overextend after it. He walks him down. That’s when you know it’s bad: the aggressor is calm, the defender is tired, and the wall is getting closer.

From a coaching standpoint, this was the first clear momentum marker. Early in the contest, AKIRA recognized that RYU-X was already absorbing more than he was returning, so he did not give him the courtesy of space. The blue fighter compressed the distance in a single explosive entry, arriving before RYU-X could square his hips. Contact came clean enough to force displacement rather than just stun: RYU-X was carried laterally and back, toward the right boundary of the arena. That matters. AKIRA was not merely striking; he was choosing where the fight would happen next. RYU-X, in red, tried to brace and turn out, but his feet were dragged into a retreating pattern. His guard stayed up, yet it looked more protective than threatening. At this point, AKIRA was clearly pressing, and RYU-X was beginning to spend energy just to survive the pace.

Rin’s single clean escape from the sand painter was a masterpiece of pettiness. The painter had spread golden dust across the museum floor and could turn every footprint into a grabbing hand. Rin was forced onto the central statue pedestal, surrounded. The painter mocked her for having nowhere to step. Rin answered by removing the statue’s bronze laurel wreath and tossing it like a frisbee. It did not hit him. It struck the velvet rope stanchion behind him, knocking it over and dragging the rope across the sand. The rope carved a clean, sweeping line through the dust, ruining dozens of half-formed hand sigils at once. While the painter flinched at the damage to his pattern, Rin hopped from the pedestal to the fallen stanchion base, balanced on the tiny metal disk, and pushed off again before the sand could claim it. Her knee caught him under the chin. The move scattered the remaining dust in a halo, and she landed on a display case, laughing because his perfect battlefield now looked like a child’s spilled glitter jar.

Look, I’m the guy in the watch party who usually says, “Relax, it’s early,” but even I couldn’t pretend after this. RYU-X had the initiative from the opening minutes, and then he just stabbed forward with this sharp, compact rush that caught AKIRA square. No fancy setup needed, just red stepping in and making blue give ground. AKIRA got driven hard toward the right side of the field, and the scary thing was how little resistance he seemed able to put into the slide. He wasn’t outclassed for the whole fight yet, but in that instant he looked like someone already carrying damage, already breathing heavier. RYU-X was hunting; AKIRA was surviving.

My notes from that point are basically underlined chaos: ‘AKIRA pressing. RYU-X fading. Right side danger.’ The exchange itself was short, but it changed the feeling of the finish. AKIRA rushed in behind a sweeping blade stroke, catching RYU-X as the red fighter tried to reset his footing. The hit snapped him sideways and drove him toward the arena’s right edge. RYU-X didn’t bounce back into stance like earlier; he staggered, shoulders sagging, guard loose. AKIRA followed with that predator posture, not frantic, just certain. It was late enough that every forced step mattered, and those steps all belonged to AKIRA.

I’m not even going to pretend neutrality: RYU-X looked vicious there. He had AKIRA backing up early, then he caught him with that arcing boot and sent him sliding right like he was clearing the lane. The red side was completely in command, stepping forward after every exchange, while AKIRA in blue looked stuck reacting. Since it came in the opening stretch, it felt like a warning shot to the whole match: RYU-X wasn’t letting him build anything.

Haruka’s paper talismans have been used as blades all night, so Densuke expects another slicing volley. He lowers his shoulder and bulldozes through the first dozen charms, letting them spark harmlessly against his armored jacket. Haruka retreats up the red staircase toward the shrine doors, scattering more talismans in an apparently panicked fan. Densuke laughs and charges faster. The trick is that none of the papers are attacking. Each one sticks to a railing post, a lantern hook, or a crack in the steps. When Densuke reaches the top, Haruka claps her hands once. Thin ink lines snap between the talismans, revealing a web that had been invisible against the night air. Densuke plows into it chest first. The web stretches, absorbs his momentum, and flings him backward, but Haruka is already running down the steps toward him. She jumps, plants a palm on his forehead as he rebounds, and vaults over him. Her heel clips the final talisman on his collar. The web contracts all at once, wrapping him into a paper cocoon that rolls down the stairs and bursts through the offering gate.

From a spacing perspective, that exchange was brutal for RYU-X. This was not the opening scramble anymore; by then both had shown their habits, and AKIRA had started taking ownership of the center. RYU-X was retreating in little reluctant steps, trying to make blue swing first, but AKIRA did not overextend. He stepped into range, lifted the line of attack, and dropped it onto RYU-X from above at exactly the wrong moment for red's defense. The hit forced RYU-X's posture to buckle and carried him toward the right perimeter. What matters is that AKIRA gained more than a clean connection. He gained the chase. RYU-X had to recover while losing ground, and you could see the fatigue in how late his feet responded.

Forum recap version: early fight, RYU-X pressure sequence, AKIRA already looking uncomfortable. Red steps in, throws that big circular leg attack, and it lands clean enough to push AKIRA toward the right edge of the arena. This is not some isolated tap either; it fits the whole opening pattern. RYU-X is the one advancing, choosing the range, and forcing reactions. AKIRA is still standing, obviously, but he’s being worn down fast, and that shove to the side made the momentum gap impossible to ignore.

Mira's most delicate exchange happened near the torn parasol stand, where Sable tried to spear her with a black lacquered cane. Mira stepped inside the thrust instead of away from it, catching the cane under her left armpit while her right hand flicked open a paper umbrella from the rack. She snapped the umbrella's ribs across Sable's wrist, not hard enough to break it, but perfectly angled to pin his thumb against the cane's carved dragon head. Then she spun the umbrella shut, trapping his sleeve in the folds, and used the collapsing canopy as a lever. Sable's arm corkscrewed behind his back, his knees buckled, and Mira guided him face-first into a display of painted masks without ever raising her voice. The joint-lock was odd, pretty, and impossible to repeat once the umbrella split into wet paper strips.

I am not even good at analyzing fights, but I knew that was bad for AKIRA. RYU-X was chasing him at the end like he had unlimited energy, and AKIRA looked so tired, like every block hurt. Then red came down on him from above, really hard, and AKIRA got knocked toward the right side. It was scary because he did not bounce back with some cool counter or anything. He just had to take it and keep moving backward. The blue guy was still trying, but you could tell he was being worn away. RYU-X looked like he wanted to end it right there.

Listen, as a RYU-X supporter, that was the delicious part. Late fight, both of them scorched, but only one of them still looked hungry. RYU-X had AKIRA backing up already, and then he went high, came down hard, and cracked through from over the top. AKIRA took it badly. Not a dramatic pose, not a clean heroic block, just that ugly stagger where you know the pressure is getting to him. Blue got hammered toward the right edge while red kept advancing like a storm with boots. That moment told me RYU-X was not just ahead on momentum; he was dictating where AKIRA was allowed to stand.

Tetsu nearly caught Koji at the aquarium restaurant when he forced him backward against the decorative fish tank wall. The spear point tapped the glass beside Koji’s cheek, daring him to move. Koji grinned and pressed two fingers to the tank instead of the spear. His shock pulse did not shatter the glass; it startled the ornamental eels inside, sending them into a frantic spiral. Their bodies stirred the colored gravel into a glittering cloud that obscured the tank’s far side. Tetsu glanced at the motion despite himself. Koji used that tiny shift to grab the spear shaft with his sleeve-wrapped hand and twist downward. The spear butt dropped into a floor drain, wedging hard. Koji vaulted over the trapped shaft, planted both feet on Tetsu’s breastplate, and bounced away just as the aquarium sprinklers misted both of them with cold water.

Sable’s one clean throw came after he lost his chain and pretended to be unarmed. Rika rushed him near the star-map mural, aiming a spinning elbow for the side of his head. Sable took the blow on his shoulder and allowed the force to turn his body. During that turn, his left hand slipped into Rika’s sash, not to grab her waist, but to hook the small lacquered charm dangling at her back. He twisted the charm cord around two fingers, dropped to one knee, and used her own forward spin against her. Rika flipped over him in a tight, involuntary cartwheel, but Sable did not release her at the peak. He guided her downward into the mural wall, scraping a chalk constellation across her shoulder blades. She kicked free before he could pin her, yet the throw changed the rhythm of the fight: for the first time, Rika landed breathing hard while Sable rose with nothing in his hands except the snapped charm cord.

I’m not saying the fight was decided there, but as an arena medic watching body language, I noticed AKIRA’s condition dip. This happened in the early third of the clash, before the big dramatic turns, and RYU-X was clearly the hunter. He stepped in red-hot, clipped AKIRA with a narrow, sudden punch to the front line, and the blue fighter recoiled toward the right perimeter. The scary part was how routine it looked for RYU-X. He didn’t overextend or celebrate; he simply advanced again, like he expected AKIRA to keep giving way. AKIRA’s reactions were still there, but they were getting slower under the pressure. That hit was less about spectacle and more about accumulation: another forced retreat, another bit of stamina taxed, another sign that red controlled the tempo.

Goro's rooftop exchange with the kite-armored courier was all momentum and bad architecture. The courier swooped between satellite dishes, cloak stretched into rigid wings, and clipped Goro's shoulder with a heel blade on every pass. Goro could not catch him, so he pretended to chase harder, stomping across the roof until tiles cracked behind him. The courier laughed and came in for the obvious finishing dive. At the last instant, Goro stopped on a cracked patch, raised both fists, and did nothing. The courier's heel struck his chest plate, but Goro absorbed it without grabbing. The roof section beneath them finally gave way. The courier's wings snagged on the jagged hole while Goro dropped cleanly through, caught a ceiling beam below, and yanked the hanging courier down by the ankle. They landed in a storage room among paint cans, and the courier emerged with one wing plastered shut in bright yellow enamel.

At the central escalator, the Oni Twin Yuko tried a wrestling finish on Hiro. She caught him around the waist from behind and lifted him for a backward slam down the moving steps. Hiro hooked both arms around the rubber handrails instead of fighting her grip. The escalator kept pulling his hands upward while Yuko tried to throw him downward, stretching the move into an awkward tug-of-war. Yuko snarled and adjusted her stance for more power. That was when Hiro tucked his knees, planted both soles against the step in front of her, and let the handrail drag his upper body forward. He slipped out of her grip like a cork from a bottle. Yuko's own lift carried her backward, and Hiro used the momentum to guide her onto the adjacent luggage conveyor. She vanished behind a curtain of suitcases, still yelling as a floral trunk gently bumped her away.

The fireworks-cart exchange ended the brawl's last chaotic push without anyone quite admitting it was an accident. Renga and Brutus were grappling beside the terrace rail, each trying to throw the other into a rack of sky rockets. Juno crawled under the rack to escape Veyra and bumped the wheel chock loose with his elbow. The entire cart rolled toward the two giants. Renga saw it first and released Brutus just long enough to hook one rocket bundle with his toe. Brutus thought it was a trip attempt and stomped down, crushing the fuse tray. Sparks leapt everywhere.
